items.title: Aldi’s Kevin the Carrot scores perfect rating for Christmas ad
items.summary: Aldi’s Kevin the Carrot has achieved the highest possible score in System1’s Christmas advertising effectiveness rankings, securing a maximum 5.9-Star Rating for the fourth time in five years. The supermarket’s…
items.body:
Aldi’s Kevin the Carrot scores perfect rating for Christmas ad
Aldi’s Kevin the Carrot has achieved the highest possible score in System1’s Christmas advertising effectiveness rankings, securing a maximum 5.9-Star Rating for the fourth time in five years.
The supermarket’s 2026 festive campaign marks Kevin’s seventh consecutive Christmas advert to achieve a 5-Star Rating, continuing a run that began after the character’s debut in 2016.
This year’s advert, which sees Kevin and his daughter Chantenay embark on a snowy adventure to find their missing family pet, Cauli Dog, scored well above the supermarket category average of 3.4 Stars.
System1’s testing found that 72 per cent of viewers felt happy watching the advert, double the UK television advertising average, while just 20 per cent reported feeling no emotion, compared with 44 per cent for a typical advert.
The campaign also achieved a Spike Rating of 1.54, classed as exceptional for its potential to drive short-term sales, alongside a Fluency Rating of 85 for brand recognition.
The result is Kevin’s fourth maximum score in five years, having previously achieved 5.9 Stars in 2022, 2023 and 2024.
Aldi also topped System1’s Christmas advertising leaderboard in 2023 and 2024.
System1 senior vice president of global partnerships Andrew Tindall said: “Eleven Christmases in, and Kevin the Carrot has scored a perfect 5.9 Stars. When Kevin debuted in 2016, he managed a respectable 3 Stars, so this is ten years of compounding you can actually see.”
He added: “Most brands spend a fortune trying to make people feel something at Christmas, and Aldi keeps doing it with a carrot.”
System1’s Star Rating measures viewers’ emotional responses to adverts to predict their potential to drive long-term brand growth, with only around one per cent of campaigns typically achieving a 5-Star score.
The result also marks the final Christmas campaign created for Aldi by McCann Manchester, bringing an end to the agency’s 21-year partnership with the supermarket.
The agency helped establish Kevin the Carrot as one of Aldi’s most recognisable advertising characters, with the mascot becoming a fixture of its Christmas marketing since 2016.

items.title: Asda rolls out Christmas gift appeal across 380 stores
items.summary: Asda has launched a nationwide Christmas gift appeal across more than 380 stores, inviting shoppers to buy presents for people supported by local charities, community groups and care homes. The…
items.body:
Asda rolls out Christmas gift appeal across 380 stores
Asda has launched a nationwide Christmas gift appeal across more than 380 stores, inviting shoppers to buy presents for people supported by local charities, community groups and care homes.
The supermarket’s Christmas Kindness Trees campaign launched on 16 November, with participating stores displaying gift tags featuring requests from people in their local communities.
Customers can pick a tag from the tree, purchase the requested gift and leave it in a collection trolley, with presents then distributed by the participating organisations in time for Christmas.
Unlike traditional Christmas gift appeals, Asda said each tag represents a specific request, helping ensure donations reach those who need them.
Asda local community advisor Carolyn Francis said: “The festive season is often associated with joy, celebration and togetherness, but for many people it can be a difficult and lonely time.”
She added: “Through our Christmas Kindness Trees, we’re giving customers and colleagues the opportunity to make a direct difference to someone’s Christmas by supporting real requests from local people and families.”
The initiative will see Asda work with local charities, community organisations and care homes, with all gifts remaining within the communities where they are donated.
Francis said: “We know even the smallest act of kindness can have a lasting impact, and we’re incredibly proud to be bringing communities together in this way across more than 380 Asda stores this Christmas.”

Ikea ditches plans for new UK stores over ‘unprecedented costs’
Ikea has “abandoned” plans for a number of new stores in Britain and could slow its expansion in the country even further, owing to the “unprecedented” costs facing retailers.
David McCabe, chief executive of the flat-pack furniture seller’s UK and Ireland business, said the Swedish retailer is considering investing instead in European markets with lower taxes, following the government’s “missed opportunity” to back the sector at last month’s Budget.
The furniture group has long enchanted British shoppers with its maze-like layout and offering of Swedish meatballs and has moved into smaller city centre stores, including on London’s Oxford Street, in recent months in a bid to get closer to the high street.
“But it is a fact that there have been planned investments that Ikea intended to make in the UK that have been abandoned due to the increases in costs that we face,” McCabe told City AM.
“I will be working with the team to be as creative as we can to ensure that we do continue to invest and expand in the UK. But it is becoming harder, of that there is no doubt.
“If we’re not able to make these cases for sustainable investments in the UK, Ikea as a company, we will invest in other European countries. That is the reality.”
The huge size of Ikea stores means the retailer inevitably pays a large amount of property tax but McCabe said the company’s business rates bill is significantly higher than the equivalent tax in any of the other European countries in which it operates.
The Ikea boss said his firm had been hoping that John Healey would take action at last month’s Budget to address “the unprecedented period of high costs and complexity” facing the UK’s retail sector.
The Chancellor claimed he would freeze the business rates bills of all high street firms, but industry bosses pointed out that this tax is still set to rise in line with inflation, piling the sector with an extra £250m in costs next year.
“We do see that it was a missed opportunity to back retail under real pressure. I do hope that the Prime Minister and his team really do urgently recognise the importance of the retail sector, and work together with us,” McCabe said.
Ikea slashes prices
He added that Ikea is “positive” about the UK and would be keen to revisit some of the projects it has been forced to shelve, but would not be able to do so unless Labour provides “a sustainable cost picture and an incentive to continue to grow in the UK”.
Ikea’s shift to scaled-down stores has been driven by the rising business rates burden facing retailers. The industry pays 20 per cent of these tax receipts despite making up only five per cent of the UK economy, according to the British Retail Consortium (BRC).
As well as moving closer to high streets, Ikea has aggressively cut prices in recent months. Across 425 products, including its Billy bookcase and Hemnes sofa, the retailer spent £54m reducing prices by an average of 20 per cent in August. The group is rolling out further price cuts across 1,000 products in the run-up to Christmas.
McCabe said: “I think it’s fair to say that people across the country are facing unprecedented pressure when it comes to cost of living.
“For us, the more challenging it is for our customers, the harder we need to work to ensure that the products that we have are accessible for our customers.”
Ikea’s boss said he was “proud” the retailer managed to grow its sales in a year that “wasn’t easy when it comes to the retail environment”. The group’s takings rose by just 0.5 per cent to £2.26bn in the last year, despite total store visits rising by seven per cent.

items.title: Citizens of Soil secures retail listing at Tesco
items.summary: Citizens of Soil has launched two single-origin extra virgin olive oils across Tesco stores, marking a significant milestone for the brand. The brand was first founded in 2021 and has…
items.body:
Citizens of Soil secures retail listing at Tesco
Citizens of Soil has launched two single-origin extra virgin olive oils across Tesco stores, marking a significant milestone for the brand.
The brand was first founded in 2021 and has a focus on creating olive oil products that are high quality and sourced from a transparent supply chain.
The Citizens of Soil Extra Virgin Olive Oil and Spanish Extra Virgin Olive Oil have launched across 425 stores this week for an RRP of £19 for 500ml.
Both oils will be discounted by 20 per cent at Tesco on a Clubcard Price Promotion at £15.20 for two weeks from 24 November.
The brand was recently selected for the Tesco Accelerator programme, which provides support for upcoming businesses.
Subscribe to Grocery Gazette for free
Sign up here to get the latest grocery and food news each morning
Citizens of Soil aims to offer a premium version of olive oil in the category and market it as a speciality ingredient compared to an everyday commodity.
Sarah Vachon, co-founder of Citizens of Soil, said: “Tesco is where thousands of people buy their olive oil, so it’s where we can make the biggest difference. Shoppers already choose coffee by origin, wine by grape, and chocolate by percentage.
“And as they trade up on everyday staples, we are confident olive oil will be next, due to its wide range of flavours and uses.
“We want to show people just that: these oils taste completely different, and putting them side by side lets shoppers discover that for themselves and find the oil that suits the way they cook.”
This comes after a year of significant growth for Citizens of Soil, and the brand collaborated with Ottolenghi to produce a speciality virgin olive oil.

items.title: Aldi snaps up boozy pickle kombucha brand after Channel 4 win
items.summary: Aldi has handed Manchester-based drinks brand Stiff Tea a nationwide listing after its alcoholic kombucha won the latest episode of Channel 4’s Aldi: The Next Big Seller. Founded by Zach…
items.body:
Aldi snaps up boozy pickle kombucha brand after Channel 4 win
Aldi has handed Manchester-based drinks brand Stiff Tea a nationwide listing after its alcoholic kombucha won the latest episode of Channel 4’s Aldi: The Next Big Seller.
Founded by Zach Taylor, the business secured a contract to supply its 3.4 per cent ABV kombucha to more than 1,080 Aldi stores after impressing judges in the show’s ‘Party’ category.
The drinks landed in stores on 13 November as an exclusive Specialbuy, priced at £1.49 for a 330ml can.
Available in two flavours, In a Pickle and Grape Cooler, the range offers an alcoholic take on traditional kombucha, with the former brewed using real juiced gherkins and the latter made with grapes and apples.
Taylor, 32, launched Stiff Tea in October 2024 after a decade working across the craft beer and kombucha industries.
The business has since partnered with larger production facilities to increase capacity, with the Aldi contract marking its biggest retail opportunity to date.
Taylor said: “Being stocked in Aldi is a dream come true. Running a bootstrapped business is almost impossibly hard, so to get the opportunity to work with a national supermarket with what is on the surface a quite niche product so early in our journey is unbelievable.”
Aldi UK chief commercial officer Julie Ashfield, who judged the competition alongside presenters Anita Rani and Jimmy Doherty, said the brand’s unusual flavours had helped it stand out.
“Taking kombucha into the party aisle with trending flavours like pickles was a bold move, but the flavours speak for themselves,” she said.
The six-part Channel 4 series sees emerging food and drink brands compete for a place on Aldi’s shelves, with products assessed on taste, price, packaging and their ability to scale.
Previous winners include Caribbean bakery brand Flake Bake, which went on to secure a permanent listing with Aldi after appearing on the show.
Stiff Tea’s two flavours are available for a limited time as part of Aldi’s Specialbuy range, with stock available while supplies last.

items.title: Boden accelerates US expansion
items.summary: British fashion brand Boden is working to unify its inventory and order flows as it continues to grow in the US, and scales its international Direct To Consumer (DTC) and wholesale operations. Therefore, Boden has worked with OneStock to modernised its Order Management System (OMS). It replatformed to one centralised system to allow it to...
items.body:
British fashion brand Boden is working to unify its inventory and order flows as it continues to grow in the US, and scales its international Direct To Consumer (DTC) and wholesale operations.
Therefore, Boden has worked with OneStock to modernised its Order Management System (OMS). It replatformed to one centralised system to allow it to manage increasingly complex order flows, segment stock and scale.
Alexander Ives, senior director of technology at Boden, explained: “As we look to grow the business through international expansion, particularly in the US, and adding new channels like wholesale and retail, we need more sophisticated order orchestration capabilities to support these ambitions.
“OneStock will bring our order orchestration together into a single platform, giving us the flexibility we need to support the business whichever direction it wants to take. This means we’ll be able to continue managing a single pool of stock while dynamically altering what we display to different channels, this will enable us to deliver seamless shopping journeys, while building the operational foundations to support our next phase of growth.”
A phased rollout will see OneStock supporting Boden’s DTC operations, orchestrating orders from its UK, North American and European Shopify storefronts, as well as its marketplace channels and new US stores.
Boden currently has three physical stores in the US. Its first in Atlanta, Georgia, opened last year. While two sites in Nashville, Tennessee, and Birmingham, Alabama were introduced earlier this year.
The retailer stressed its US stores “complement its strong digital business with carefully selected physical retail locations in key US markets”.
In September, Boden credited its US growth for an increase in profits. The US has become the retailer’s fastest-growing market, and now represents nearly half of group revenue.

items.title: Black Friday sales tipped to hit £12.8bn but smaller retailers face profits wipeout
items.summary: UK shoppers are expected to spend £12.8bn online during this year’s Black Friday sales period, although smaller retailers could find their profits swallowed up by heavy discounting and costly returns. Research from Parcelhero forecasts online sales will climb five per cent from £12.2bn last year, with £1.24bn expected to be spent on Black Friday itself,...
items.body:
UK shoppers are expected to spend £12.8bn online during this year’s Black Friday sales period, although smaller retailers could find their profits swallowed up by heavy discounting and costly returns.
Research from Parcelhero forecasts online sales will climb five per cent from £12.2bn last year, with £1.24bn expected to be spent on Black Friday itself, up 7.1 per cent.
The four-day Cyber Weekend is also expected to bring in £4.05bn, while Cyber Monday spending could top £1bn for the first time.
But while the figures make encouraging reading for the likes of Amazon and other major retailers, Parcelhero warned that smaller businesses may struggle to turn the sales rush into profit.
Discounts are expected to deepen as Black Friday approaches, with Adobe predicting average online markdowns will reach 25 per cent over Cyber Weekend.
For independent toy shops, craft retailers and other specialist sellers that rely heavily on Christmas trading, matching those promotions could leave little room for profit.
Parcelhero head of consumer research David Jinks said: “The sad truth, however, is that many of Britain’s favourite smaller retailers are very unlikely to see their final profits rise by anything like 5%.”
And the squeeze may not end when the sales finish.
Parcelhero estimates £1.55bn worth of gifts were returned to retailers following last year’s Christmas shopping peak, with smaller online businesses bearing a disproportionate share of the costs.
Processing a return can cost a small retailer as much as 66 per cent of an item’s original price once shipping, labour and inspections are taken into account.
Some online sellers have reported return rates reaching 60 per cent after the Christmas rush, while marketplace traders told Parcelhero that handling returns costs them at least 13 per cent more than high street-only retailers.
Jinks warned: “A seller who thinks they’ve banked a healthy Black Friday profit can find it has disappeared by the end of January.”
He argued that retailers with both physical stores and online operations are better placed to withstand the pressure, particularly as returns continue to eat into the gains made during peak trading.

items.title: Waitrose signs landmark global Regen Compact after UK’s smallest harvest on record
items.summary: Waitrose has signed a global initiative to support farmers, as they adopt regenerative practices that build healthier soil and help farms cope with extreme weather. Signing the Regen Compact builds…
items.body:
Waitrose signs landmark global Regen Compact after UK’s smallest harvest on record
Waitrose has signed a global initiative to support farmers, as they adopt regenerative practices that build healthier soil and help farms cope with extreme weather.
Signing the Regen Compact builds on years of its own work with British farmers, with its Leckford Estate acting as a living lab.
The Regen Compact, led by the Circular Bioeconomy Alliance, a charity founded by His Majesty the King in 2020 when he was Prince of Wales, is signed by 14 businesses. It comes after a year of extreme weather in which the UK is heading for its smallest cereal and oilseed harvest on record.
Each business that signs develops its own approach to supporting the farmers it buys from. Signatories will track progress transparently, and their actions will be independently benchmarked against the Compact’s principles.
Tom Denyard, managing director, Waitrose, said: “If we want British food on our plates in years to come, our farms have to be able to cope with summers like this one, which gave the UK its smallest harvest on record. Regenerative farming is about looking after the soil, so it can keep feeding us through the good years and the bad.”
Subscribe to Grocery Gazette for free
Sign up here to get the latest grocery and food news each morning
“Farmers are leading the biggest change in how British food is grown for a generation, and backing them has never been a side project for us,” he added.
“We’ve done it for years, on our own farm and with every one of our UK farmers and growers, and we intend to go further. But this is a challenge for the whole food industry, and this landmark Compact brings us together behind them, with farmers and nature at its core.”
The Compact is designed to give long-term commercial certainty for farmers and direct investment in farmer support as examples of what signatories can do. Waitrose already does both through Farming for Nature, launched in 2024 to build resilience into British farming.

items.title: Beckham kicks up a stink over Poundland perfume sales in £32m legal battle
items.summary: David Beckham‘s company has launched a £32m legal battle against fragrance giant Coty after claiming his perfumes were sold in Poundland and petrol station bargain bins, damaging his luxury brand image. The former England football captain’s business, DB Ventures, has accused the beauty giant of distributing Beckham-branded fragrances through retailers that had not been approved...
items.body:
David Beckham‘s company has launched a £32m legal battle against fragrance giant Coty after claiming his perfumes were sold in Poundland and petrol station bargain bins, damaging his luxury brand image.
The former England football captain’s business, DB Ventures, has accused the beauty giant of distributing Beckham-branded fragrances through retailers that had not been approved under their licensing agreement.
According to court documents filed in New York, Beckham’s company reacted with “shock and dismay” after discovering the fragrances being sold in Poundland and in a petrol station bargain bin.
The business claims Coty sold at least £18m worth of Beckham products through unauthorised distribution channels, undermining the premium positioning of the former footballer’s global brand.
Lawyers acting for DB Ventures argued that the discount sales associated Beckham’s fragrances with cheap products, potentially damaging the luxury image he has built over several decades.
The company is seeking approximately £32m in compensation and damages over the alleged breaches of its licensing agreement.
It has also accused Coty of under-reporting net sales by around £93m, resulting in approximately £4.5m in unpaid royalties.
However, Coty has denied ever selling Beckham fragrances to Poundland and has asked the New York court to dismiss the lawsuit.
The company maintains that it has the contractual right to determine which retailers stock the products.
Coty has worked with Beckham’s fragrance brand for more than a decade, producing over 30 scents bearing his name, with bottles typically retailing for around £20 in the UK.
The fragrance partnership is set to go through a significant change, with rival perfume manufacturer Interparfums set to take over the Beckham licence in 2028.
The company has signed a 20-year global licensing agreement to develop, manufacture and distribute fragrances under the Beckham name.

items.title: Waitrose to expand digital broadcasting after festive ad launch wins 2m views
items.summary: Chief executive of supermarket says it is considering new projects after success of Dish podcast and YouTube channel Waitrose is to expand its digital broadcasting portfolio after this year’s Christmas ad launch with Keira Knightley attracted more that 2 million viewers. “There are not many brands that would command an appointment of you for six minutes on ITV to launch their Christmas ad and have 2.3 million people show up to watch,” said the supermarket’s chief executive, Tom Denyard. Continue reading...
items.body:
Waitrose is to expand its digital broadcasting portfolio after this year’s Christmas ad launch with Keira Knightley attracted more that 2 million viewers.
“There are not many brands that would command an appointment of you for six minutes on ITV to launch their Christmas ad and have 2.3 million people show up to watch,” said the supermarket’s chief executive, Tom Denyard.
Showing the Guardian around Waitrose’s latest shop which opened in the wealthy Greater Manchester neighbourhood of Hale Barns last week, he said the company was looking at more digital ideas. “We would be daft not to think about that as an opportunity,” he said.
Waitrose is already a serious digital player with the Dish podcast, hosted by the DJ Nick Grimshaw and the chef Angela Hartnett, which has been downloaded more than 1.3bn times. It says its social media following has risen 8% year on year and fans spent more than 1m hours watching its YouTube channel in the last 12 months, double the previous year.
It launched a weekly recipe and tutorials series, Let’s Cook, this summer and has taken Dish live, selling more than 2,000 tickets for an event at the Royal Opera House. It also has a growing presence on TikTok with 128,000 followers.
Denyard said: “Waitrose as a brand punches well above its weight in food culture. We have the fastest growing channel for food in the UK.”
He said the retailer was thinking carefully about how to ensure it kept the trust it had gained from food fans. “We want to do it in a way that’s right for the community that we’re part of.”
Denyard, who joined Waitrose in January after four years leading Tesco’s online business, wants to link Waitrose stores and the digital world more closely with a host of ideas including AI assistants for staff and shoppers.
Staff across the chain are now equipped with handheld gadgets that give them access to AI-assisted information. The Rosie system, which began trials last year and is now in most shops, can help staff provide advice on suitable wines for different meals, and where in store to find products.
Denyard says the introduction of electronic pricing labels in almost all its shops over the past year will, from this week, also help staff, including those picking shelves for online orders, to find products. Rosie will indicate product locations with a flashing light on the electronic shelf label.
The system is said to have freed up thousands of hours of staff time, amid pressure to cut costs as a result of higher minimum wages and tax.
After opening two supermarkets this year, its first in eight years, Waitrose is to open as many as six new outlets of various sizes in 2027 as part of a £1bn investment plan.
Despite industry chatter about consolidation, Denyard says Waitrose is not looking to buy a rival chain. But in the event of a widely expected move by the UK’s second biggest supermarket chain, Sainsbury’s, to buy up either Asda or Morrisons, or any attempts by rivals to downsize, Waitrose will be waiting in the wings to pick up store locations.
“We will remain acquisitive and we are keen to make sure that we’re at the table taking those opportunities,” he said.
Next year’s plans include a supermarket in Oakham, Rutland, and three convenience shops in Bedminster inBristol, Chalk Farm in London and Springstead Village in Cambridge, as well as refurbishing 29 existing branches.
Denyard says he is keen for more larger supermarkets, such as those recently opened in Hale Barns and Cricklewood in north London, where the company can show off its full foodie credentials with fresh food counters, something removed by most rivals.
Waitrose, which has more than 300 supermarkets, is introducing meat, fish and sushi counters, on-site bakeries and fine wine sections in more stores. It is also using pop-ups, such as a mini cheese tasting table in Hale Barns.
Denyard says counters are “a core part of our offer” as the foodies Waitrose wants to attract “really want to shop them”.
Those foodies are also being courted with an ever-expanding own-label range, particularly at the premium end with Waitrose No.1. Sales of the luxury own brand are growing by more than 10% year on year despite the squeeze on household budgets, as many buy ready meals instead of takeaways and dining out.
Denyard says there is “lots of headroom” to expand the range and that own-label is a key part of what makes Waitrose distinctive.
After a difficult period, when sales were hit by IT problems that led to gaps on shelves, Waitrose is holding market share, according to the latest figures from the market analysts Worldpanel by Numerator. It is coming under pressure from Marks & Spencer, however, which has a higher share of the grocery market by some measures after opening a number of new food-led outlets.
Denyard nonetheless says Waitrose is “resilient and competitive in the market”. “Customers have a repertoire of places that they go for different missions and fulfil different needs across the course of a given week or month,” he said. “Our job is to make sure in that mix we are brilliantly differentiated and give food lovers more reasons to come to Waitrose, and we feel like we’re getting well down the path.”

items.title: David Jones: what went wrong and what happens next? Five takeaways from first creditors meeting
items.summary: Upmarket retailer, which recorded a net loss of $228m last financial year, has total debt over $400m including $11m owed to staff Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Upmarket retailer David Jones owed hundreds of millions of dollars when it collapsed into administration, after accelerating financial losses and reputational damage threatened its ability to stock shelves for Christmas. About 500 creditors attended its first meeting on Tuesday, where administrators McGrathNicol started to break down who is owed what, when those left out of pocket will know where they stand, and what ultimately went wrong. Continue reading...
items.body:
Upmarket retailer David Jones owed hundreds of millions of dollars when it collapsed into administration, after accelerating financial losses and reputational damage threatened its ability to stock shelves for Christmas.
About 500 creditors attended its first meeting on Tuesday, where administrators McGrathNicol started to break down who is owed what, when those left out of pocket will know where they stand, and what ultimately went wrong.
Here are five things we learned.
How much is owed?
David Jones collapsed early this month owing in excess of $400m to an assortment of creditors, including $180m of debts to trade creditors, mainly consisting of the brands that stocked its shelves.
There are also outstanding employee entitlements, such as annual and long service leave, worth about $11m, and about $33m in unredeemed gift cards, which the retailer is still accepting.
The rest is owed to large secured creditors, led by the retailer’s main financier, Hilco, which has a controlling hand over the current process and even has its own representatives in the 19 stores marked for closure.
Taken together, the debts are well over $400m, but that total is almost certain to climb as landlords tally up their losses.
On top of unpaid rent up to the appointment of administrators, shopping centre owners will also claim for broken leases after the chain’s receivers moved to close half of its 38-store network.
How much will creditors get back?
What, if any, money suppliers get back hinges on whether a buyer steps in and how much they are willing to pay, or whether the chain ends up liquidated, as well as how much cash David Jones can bring in through the crucial Christmas trading period.
Because product suppliers sit near the bottom of the creditor priority list, they won’t receive any money until secured lenders and employees are paid out.
Given the size of the outstanding debts, and poor financial state of the department chain, many suppliers are bracing for a near total loss of outstanding amounts.
Shaun Fraser, a founding partner at McGrathNicol, told creditors there were “too many variables” to indicate how much, if any, suppliers would receive.
“We haven’t yet got to a point where we’re engaged enough with bidders to have a sense of what value might be there,” Fraser said.
“We haven’t reached a point in the sale process where people are talking value or price.”
How are creditors feeling?
Out of pocket suppliers are particularly frustrated, though the modern practice of holding meetings online kept any real anger contained behind muted microphones.
There were questions over whether there had been preferential treatment to some suppliers, and if the retailer had been trading insolvent before the appointment of administrators.
McGrathNicol said it would investigate when the company might have been insolvent, and if preferential payments were made.
One brand representative said they had also repeatedly asked for stock lists and weekly sales figures without response.
What went wrong?
The administrators provided updated financials at the meeting that showed the poor state of affairs at David Jones.
The 188-year-old retailer recorded a net loss of $228m in 2025-26, before losing a further $69m in the first four months of the new financial year leading up to the administration.
Creditors were told that the funding pressures it was facing, coupled with reputational damage, was affecting its ability to get stock for the Christmas trading period.
David Jones ultimately got tipped into administration when negotiations with its main landlord, Westfield owner Scentre Group, broke down.
The retailer’s private equity owner, Anchorage Capital, wanted to radically reduce store numbers – something that is now happening during receivership – to rid the network of underperforming suburban stores.
The directors of David Jones listed several causes of the retailer’s problems, including everything from cost-of-living pressures and soft luxury demand to fierce online competition.
Fraser said there was also “clearly a business model problem” with the retailer.
What happens next?
Under a dual appointment, receivers FTI Consulting have taken day-to-day control of the business while administrators McGrathNicol hunt for a buyer, having called for “non-binding indicative offers” for the retailer by the end of the month.
That will trigger a process that could see formal bids lodged either late this year or early in 2027, giving some clarity to employees and suppliers ahead of the next creditors’ meeting, due by March.
The road ahead is, however, complicated by the breakdown in relations between Anchorage and the Westfield owner, which is threatening the retailer’s ability to operate at any of its complexes.
The Scentre Group chief executive, Elliott Rusanow, told Guardian Australia the landlord now had a “unique opportunity to facilitate the entry and growth of businesses that are more relevant to customers today and into the future”.
“That is the opportunity we will pursue at each of the 17 destinations with a David Jones store,” Rusanow said.

items.body:
innni - stock.adobe.com
Fintech pioneer Anne Boden back with agentic AI-focused bank
Anne Boden returns two and a half years after leaving Starling bank, with latest venture driven by AI
Starling bank founder Anne Boden has revealed her next venture to be an agentic artificial intelligence (AI)-focused bank.
The bank, Lockwood, will initially attempt to gain an Electronic Money Institution (EMI) licence from the Financial Conduct Authority next year, before a full banking licence in 2028. It is targeting one million customers in its first year.
Boden, who left Starling in 2023, sold her shares in the firm, and is reported to be providing the new company’s initial funding.
She told The Sunday Times that the bank is “going to be built by agents, to serve customers that want to use agents, and then be defended by agents”.
On its website, Lockwood describes its approach to AI and its security. “You’re ready to welcome AI assistants into your life, with all the convenience and financial freedom they offer,” she said. “Yet, at the same time, more fraudsters are using AI to try to break into people’s accounts. Most banks will respond with more passwords, more checks and more tracking. Lockwood is different. Lockwood is building its current account with fewer ways in, and Lockwood guards every one of them.”
According to Lockwood, it is a current account that “lets your AI agent pay for things safely, within limits you set, for people and small businesses in the UK.”
“Ten years ago, we built digital banking around the smartphone,” she said. “Today, the interface of personal finance is shifting again – from apps that you tap to intelligent agents that act on your behalf. If an AI agent is going to shop for you, pay your bills or manage your money, your bank account needs to be engineered specifically to govern that relationship safely. Lockwood is about giving people the confidence to embrace agentic AI while keeping absolute control over their finances.”
Boden founded Starling in 2014, and it received its banking licence in 2016, launching the following year. In October 2020, it made its first monthly profit of £800,000, becoming the first UK digital challenger bank to do so, and it reached fintech unicorn status in 2021.
Read more about Boden: Banker’s startup experience feathers the nest for Starling Bank
Boden is an IT professional who got into banking. She gained a BSc in computer science and chemistry, and an MBA.
Boden joined Lloyds Bank in the early 1980s, when, as she told Computer Weekly in a 2015 interview, she was “doing fintech before fintech was fashionable”.
After Lloyds Bank, her career has included a period heading up UK IT at Standard Chartered; being one of the original designers of the Clearing House Automated Payments System; a role as a strategy and technology consultant at PWC; restructuring European operations at UBS; holding the global chief information officer job for reinsurance at Aon; and running business in 34 countries for ABN Amro, and subsequently RBS, when it took over the Dutch bank.
But it was after leaving RBS in 2011 – to spend time working with startups to find out what was going on in financial services outside the big organisations – that she realised how banks needed to change. She joined Allied Irish Bank as chief operating officer and began implementing some of the ideas she’d had while working with small fintech groups. This was successful for the bank, but Boden wanted more – and realised the only way to get it was by starting from scratch with a new bank when the time was right.

items.title: US focused British fashion brand Boden taps OneStock order management system
items.summary: Boden has selected OneStock to unify its inventory and order flows as it accelerates US expansion and scales its international direct to consumer (DTC) and wholesale operations.To support its expansion plans, Boden recognised the need to modernise its order management system (OMS), seeking a ce
items.body:
Boden has selected OneStock to unify its inventory and order flows as it accelerates US expansion and scales its international direct to consumer (DTC) and wholesale operations.
To support its expansion plans, Boden recognised the need to modernise its order management system (OMS), seeking a centralised platform to allow it to manage increasingly complex order flows, segment stock and scale seamlessly.
Alongside its track record in DTC fashion, including partnerships with JD Sports Fashion, Orlebar Brown, Jigsaw and Longchamp, OneStock was selected for its native Shopify integration, which allowed Boden - one of Shopify’s largest EMEA clients - to reduce technical complexities during implementation.
“As we look to grow the business through international expansion, particularly in the US, and adding new channels like wholesale and retail, we need more sophisticated order orchestration capabilities to support these ambitions,” says Alexander Ives, Senior Director of Technology at Boden.
“OneStock will bring our order orchestration together into a single platform, giving us the flexibility we need to support the business whichever direction it wants to take. This means we’ll be able to continue managing a single pool of stock while dynamically altering what we display to different channels, this will enable us to deliver seamless shopping journeys, while building the operational foundations to support our next phase of growth."
A phased roll-out will see OneStock supporting Boden’s DTC operations, orchestrating orders from its UK, North American and European Shopify storefronts, as well as its marketplace channels and new US stores. This will bring delivery promises at checkout and returns management together on one central platform, with a view to providing a unified view of stock across all channels.
OneStock will also support Boden’s wholesale channel, including a stock reservation and reallocation system which keeps inventory set aside for specific wholesale partners. It will also allow Boden to scale its wholesale operations, moving from writing code to add new wholesale partners to configuring OneStock, to reduce the time to market for implementing new relationships.
“Retailers are increasingly operating in a Promise Economy,” says Romulus Grigoras, CEO and Co-Founder at OneStock. “And that means giving customers confidence that the commitments made at the point of purchase will be fulfilled, every time - whether they’re an individual shopper or a wholesale partner.”
“By unifying inventory and intelligently orchestrating orders across channels, Boden can extend the same precision, reliability and transparency of delivery promises to its wholesale partners as its DTC customers, ensuring every promise made is a promise kept."

items.title: Retail sales hit £2.26 billion in FY26 as Ikea UK invests in AI and automation technology
items.summary: Ikea UK has announced retail sales of £2.26 billion for financial year 2026 (FY26), an increase of 0.5% compared with the previous year (£2.25 billion).The retailer says that its expanded store footprint helped deliver a strong start to the year, with sales revenue growing 4.7% year-on-year in the f
items.body:
Ikea UK has announced retail sales of £2.26 billion for financial year 2026 (FY26), an increase of 0.5% compared with the previous year (£2.25 billion).
The retailer says that its expanded store footprint helped deliver a strong start to the year, with sales revenue growing 4.7% year-on-year in the first four months of FY26. However, a challenging trading environment with weakened consumer confidence and sustained pressure on household budgets saw sales revenue dip in the second half of the year.
David McCabe, CEO and CSO at Ikea UK&IE, says: “I’m incredibly proud that in extremely challenging market conditions, we’ve managed to close financial year 2026 in growth. In a year when many households continued to manage their budgets carefully, we saw just how important the home remains to people’s everyday lives. This growth reflects the trust people place in Ikea to offer quality, sustainable and well designed home furnishing solutions at prices as low as possible."
“In September, we started financial year 2027 with a clear priority: to continue giving customers the best possible value for money at a time when every pound matters. While cost of living pressures continue, we know a well-functioning home can make a real difference to everyday life. That’s why we’re continuing to invest in lowering our prices, helping more people create the home they want at a price they can afford.”
As consumer shopping habits evolve, Ikea has been looking to bring its offer closer to customers through a mix of store formats and online services. Building on the openings of Oxford Street, Brighton, Norwich and York towards the end of FY25, it expanded its presence further in FY26, with the opening of a small format store in Chester and a Plan and Order Point in Dundee. A further Plan and Order Point opened in Aberdeen in October, at the start of FY27.
Across its UK network of 31 stores, total store visits increased by 7% in FY26, with visitation bolstered by the retailer's expanded footprint, including those located in city centres and retail parks. It also opened a standalone Decathlon store within Ikea Croydon in April.
The UK is one of Ikea’s most advanced omnichannel markets in Europe. Online and remote sales grew by 0.7% compared with FY25 and accounted for 43.3% of total home furnishing sales in FY26. Through investment in digital innovation, including AI powered planning tools such as an AI room designer, and the Ikea app, it says it is creating a more connected and personalised omnichannel experience, making it easier for customers to explore the range, shop seamlessly across channels and access services whenever and however they choose.
In FY26, Ikea invested £31.5 million across its customer distribution centres in Peterborough and Doncaster to make online fulfilment more efficient and sustainable. In Peterborough, new technology is helping teams manage inventory and fulfil orders more efficiently. This includes using drones to support inventory management and machinery that packages orders to size, reducing material usage by up to 30%.
A further £1.5 million investment in Doncaster has expanded the centre’s capacity to fulfil more orders, enabling it to service the Gateshead, Edinburgh and Glasgow areas while creating 80 additional jobs at the site. By fulfilling these orders from Doncaster, rather than Peterborough, Ikea expects it will reduce emissions from delivery journeys by an estimated 280 tonnes of CO2 annually.
In FY26, 86% of UK deliveries were made using electric vehicles. Ikea is also planning to launch EV charging hubs at its Edinburgh and Glasgow stores, including charging facilities for electric heavy goods vehicles. Beyond fulfilment, it recorded growth in its circular business areas, with spare parts sales increasing by 13% and second-hand sales rising by 17%.
It has also continued to focus on other elements of its total cost transformation programme aimed at increasing operational efficiency, reducing costs and building a more sustainable business. Specifically, Ikea has optimised the utilisation of assets by increasing the proportion of online sales fulfilled through stores by 1.4% compared with FY25, while also generating additional value through the rental of excess space to third parties. It has also worked with external partners to invest in technological advancements that help reduce facility management costs and improve energy, water and waste efficiencies.
The retailer sees significant opportunities for future growth in the UK. However, while the recent budget avoided introducing significant new costs for retailers, it says structural cost pressures continue to impact investment and competitiveness across the sector.
McCabe says: "The UK has the highest business rates burden of any Ikea market in Europe and the third highest globally. While the budget avoided adding further costs, it missed an opportunity to back retailers under real pressure, stopping short of addressing the structural challenges holding the sector back. Retail is a vital part of the UK economy and communities nationwide and a more competitive operating environment would help businesses invest with confidence, while continuing to keep prices as low as possible for customers."

items.summary: Fermat, a Barcelona-based AI platform for the fashion industry, has raised $8 million in seed funding to open a New York office and expand its software from a design tool to full garment production. To begin, the company, which launched in 2022, is launching Techpacks, a tool which turns designs int
items.body:
Fermat, a Barcelona-based AI platform for the fashion industry, has raised $8 million in seed funding to open a New York office and expand its software from a design tool to full garment production.
To begin, the company, which launched in 2022, is launching Techpacks, a tool which turns designs into factory ready specifications.
The seed round was led by Kibo Ventures and Lunar Ventures, with participation from London-based PROfounders Capital, whose combined portfolios include companies such as Unity, Flywire, Job&Talent and Zama. Other participating investors include Masia Ventures, Blue Wire Capital, Common Magic, Betaworks and tech entrepreneur Dídac Lee.
Fermat is used by more than 350 customers across 14 countries, including Asos, J.Crew Group, New Look, S. Oliver, and Tendam, with designers tapping the platform to integrate AI into existing product development workflows.
With the launch of Techpacks, Fermat says it is reducing the bottleneck between designers and factories by speeding up tech pack creation, allowing for the creation of technical flats, construction details, measurements, bills of materials, and colourways in seconds.
Pol Baladas, CEO and Co-founder at Fermat, comments: “Fashion is an industry starving for good software tools, and generative AI is the first technology that can match its need for speed. In five years, no brand will work without it. We’re building Fermat to be the tool designers use from first sketch to production. It feels like the right time to open an office in the US as a third of our revenue already comes from there, without a single person being on the ground–until now.”
Nick Eley, Head of Digital Product Creation at Asos, comments: “Fermat transforms our sampling process from weeks to minutes. Designers communicate vision to suppliers without physical samples. This isn’t just time saved – it’s a fundamental change in how we develop products.”
Jordi Vidal, Partner at Kibo Ventures, says: “We invested in Fermat because it’s the emerging category leader in AI native fashion design, with rare early proof: explosive growth, near-zero customer churn, and tier-1 brands like New Look, J.Crew Group, and Asos adopting it bottom-up, designer by designer. Pol, Uri, Oscar and the team have shown that embedding AI directly into designers’ own workflows - not just generating images - is how you build the defining vertical AI product for fashion.”

items.body:
Best Buy is joining Circana’s Gateway programme with a view to giving suppliers a clearer view of how their products sell and how customers shop with the retailer.
Built on Circana's Liquid Data platform and Liquid AI technology, Gateway brings Best Buy's first-party data together with Circana's analytics and AI powered tools in one place. Best Buy’s suppliers will be able to better understand their sales performance and customer behaviour, spot opportunities and make more informed decisions.
“Suppliers want to understand what's happening in a retailer's business, and they want it fast to act on,” says Brad Shelton, President of Global Gateway Solutions at Circana. “With Best Buy Gateway, we're bringing Circana's analytics and AI tools together with Best Buy's data so suppliers can spot opportunities, make more informed decisions and grow together.”
“We have a shared goal with our vendor partners, and that’s to create the best possible experience for our customers,” says Blake Hampton, Chief Merchandising Officer at Best Buy. “Best Buy Gateway allows us to work with our partners to better understand our customers, so together we can deliver even more of what they want and need.”

He will lead Evolve’s client services team and drive continuous improvement in
items.body:
Evolve, which powers network connectivity for retailers, has made two senior appointments in client services and AI.
Kevin Breheny joins as Services Director from Places for People, where he was Director of IT Operations. He will lead Evolve’s client services team and drive continuous improvement in how the business supports around 100 brands across 12 countries.
Ben Cleary comes onboard from Neuven Solutions as the new Head of AI & Automation and will be responsible for using technology to strengthen and drive efficiency across the business’s client services proposition, which will give teams more time to focus on its growing customer base.
Founded in Wigan in 2005, Evolve specialises in providing internet connectivity and secure network solutions to multi-site brands and is set to manage more than 9,000 sites by the end of this year.
It received backing from BGF in August 2024 to support its UK and international expansion plans, with a particular focus on growth in the US, where it currently operates over 1,500 sites across multiple states, mainly in the fuel forecourt industry.
Alan Stephenson-Brown, Chief Executive at Evolve, says: “We’re excited to welcome Ben and Kevin to Evolve. Their roles will be key to driving continued growth as we bring more of the UK’s biggest multi-site brands onboard."
“The strength of our business reflects the increasing importance of reliable digital infrastructure across retail, hospitality and the forecourt industry. When brands can’t deliver the experiences customers expect in store, they walk away."
“Every payment, order and loyalty transaction in a modern store depends on connectivity. The household names we work with treat it as a customer priority rather than an IT issue, and they want one partner that takes accountability for their whole network. That is where we win.”
Stephenson-Brown adds: "We're focused on continuing our growth and delivering excellent service to our customers. The business is in great shape and we're well-positioned to continue winning major contracts as more brands recognise that reliable network infrastructure is a critical foundation to trading."

Jen Price has joined Allwyn UK, operator of the National Lottery, as Customer Transformation Director. She was previously at Morrisons, where she spent almost 12 years, most recently serving as Customer Director.
In a LinkedIn post, she said: "After a brilliant 12 years at Morrisons, it’s time for a new chapter. I’m sad to say goodbye to so many awesome colleagues, but thrilled to be joining Allwyn UK as Customer Transformation Director."
"As the operator of The National Lottery, Allwyn UK is a business with such an incredible purpose, and that has been evident in everyone who I have met in my first week."
She added: "A huge thank you to the team at Allwyn for making me feel so welcome already. It’s such an exciting time to join and I’m really looking forward to what’s ahead!"
Vusion
In what is claimed to be a UK supermarket first, Morrisons is launching new in-store technology that helps customers quickly find exactly what they're looking for.
The new ‘shop to light’ feature uses blinking electronic shelf labels, installed by Vusion. To use it, customers need to open the Product Finder tool on the homepage of their More Card app, search for the product they need and select ‘flash price label’. The app will share the in-store location, ask the customer to confirm if they are in the right aisle, and then the corresponding digital shelf label will flash magenta.
The new technology is being rolled out to Morrisons stores as they are installed with digital shelf edge labels. Currently over 270 of its supermarkets have them.
Gordon Macpherson, Group Productivity Director at Morrisons, says: “We know that Christmas is one of the busiest times of the year for our customers, and we're always looking for new ways to make their shopping experience as easy and convenient as possible."
"Our new ‘shop to light’ feature is a great example of how we're using technology to make a real difference in-store, helping our customers find the products they need quickly, whether they're shopping for their Christmas dinner or just popping in to pick up a few last minute essentials.”
Roy Horgan, UK & Ireland CEO at Vusion, says: “Technology has a huge role to play in making the shopping journey simpler, faster and more enjoyable for customers. ‘Shop to light’ is a great example of how we can help customers find what they need while making stores more seamless. Morrisons has been a fantastic partner in embracing innovation, and we are incredibly proud to be working together to help shape the future of retail.”

items.title: Change the law to protect millions from scourge of bank closures, ministers urged by independent review
items.summary: Labour has been urged to change the law urgently to protect millions from the scourge of bank closures on Britain's high streets following an independent review.
items.body:
Change the law to protect millions from scourge of bank closures, ministers urged by independent review
Labour has been urged to change the law urgently to protect millions from the scourge of bank closures on Britain's high streets following an independent review.
The review laid bare the damaging impact of thousands of branches shutting their doors on customers who rely on them including the elderly or those in rural areas.
It revealed that four million people still rely on face-to-face banking services – even as lenders desert high streets because more people are choosing to bank online instead.
The government said it had accepted a key recommendation for new laws 'to ensure people can continue to access the essential face to face banking services they need'.
The review said that since January 2021, banks and building societies have closed 2,382 branches, or 45 per cent of the network.
Consumer group Which? estimates that 6,896 have closed since January 2015, at a rate of around 53 each month, representing 70 per cent of the branches that were open at the start of 2015.
Some experienced anxiety and frustration when they could not access banking services
Since the 1980s, around 15,000 have shut, the review said.
Led by former Which? director Richard Lloyd, it gathered more than 18,000 responses, mainly from individual members of the public.
Many reported 'anxiety, frustration and a sense of disconnection' as issues such as lack of public transport, poor internet connectivity and the cost of mobile or broadband made it hard for them to access banking.
Mr Lloyd said: 'It is clear… that there are significant numbers of people who require in person services, and that existing banking provision falls short of meeting that need. Urgent action is necessary to prevent further harm.'
He said voluntary measures would not be enough and that Labour 'should introduce legislation as soon as possible to create an access to banking services obligation on designated banks'.
The review called for larger banks to 'be required to assess and fill gaps, or potential gaps, in in-person banking provision that significantly impact their customers' and consult with local authorities, charities and other bodies.
It was estimated that 40 per cent of consumers have experienced being unable to access banking services due to branch closures and that nearly one in five of those affected had been left unable to carry out the activities they needed to do.
While regular use of branches has declined, they 'continue to play a role for a significant number'.
Lack of access can lead to financial harm to consumers including those who fall victim to scams.
Figures this year showed 15 per cent of people reported that they had lost money to a fraud that they had been unable to resolve due to difficulty accessing banking services.
Others found they had incurred charges due to missing or delayed payments while others pointed to loss of financial independence.
The report added: 'Branch closures can create feelings of fear or abandonment among regular users, reducing trust in banks and discouraging engagement.'
Research found those experiencing the most difficulty accessing in-person banking services included older people and those in people poor physical or mental health, and people with disabilities.
Small businesses have also been hit by banks disappearing from town centres.
Some found it harder to deposit cash and cheques or carry out routine banking they needed to carry on operating, while others said holding more money on the premises or travelling with it over longer distances increased their exposure to theft and robbery.
In some cases, firms believed branch closures led to reduced footfall on the high street and weaker local trade.
The government said it would work with the Financial Conduct Authority as well as industry and consumer groups to work out what constitutes 'reasonable access for different types of essential banking services' under a new framework.
It said this would be 'carefully targeted and proportionate, whilst remaining responsive to changes in how people are increasingly banking digitally, and supporting competition and innovation'.
City minister Lucy Rigby said: 'Millions now rely on banking digitally but for people and businesses who rely on face-to-face services, being able to speak to someone in person really matters. We will act to protect the access they need.'
A spokesperson for trade body UK Finance said: 'Most retail banking transactions are now carried out through mobile banking. The framework should build on what already works and remain flexible as customer needs change over time.'

By Daniel Wolfenden, design and marketing director at retail design agency Ripple
“2027 will be a year when retailers expect their physical spaces to work harder, both commercially and in terms of customer experience. Rising energy bills, business rates and staffing costs are making physical stores increasingly expensive to operate, putting greater pressure on retailers to maximise the value of every square foot. Against this backdrop, store design will increasingly be judged on its ability to deliver long-term commercial value, rather than creating an immediate visual impact.
“Flexibility will be a major priority for retailers that need environments that can adapt to changing product ranges, seasonal campaigns and evolving customer demands without the expense and disruption of a complete refit. We’re expecting greater investment in modular displays, adaptable fixtures and design systems that allow retailers to refresh their spaces while protecting their existing investment.
“We’ll also see a shift in how showrooms support the customer journey. Online and physical shopping are no longer separate experiences. Research from Visa Acceptance Solutions found that 38% of UK in-store shoppers used their phone as part of their most recent physical purchase, demonstrating how closely the two channels are becoming connected.
“Shoppers are increasingly researching and comparing products online before visiting a store, physical environments need to offer something they can’t get from a screen. Particularly in sectors such as flooring, interiors and home improvement, showrooms will need to help customers visualise products, compare materials and finishes, and make more confident purchasing decisions.
“Sustainability will remain important, but the focus will increasingly move beyond material selection towards longevity. Designing fixtures that can be repaired, reconfigured and reused makes both environmental and commercial sense. The same scrutiny will apply to digital technology. Screens and interactive features need to earn their place by making shopping easier, rather than simply adding another layer of technology.
“Ultimately, I think 2027 will see commercial performance become an even greater consideration from the earliest stages of the design process. Retailers will want environments that not only reflect their brand, but improve product visibility, encourage engagement, support sales and remain practical to operate and maintain. The most successful store designs will balance creativity with flexibility, functionality and a clear return on investment.”

items.title: Understanding what Martyn’s Law means for retailers

Although the exact commencement date has yet to be confirmed, this new law will make preparing for and protecting against terrorist attacks in qualifying premises […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
The Terrorism (Protection of Premises) Act 2025 – also known as Martyn’s Law – is expected to be implemented in Spring 2027 impacting public venues and events across the UK. Although the exact commencement date has yet to be confirmed, this new law will make preparing for and protecting against terrorist attacks in qualifying premises and events a legal requirement, with the likes of retail parks and outlets, shopping centres, and larger individual retail units all affected by the changes.
As retailers prepare for Martyn’s Law, loss prevention and health and safety teams have rightly focused on finalising in-store emergency procedures that are compliant with the new legal requirements. What retailers may not realise, however, is that updating procedures is only one part of preparing for the legislation. Whilst the majority of those in the retail sector have heard of Martyn’s Law, there are some disparities between what organisations believe is compliant and what the legislation actually requires.
Retailers specifically face unique challenges when it comes to implementation of the law compared to other sectors. In a busy store with varying footfall, for example, will every colleague know what to do if an incident occurs? For smaller stores, that don’t have the resources or corporate health and safety teams available, implementing any changes effectively can prove difficult. For outlets within shopping centres, is it clear which responsibilities lie with the landlord, and which lie with the tenant? With this in mind, all retailers must now put the right plans, communication processes and resources in place to ensure full compliance with Martyn’s Law, without overburdening already stretched teams.
Having a thorough understanding of what Martyn’s Law means for, and which parts apply to, individual retail premises is the first step in making sure your business is prepared for the legislative change. Knowing about Martyn’s Law is one thing, but understanding the intricacies of what the law means in practice is often overlooked, leaving retailers unsure of how the law specifically applies to them. The key to compliance is establishing where your retail store sits within the scope of legislation, and therefore what requirements apply to the space.
The first step for retailers is to establish whether their premises falls within the scope of Martyn’s Law which is divided into two tiers; standard tier for venues or events with 200-799 occupancy, and enhanced tier for 800+ people. These thresholds relate to the number of people reasonably expected to be present at the same time on at least one occasion, including staff meaning knowing what tier your establishment falls into is key to understanding what action needs to be taken. Predicting occupancy in the retail sector can be difficult, especially when footfall fluctuates so vastly with spikes in seasonal sale periods like Black Friday or January sales. Martyn’s Law uses the number of individuals reasonably expected to be present in qualifying premises at the same time, from time to time. Whilst larger retailers might use existing footfall data to assess occupancy levels, and therefore which tier they fall into. Retailers should therefore assess peak simultaneous occupancy, rather than relying solely on daily footfall totals or average visitor numbers. This assessment should take account of relevant seasonal peaks, historical occupancy data, and expected customer numbers. Capacity records and manual counts can help form an assessment In addition to customer numbers, retailers must also account for employees or contractors reasonably expected to be on site who could push occupancy numbers over a tier threshold. Understanding which tier a premises falls into will help retailers understand their obligations, and implement appropriate and reasonably practicable changes as needed.
Aside from understanding the new protection obligations, retailers should identify the responsible person for each qualifying premises and establish clear internal accountability for implementing the relevant requirements. For Enhanced Tier premises, where the responsible person is a company or organisation, a senior individual must be designated to ensure compliance with the Act. Standard Tier premises must also establish who will take responsibility for implementing necessary measures in the event of an attack. Enhanced tiers need a designated responsible person in order to comply with Martyn’s Law but even retail stores in the standard tier should assign an individual to oversee preparations and co-ordinate activity across the business Collaborative co-ordination is especially important for retailers inside shopping centres. Both the individual units and the wider shopping centre will have responsibilities under Martyn’s Law, for example a large retailer will be responsible for its own premises, but the shopping centre management will oversee the wider site and shared communal spaces. Forming a strong relationship between retailers and centre management is imperative, and having a robust communications system – such as a smart alarm and communications system that can send different signals to different zones – paired with a co-ordinated plan is vital for keeping the public safe across multi-venue sites. Communication throughout your own team must also not be overlooked. Whether they are a long-serving supervisor or it’s their first day on the job, procedures are only effective if they are understood by employees and they know how to respond during an incident.
Retailers should prioritise simple, accessible training that helps every employee understand what different emergency procedures mean in practice, including evacuation and lockdown. Relevant plans should be incorporated into staff inductions, supported by visual materials, such as maps or information stored in an emergency grab bag, or a demonstration of the alarm signalling equipment used onsite. Staff should understand their roles and the procedures they may need to follow. In busy retail environments, members of the public are likely to look to store colleagues for guidance and leadership in the event of an incident.
Appropriate practical exercises and reviews of emergency procedures, including evacuation and invacuation drills, that mimic the dynamic nature of an attack, can also help preparation by testing different approaches and identifying overlooked areas for improvement. For smaller retailers without dedicated loss prevention teams, area managers or head office teams could support training and assess employee understanding by speaking directly with store colleagues.
Meeting the requirements of Martyn’s Law may feel overwhelming to retailers, but in reality, making preparations that take reasonable and proportionate action in protecting the public will help support compliance. Following today’s release of ASDA’s figures for the 13 weeks ending 30 September 2026; Eleanor Simpson-Gould, senior retail analyst at GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform, offers her view: “ASDA’s Q3 update leads with 3.1% growth in total revenue to £6.5bn, yet that figure includes fuel and gives a flattering picture of the grocer’s […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
Following today’s release of ASDA’s figures for the 13 weeks ending 30 September 2026; Eleanor Simpson-Gould, senior retail analyst at GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform, offers her view: “ASDA’s Q3 update leads with 3.1% growth in total revenue to £6.5bn, yet that figure includes fuel and gives a flattering picture of the grocer’s recovery. Excluding fuel, revenue was £5.1bn, level with last year, and like-for-like (l-f-l) sales fell 0.1% for the 13 weeks to 30 September 2026. Diesel prices reached their highest level on record in the UK during the final week of ASDA’s quarter as conflict in the Middle East pushed pump prices close to £2 a litre. As a result, the headline growth reflects higher forecourt prices rather than more spending in ASDA’s stores.
“The split between food and non-food is telling. Food sales grew just 0.1% while group l-f-l sales excluding fuel fell 0.1%, highlighting that non-food is likely to have declined in the quarter. ASDA did not disclose George’s performance, which suggests the brand is not currently contributing to ASDA’s recovery. That raises questions about ASDA’s investment in standalone George stores when the brand is struggling to grow within its existing estate. Christmas is now a key test for George. ASDA should give value-led gifting, partywear, and nightwear prominent space in its large supermarkets and use ASDA Rewards to target grocery shoppers with clothing offers, turning high footfall into extra non-food spending.
“Price has become ASDA’s main lever, but it is not yet producing growth. ASDA has cut prices on more than 1,000 everyday lines and pledged to hold them until Christmas, which should resonate as household budgets tighten. However, a year of price investment has barely moved l-f-l sales, and it has come at a significant cost; group adjusted EBITDA fell 33.1% in FY2025. With net debt of £3.1bn, ASDA cannot keep funding price cuts indefinitely without a recovery in volumes. It must extend its cuts into the new year, when spending is typically squeezed, but it also needs to make price leadership one part of a broader offer, rather than its only argument. The appointment of David Potts as Group CEO gives ASDA a leader with a proven record having turned around Morrisons. Potts’s priority must be to turn competitive prices and better availability into sustained growth. That will require improving fresh quality and range, raising store standards consistently across the estate, and making sure stores have enough staff to deliver a reliable shopping trip.”

items.title: Sephora plans 10 new UK stores
items.summary: Sephora is planning to open at least 10 new stores across the UK next year as the beauty retailer accelerates its expansion, according to reports. The LVMH-owned retailer is understood to be targeting further locations following its return to the UK physical retail market in 2023. New sites have already been secured on High Street...
items.body:
Sephora is planning to open at least 10 new stores across the UK next year as the beauty retailer accelerates its expansion, according to reports.
The LVMH-owned retailer is understood to be targeting further locations following its return to the UK physical retail market in 2023. New sites have already been secured on High Street Kensington in London and at the Harlequin shopping centre in Watford.
Sephora currently operates 18 UK stores, including four in London and 14 across the rest of the country. It is also preparing to open a 4,500 sq ft store at Brent Cross shopping centre in north London this winter.
The latest expansion plans build on the retailer’s strategy to establish a stronger presence across the UK, following its departure from the market in 2005.
Sephora has also been experimenting with smaller store formats, opening its first boutique on Carnaby Street in July, before launching a second at Old Spitalfields Market. The format is designed to offer a more accessible, curated shopping experience alongside its larger destination stores.
Sarah Boyd, managing director of Sephora UK, said: “We see a significant opportunity to continue building our presence and bringing our unique beauty experience to more customers across the country.”
Its UK growth will also be supported by a new partnership with M&S, announced in September. The agreement will see Sephora introduce shop-in-shops at 100 M&S locations from spring 2027, alongside a dedicated beauty offer on M&S.com.
The move will extend Sephora’s reach beyond its standalone stores, giving it access to M&S’s established high street and retail park locations.
Its expansion comes as competition in the UK beauty market intensifies. Boots has been investing in its own beauty proposition, including dedicated beauty stores and upgrades to its existing beauty halls, while Space NK continues to grow its physical estate.
Sephora’s combination of larger experiential stores, smaller boutiques and partnerships signals an increasingly multi-format approach to winning UK beauty shoppers.
The retailer’s latest plans underline its confidence in the UK market as it looks to challenge established players for a greater share of beauty spending.
