items.title: Energy costs could force disabled consumers to cut back on clothing and food
items.summary: Disabled consumers are facing increasingly difficult spending decisions as higher winter energy bills threaten to squeeze household budgets, with food, fashion and leisure among the areas expected to bear the brunt. Consumer spending could be squeezed once again this winter as rising energy costs force households to cut back, with disabled consumers likely to reduce...
items.body:
Disabled consumers are facing increasingly difficult spending decisions as higher winter energy bills threaten to squeeze household budgets, with food, fashion and leisure among the areas expected to bear the brunt.
Consumer spending could be squeezed once again this winter as rising energy costs force households to cut back, with disabled consumers likely to reduce spending on clothing, groceries and other everyday purchases, according to new research from Purpl.
The Autumn 2026 Purpl Pulse Consumer Insight Report, The Hidden Cost of Having Less Choice, found that seven in 10 disabled consumers expect higher energy bills to mean cutting spending elsewhere.
The findings highlight how the impact of rising household costs extends beyond energy providers, creating a knock-on effect for retailers as consumers are forced to prioritise essential bills over discretionary purchases.
The pressure is particularly acute for disabled consumers because reducing energy consumption is not always a realistic option. Around 68 per cent of respondents said their disability or health condition limits how much they can reduce their energy use.
Heating and electricity can be closely linked to health, comfort and independence, with some consumers relying on powered beds, wheelchairs and other medical equipment. Others spend more time at home because of mobility limitations or health conditions, increasing their energy requirements.
Consequently, 53 per cent expect higher energy costs to create a choice between adequately heating their homes and paying for other essentials.
The report, based on a survey of 1,117 respondents, suggests that when energy consumption cannot easily be reduced, households are instead having to make savings elsewhere.
Food and groceries are among the most frequently identified areas for cutbacks, alongside clothing, eating out, leisure and days away.
Some 44 per cent of respondents said they would consider cutting back on grocery spending, and 40 per cent on clothing.
The impact is particularly pronounced among respondents whose disabilities most limit their ability to reduce energy consumption. Around half of this group expect to cut grocery spending, while almost two thirds anticipate having to choose between adequate heating and other essentials, including food.
Additionally, the findings point to further pressure on discretionary spending as consumers reassess purchases and delay replacing clothing.
However, the report suggests the impact could extend beyond traditionally non-essential categories. Some respondents also expect to reduce spending on health-related costs and disability-related products and services.
More than half of all respondents (56 per cent) strongly agreed that they had already cut spending on things that improve their quality of life to protect money for essential household bills.
This suggests consumers are increasingly having to make difficult decisions about which purchases to sacrifice, rather than simply reducing overall spending.
The research also highlights the limited financial resilience available to many households. Just 12 per cent of respondents strongly agreed that they had enough savings to cope with an unexpectedly high winter energy bill, while six in 10 scored at the bottom of the scale.
This leaves little room to absorb unexpected costs without making further adjustments to spending. The changing financial landscape is also influencing how consumers shop.
The report found that behaviours identified in its Summer 2026 research, including comparing prices, checking offers and taking longer to make purchasing decisions, have remained largely unchanged.
Consumers are continuing to look for value, but the research suggests they are becoming increasingly selective about what they buy and where they spend.
Purpl said this distinction was important because comparing more products does not necessarily mean consumers have more choice. Instead, financial pressure can narrow the range of products and retailers that remain affordable and practical.
This is particularly relevant for grocery retailers, where a squeeze on household finances caused by higher energy bills can translate directly into reduced food budgets.
The report also highlights how accessibility and convenience influence purchasing decisions. A cheaper product or retailer may not represent better value if delivery costs, accessibility barriers or practical considerations make it difficult for a disabled customer to use.
Clear pricing, meaningful promotions, accessible shopping journeys and dependable delivery will therefore remain important in helping customers identify genuine value.
This winter retailer and brands will be looking to demonstrate value while recognising that customers may have increasingly little flexibility over where their money goes.

items.title: Government extends jobs guarantee for young people looking for work
items.summary: Convenience retailers have welcomed the extension of the Jobs Guarantee, funding more than 90,000 young people in their first six months of work. The announcement from the Department for Work and Pensions comes ahead of the publication of the Milburn review later this week, which… This story continues at Government extends jobs guarantee for young people looking for work Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The announcement from the Department for Work and Pensions comes ahead of the publication of the Milburn review later this week, which will make recommendations on making it easier to employ people, especially those aged between 18 and 24.
The Jobs Guarantee scheme will be available across all areas of England, Scotland, and Wales, providing jobs for eligible young people that are claiming Universal Credit and have been looking for work for at least 12 months.
The nationwide expansion of the scheme follows a rollout in six areas with some of the highest levels of youth unemployment.
The scheme intends to help more than 90,000 young people into work by March 2029.
Ed Woodall, chief executive at the Association of Convenience Stores (ACS), said: “Local shops are often where young people get their first experience of work, developing the skills and confidence that support them throughout their careers. We welcome the expansion of the Jobs Guarantee and efforts to help young people into employment sooner.”

items.title: Makeup giant Sephora to open new stores in the UK as it steps up its battle with Boots
items.summary: Sephora, which is owned by French giant LVMH, is planning to open 10 more shops in the UK over the next year, bringing its total to 28 stores.
items.body:
Makeup giant Sephora to open new stores in the UK as it steps up its battle with Boots
Global make-up retailer Sephora is to open a slew of new stores in its latest expansion in Britain, as it steps up its battle with rival Boots.
Sephora, owned by French giant LVMH, is planning to open 10 more shops in the UK over the next year, bringing its total to 28 stores.
It includes a new shop in High Street Kensington, London and at the Harlequin shopping centre in Watford, according to reports in the Times.
Retailers are under pressure to win customers amid a booming beauty market, worth £5.2billion in the UK.
British chemist Boots has been pinning its hopes on its beauty arm, having added 61 new cosmetics and fragrance brands to its roster since last August, as well as opening two ‘beauty only’ stores in London and Bristol.
Sephora stocks popular beauty brands, including Rihanna's Fenty Beauty - which is also backed by LVMH.
Department store chain John Lewis has also plugged millions of pounds into opening glossy new ‘beauty halls’, selling both newer and more established brands.
And the latest on Sephora’s expansion follows news of a tie-up with Marks and Spencer that will see 100 ‘shop in shops’ launch across Britain.
Sarah Boyd, managing director of Sephora UK, said: 'We see a significant opportunity to continue building our presence and bringing our unique beauty experience to more customers across the country.'
Sephora, which was founded in 1969 by perfume seller Dominique Mandonnaud, operates 3,400 stores in 35 countries.
Last summer, hundreds of shoppers rushed to the opening of a Sephora at the Arndale Shopping Centre in Manchester, with one couple sleeping overnight to be the first to experience the new beauty store.
It was a resounding welcome for the business, which had only returned to the UK in March 2023 with a shop in Westfields in White City, London.
It had left the UK in 2005, shutting six shops after five years, due to the dominance of existing retailers Superdrug and Boots, as well as department stores like Debenhams.
In recent years, Sephora has been a stand-out for LVMH, which also owns Dior and Louis Vuitton.
Despite a gloomier performance in its more luxurious divisions, the business said last month that the arm housing Sephora saw sales rise 8 per cent over the three months to September 1.
Bernard Arnault’s behemoth hailed ‘strong growth’ in Sephora’s revenue and said it had seen ‘sustained growth in its many historic brands and the ongoing ramp-up of exclusive launches, including Rhode and several C-Beauty brands.’
As the luxury industry faces a protracted down-turn, experts believe that fragrances and beauty are benefiting from a ‘lipstick effect’, where consumers want to make themselves feel better with affordable treats.

items.summary: Ineos wanted £10m for alleged refusal to return yacht Out-of-court settlement ends plan for a 2028 trial Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos Group has reached an out-of-court settlement with Sir Ben Ainslie over the £180m yacht their companies built for the 2024 America’s Cup. Ratcliffe and Ainslie worked closely together during two cycles of the America’s Cup culminating in Ineos Britannia becoming the first British crew to win the challenger series two years ago, but they fell out over plans for a third bid, with Ineos announcing last year that it had “reluctantly withdrawn its challenge” for next year’s event in Naples. items.body:
Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos Group has reached an out-of-court settlement with Sir Ben Ainslie over the £180m yacht their companies built for the 2024 America’s Cup. Ratcliffe and Ainslie worked closely together during two cycles of the America’s Cup culminating in Ineos Britannia becoming the first British crew to win the challenger series two years ago, but they fell out over plans for a third bid, with Ineos announcing last year that it had “reluctantly withdrawn its challenge” for next year’s event in Naples.
Ineos launched a legal action in March after expressing “surprise” that Ainslie’s Athena Racing had opted to keep using Britannia, which was beaten 7-2 by Emirates Team New Zealand in 2024, in the 2027 challenge.
Court documents filed this year showed Ineos was claiming more than £10m for Athena’s alleged refusal to return the boat. The dispute had been set for a trial in January 2028 in the Admiralty Division of the Court of England and Wales, but their claim has been withdrawn.
“Ineos has reached a settlement with Athena Racing and considers the matter now closed,” the statement read. No further details, such as whether the yacht has been returned, were provided.
In a statement issued to members of Ainslie’s club, Royal Yacht Squadron Ltd, its chair, Michael Grade, said: “Members will no doubt be aware of the ongoing commercial dispute between Ineos and Athena Racing/GB1.
“I am delighted to announce that this dispute has now been settled, with any and all claims between the parties now withdrawn. This is excellent news indeed as GB1 prepares to challenge for the 38th America’s Cup in Naples next year. We continue to offer Sir Ben Ainslie and his team our full support as they look to build on their great success in Barcelona in 2024.”
Ineos had claimed when withdrawing from the partnership last year that delays in reaching an agreement with Athena Racing had “undermined its ability to prepare” for the event, adding that it had spent £180m on Britannia on top of £170m on the boat used in the 2021 America’s Cup campaign. In response, Athena claimed they had always owned the assets and intellectual property from the two campaigns and that Ineos had been a sponsor.
In a defence filing in June, Athena alleged that Ainslie was warned on the eve of the 2024 America’s Cup by Rob Nevin, Ineos Sport’s chair, that Ratcliffe would “burn his house down” if he failed to give the billionaire what he wanted.
“We have a phrase at Ineos: ‘scorched earth’,” Ainslie claimed Nevin warned him in the defence filing. “It means that if you don’t give Jim what he wants, he will burn your house down.”
An Athena Racing/GB1 spokesperson told the Guardian: “Athena Racing/GB1 have always been, and remain, the owners of the assets, including the AC75 race yacht.”
Ineos has had a chequered record since Ratcliffe took the decision for the petro-chemical giant to invest in sport in 2019. Since buying the dominant cycling team Team Sky, who had won eight Grand Tour titles in eight years including six at the Tour de France, Team Ineos has added only the 2019 Tour de France and 2021 Giro d’Italia to the tally in seven years.
A sponsorship deal with the All Blacks also ended in an acrimonious dispute, with New Zealand Rugby taking legal action last year accusing Ienos of failing to pay the first instalment of a six-year deal, which was settled out of court.
Ineos also reached a settlement with Tottenham, who had alleged they were owed money after the early termination of a sponsorship agreement last year.
Ineos’s current sporting investments are Nice, which has been up for sale for more than a year, and Manchester United, who are in the Premier League’s relegation zone and last week appointed Mauricio Pochettino as their third permanent manager in less than three years since the company bought a 29% stake in the club.
Ineos declined to comment.

items.title: Beckham firm sues after fragrance found for sale in Poundland
items.summary: Brand reacted with ‘shock and dismay’ after products were also found in a ‘bargain bin inside a gas station’ Business live – latest updates David Beckham’s company reacted with “shock and dismay” after discovering his branded fragrance range was on sale in petrol stations and in Poundland, court documents have revealed. The former England football captain’s brand, DB Ventures, has launched a lawsuit against the distributor of the products, arguing it allowed them to be sold in stores that had not been agreed upon. Continue reading...
items.body:
David Beckham’s company reacted with “shock and dismay” after discovering his branded fragrance range was on sale in petrol stations and in Poundland, court documents have revealed.
The former England football captain’s brand, DB Ventures, has launched a lawsuit against the distributor of the products, arguing it allowed them to be sold in stores that had not been agreed upon.
DB Ventures claimed to have discovered the perfumes for sale in the troubled UK budget retailer and in a “bargain bin inside a gas station” at an unspecified location, according to court papers filed in New York.
Lawyers acting for Beckham’s company said it reflected “desperation and greed” by the perfume company, Coty.
Coty, which is headquartered in the Netherlands, has worked with Beckham’s brand for more than a decade and has produced more than 30 different fragrances bearing his name. In the UK, they sell at about £20 per bottle.
Lawyers claimed that Coty sold at least $24m (£18m) of Beckham products through “unapproved distribution channels”.
In the court filing, they said: “DB Ventures, the licensor of the David Beckham brand, ensures that all of its brand licensing partnerships maintain the lifestyle and luxury image of the brand that Sir David has carefully cultivated for decades.
“Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station. How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.”
The legal documents, filed at the supreme court in New York and first reported by the Daily Mail, allege that Coty had “distributed David Beckham fragrances through the budget retailer Poundland, allowing the product to be sold for dollar store prices and associating the David Beckham brand with cheap, discount products.”
The lawyers asked for compensation and damages totalling $41m. They also claimed Coty under-reported net sales by $123m, which would mean that DB Ventures lost $6m in unpaid royalties.
Coty filed its defence, asking for the case to be dismissed. It denied that it had ever sold the fragrances in Poundland, but argued that it had the right to decide where it wanted to sell its David Beckham range.
Beckham, who retired from professional football in 2013, has built a multimillion-pound business empire, DRJB Holdings, around his brand. The group is made up of three divisions, the largest of which is DB Ventures, which covers most of his commercial partnerships with brands such as Hugo Boss.
The Seven Global division contains licensing agreements with companies such as Adidas, and the remainder of the business is Studio 99, the production studio that made Netflix documentaries about the lives of himself and of his wife, the former Spice Girl and fashion designer Victoria Beckham.
This year David Beckham received a $51m dividend from the group, after a series of lucrative brand deals for the Fifa World Cup. He appeared in about a dozen ad campaigns during the tournament this summer, working with brands such as Lenovo, McDonald’s and Bank of America.
The Beckhams are together worth an estimated £1.2bn, according to the most recent Sunday Times Rich List.
DB Ventures and Coty were approached for comment.

items.body:
Vapers rushed to stock up on e-liquids, nicotine salts and other taxable products ahead of the Government’s new vaping duty, with sales increasing by 123% in the final seven days before its introduction, new data reveals.
The online retailer Vape and Go analysed their sales data ahead of the new Vaping Products Duty, which came into force on 1 October 2026, revealing that sales of affected products were 50% higher per day throughout September compared with normal levels.
Key findings:
- Last-minute stockpiling intensified dramatically ahead of the 1 October deadline, with daily sales 123% above normal during the final seven days of September.
- Sales peaked at 390% above average on 30 September, the final day before the tax came into force.
- Customers bought 27% more taxable vape products per order
- Stoke-on-Trent recorded the biggest regional increase, with daily sales 164% above normal between 14 and 30 September.
- The new vape duty did not immediately apply to all products on 1 October, as retailers could continue selling eligible pre-existing stock without the new tax, meaning prices didn’t necessarily rise straight away.
The rush intensified as the tax deadline approached, with daily sales increasing by 45% between 14 and 20 September, before climbing by 69% the following week. On Wednesday 30 September, the final day before the tax was introduced, sales increased a massive 390% above the normal daily average.
The figures suggest many consumers brought forward their purchases to get ahead of the new duty, which introduced a £2.20 charge per 10ml of vaping liquid, before VAT.
Vapers stockpile e-liquids and nicotine salts
E-liquids and shortfills experienced the biggest increase in demand ahead of the tax, with sales rising by 78% throughout September compared with normal daily levels.
Nicotine salts also saw a significant increase of 55%, while sales of pre-filled pods rose by 31%. Pre-filled kits, meanwhile, remained relatively unchanged, with sales falling by 2%.
The trend became even more apparent during the final seven days before the tax came into force, with sales of e-liquids and shortfills increasing by 153%, followed by nicotine salts at 132%, pre-filled pods at 91% and pre-filled kits at 62%.
Customers also appeared to be purchasing larger quantities in anticipation of the price changes. The average September order saw an increase of 27% in order size compared to normal periods.
Which UK cities saw the biggest pre-tax buying rush?
The sales surge was particularly pronounced in some parts of the UK, with Stoke-on-Trent recording the biggest increase in daily sales between 14 and 30 September.
Nottingham and Plymouth followed closely behind, while several other towns and cities also experienced substantial increases.
The ten locations with the biggest increases were:
| Rank | City (delivery address) | Increase in taxed units sold a day, 14–30 Sep vs normal | Taxed units a day, all September vs normal | Orders a day, 14–30 Sep vs normal | 
| 1 | Stoke-on-Trent | +164% | +99% | +75% | 
| 2 | Nottingham | +148% | +101% | +63% | 
| 3 | Plymouth | +126% | +83% | +55% | 
| 4 | Rotherham | +125% | +69% | +40% | 
| 5 | Doncaster | +119% | +68% | +51% | 
| 6 | Glasgow | +117% | +82% | +46% | 
| 7 | Leeds | +114% | +66% | +40% | 
| 8 | Lincoln | +107% | +65% | +49% | 
| 9 | York | +102% | +67% | +36% | 
| 10 | Bristol | +100% | +59% | +38% | 
Across the UK as a whole, daily sales of products covered by the new duty increased by 84% between 14 and 30 September.
Sales return to normal after vape tax introduction
The data also reveals how purchasing habits changed once the new duty came into force.
Although sales remained 2.3 times higher than normal on 1 October, they had already fallen to 1.2 times the usual da ily average by 2 October.
From 3 October onwards, sales returned to broadly normal levels, with daily sales between 3 and 31 October sitting just 1% below the June – July average.
Salman Essap, founder at Vape and Go, said:
“There was clearly a lot of uncertainty surrounding the introduction of the new vape duty, and we believe this may have encouraged customers to stock up before the October deadline. Some customers may have assumed that prices would increase immediately across all products from 1 October, when in reality retailers could continue selling eligible existing stock without the new duty until 31 March 2027.
“We decided not to rush into increasing our prices and wanted to take a considered approach as duty-paid stock gradually entered the market. We were conscious that customers were already facing uncertainty around the changes and didn’t want to introduce unnecessary price increases before they were required.
“The sales figures show just how strongly the deadline influenced buying habits, with customers purchasing larger quantities ahead of the change. However, the introduction of the duty didn’t mean every product would automatically become more expensive overnight.”

items.title: Reading off-licence owner hit with six-year director ban over unexplained payments
items.summary: The owner of a Reading off-licence and convenience store has been banned as a company director after failing to account for hundreds of thousands of pounds in transactions. Pal Chopra was the director of Reading Food & Wine Ltd, which traded from Friar Street in… This story continues at Reading off-licence owner hit with six-year director ban over unexplained payments Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Pal Chopra was the director of Reading Food & Wine Ltd, which traded from Friar Street in the town centre.
Insolvency Service investigators found Chopra failed to ensure adequate accounting records were maintained or provided to the liquidator for Reading Food & Wine Ltd.
The 52-year-old received more than £200,000 directly from Reading Food & Wine Ltd’s bank account, but inadequate records meant investigators could not establish the nature of the payments.
Chopra, of Lady Margaret Road, Southall, London, has been disqualified as a company director for six years.
Neil North, chief investigator at the Insolvency Service, said: “Directors running businesses on our high streets have a responsibility to keep proper records and account for company money.
“Chopra failed to do that, leaving more than £200,000 paid directly to him unexplained, alongside substantial cash withdrawals and other transactions.
“We are working with partners across government and law enforcement to tackle misconduct on our high streets and protect local communities.
“This six-year ban demonstrates the action we can take when directors fail to meet the standards expected of them.”
The lack of records meant Insolvency Service investigators could not establish the nature of £219,402 in payments made from Reading Food & Wine Ltd’s bank account to Chopra between March and August 2024.
Investigators were also unable to establish the purpose of £27,290 in cash withdrawals, as well as the nature or business benefit of other transactions totalling almost £9,500.
They could not establish what happened to £163,500 of stock recorded in Reading Food & Wine Ltd’s accounts for the year ending July 2023 but which did not appear in its Statement of Affairs in December 2024.
The inadequate records ultimately meant the true financial position of Reading Food & Wine Ltd could not be established.
Reading Food & Wine Ltd went into liquidation in December 2024 with assets of £6,000 and liabilities of £228,641.
The Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade accepted a disqualification undertaking from Chopra, and his ban started on Friday 13 November.
It prevents him from being involved in the promotion, formation or management of a company without the permission of the court.

items.title: M&S set to introduce home delivery subscription
items.summary: Marks & Spencer is planning to launch a new home delivery subscription for customers early next year, as the retailer looks to drive online sales and increase shopping frequency. The proposed service will offer unlimited home delivery for a subscription fee, according to reports in The Times, with the plans revealed at M&S’s Capital Markets...
items.body:
Marks & Spencer is planning to launch a new home delivery subscription for customers early next year, as the retailer looks to drive online sales and increase shopping frequency.
The proposed service will offer unlimited home delivery for a subscription fee, according to reports in The Times, with the plans revealed at M&S’s Capital Markets Day on 10 November.
The move comes as the retailer looks to strengthen its digital proposition and encourage customers to shop more frequently across its fashion, home and beauty ranges.
The subscription will mark a return to a delivery-based membership offer for M&S, which withdrew its Sparks Delivery Pass from sale to new customers in March 2026. The previous scheme offered unlimited standard, next-day and nominated-day delivery on eligible orders for an annual fee of £25.
It is not yet clear how much the new subscription will cost, which product categories will be covered or whether it will include minimum spending requirements.
The delivery subscription is one of two new customer propositions being developed by M&S, alongside the introduction of M&S Pay, a flexible credit service due to launch in the 2027 financial year.
The credit scheme will allow shoppers to spread payments across instalments, with M&S director of online and omnichannel for fashion, home and beauty David Clark suggesting it could encourage more frequent purchases and higher average transaction values.
Clark told investors that securing just one additional annual purchase from 10 per cent of M&S customers could generate £39m in incremental revenue.
Both initiatives form part of M&S’s wider growth strategy, which includes increasing the contribution of online sales to its fashion, home and beauty business.
The retailer is targeting online sales accounting for almost half of fashion, home and beauty revenue, up from 35 per cent in the first half of 2026.
The plans come as M&S continues to invest in its digital and operational capabilities following the disruption caused by its 2025 cyberattack.

items.title: Cyber insurance premiums climb as fridge hacks and Binance expose rising uncovered losses, reveals GlobalData
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. However, recent attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe and the record $6.3 billion theft from crypto exchange Binance show that a growing share of cyber losses fall outside what standard […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
Global cyber insurance premiums are set to grow at a faster pace over the next two years as businesses respond to rising attack frequency. However, recent attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe and the record $6.3 billion theft from crypto exchange Binance show that a growing share of cyber losses fall outside what standard policies cover, says GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform.
GlobalData’s Global Insurance Database forecasts that global cyber insurance premiums will grow by 6.9% to $16.6 billion in 2026. Growth is then expected to accelerate to 10.0% in 2027, taking premiums to $18.3 billion, as rising attack frequency, greater awareness among businesses, and the growing use of internet-connected technology push more organizations to seek protection.
The forecasts come as a cyberattack that switched supermarket fridges into defrost mode has reached the UK. Hackers disrupted refrigeration at approximately 350 supermarkets in France in October, before a second wave hit stores in seven countries, including Ireland. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre has confirmed that UK organizations were also affected.
Much of the resulting loss is unlikely to be insured. Standard cyber policies typically exclude physical losses such as spoiled stock, while property policies with spoilage cover often carry cyber exclusions. French retailer Intermarché said its insurance did not cover the incident, while David Molony, Aon’s head of cyber solutions for Europe, the Middle East, and Africa, said most UK retailers lack the specialist endorsement required.
Elsewhere, Binance has published an incident report on its $6.3 billion theft, the largest crypto theft on record, which the FBI has attributed to North Korean state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor. The five-month attack relied heavily on social engineering, including a fake job offer that led an engineer to download malicious code. Bloomberg Law reported that Binance had been unable to buy cyber insurance, as is the case for many crypto firms.
Charlie Hutcherson, Senior Insurance Analyst at GlobalData, comments: “Demand for cyber insurance is clearly picking up, but these incidents show that the cover businesses buy does not always match the attacks they face. A supermarket losing chilled stock to a hacked refrigeration system, or a crypto firm losing funds to a state-backed group, can find that the loss sits outside its policy. Without clearer protection, businesses risk paying for cover that does not respond when it matters most.”
Losses are increasingly falling between policy lines, from physical damage caused through operational technology to digital asset theft and state-backed attacks.
Hutcherson continues: “Even where crypto firms can find cover, most cyber policies exclude fund losses unless digital asset cover is added. The attribution of the Binance attack to a state-backed group adds a further complication, as it could trigger war and state-backed attack exclusions. Businesses need to understand these exclusions before an incident, not after.”
For insurers, this creates both a risk and an opportunity as premium growth accelerates.
Hutcherson concludes: “As more operational technology is connected to the internet, attacks that cause physical damage are likely to become more common. Insurers that offer clearer wordings, specialist endorsements such as perishable goods cover, and greater certainty around war and state-actor exclusions will be best placed to capture the growth expected over 2026-27. Brokers also have an important role to play in helping businesses identify coverage gaps they may not know they have.”
*GlobalData’s Global Insurance Database supplies actual, historical, and forecast data on key insurance indicators for over 172 markets worldwide. Its dedicated cyber insurance view covers premiums in 83 markets, including both standalone and packaged policies. Where available, cyber premiums are collected directly from insurance regulators and industry associations. Where direct reporting is not available, GlobalData applies a proprietary modeling methodology, anchoring estimates on each market’s broader general insurance base and comparable regional growth trends and incorporates an estimate of cyber premium placed through Lloyd’s. Forecasts are revised monthly based on the latest driver trends for the cyber insurance market.

American Pecans is bringing a new sweet-and-savoury format to UK shoppers with the launch of its new Caramelised Pecans (RRP: £3.00), now set to debut as a Tesco Finest 150g SKU.
Launching from 17 November, the new listing will go live ahead of the key Christmas shopping period. The festive pack features holly and berries, positioning caramelised pecans as a seasonal, versatile snack for sharing, gifting and entertaining.
The new product combines crunchy caramelised pecans with a touch of salt, delivering a distinctive sweet-and-savoury bite designed to bring something new to the premium snacking fixture.
The Tesco listing comes as the UK market for American pecans continues to see strong growth. According to recent data, UK imports of American pecans reached 3,090 metric tonnes in 2025 (ISE 2024–25), demonstrating a 38% increase on 2023–24. The growth reflects pecans moving beyond traditional baking occasions, into more nutritious snacking, entertaining and premium seasonal formats.
The UK is currently the third-largest European market for American pecans, and is continuing to build momentum in 2026, underlining the market’s growing demand for American pecans.
Serena Schaffner, chief marketing officer at American Pecans, said: “Our new caramelised pecans launch is part of American pecans’ continued focus of showcasing the versatility of pecans and creating new ways for UK consumers to enjoy them, from everyday snacking to festive sharing occasions. As we see growing interest in pecans across the UK, we’re excited to bring this sweet and savoury format to shoppers, particularly ahead of Christmas as a key, seasonal shopping moment.”

items.body:
Tesco launches Climate Supplier programme to lower emissions
Tesco has launched a Climate Supplier programme in partnership with OpenClimat to increase decarbonisation across the sector.
The retailer is inviting 400 of its key suppliers to join a data sharing platform with the goal of cutting emissions and achieving measurable reductions across its operations.
This is part of the supermarket retailer’s wider commitment to sustainability, with a target of achieving net zero across its full value chain by 2050.
The programme was designed to streamline climate data sharing and aims to build a clearer understanding of emissions while offering suppliers with tailored guidance, practical resources and opportunities for collaboration.
At the beginning of the programme, suppliers will fill in a questionnaire and submit their data prior to the engagement stage of the process, which is set to start in February next year.

OpenClimat currently operates an established network of retailers and manufacturers collaborating to lower greenhouse gas emissions according to the business.
Some of the brands under OpenClimat’s banner include retailers such as Carrefour, Tesco, General Mills and McCain.
Claire Lorains, group quality and sustainability director at Tesco said: “At Tesco, we know reaching net zero across our full value chain by 2050 will require collaboration with all our suppliers to drive emissions reduction.
“We’re pleased to be partnering with OpenClimat to help streamline emissions data sharing while strengthening collaboration and driving meaningful action. Manufacturers asked us to bring our collaborative model to the UK. Tesco has made it happen.
“We’re proud to be opening a new chapter in retailer-manufacturer collaboration to accelerate decarbonisation across the value chain.”

items.title: Retail workers lag behind rest of UK workforce in AI productivity gains

Adoption of GenAI varies across the retail sector, with over two-thirds (69%) of retail workers in desk-based […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
Workers in the retail sector are not yet seeing material productivity gains from the use of Generative AI (GenAI). Only half (48%) of UK retail workers who have used GenAI at work agree that it saves them time.
Adoption of GenAI varies across the retail sector, with over two-thirds (69%) of retail workers in desk-based roles* having used GenAI at work, compared with half (50%) of retail workers overall. Comparatively, less than two-thirds (63%) across the wider UK workforce have used GenAI at work.
The findings come from Deloitte UK’s inaugural GenAI Workforce Survey, the largest study of workplace GenAI use conducted in a single country. It surveyed 25,000 workers across the UK to understand how they are using GenAI in their jobs and how organisations are responding. More than 1,700** retail workers responded to the survey.
Training is a key issue for retail workers and their use of GenAI tools. The main support retail workers want from their employer to help them include GenAI in their daily tasks at work is training on how to fact-check the output of tools (21%) and more GenAI skills training (20%). Less than a quarter (23%) of retail workers said they had already received formal training from their employer on how to use GenAI at work.
However, retail workers are more optimistic than the general UK workforce around the security of their jobs in an AI world. Half (50%) of all retail workers believe that none of their current role will be done by GenAI in five years, with an additional third (33%) believing that their role will only partially be done by GenAI.
Oliver Vernon-Harcourt, partner and head or retail and consumer products at Deloitte UK, added: “GenAI has created a new opportunity for businesses to boost productivity, and the retail sector is no different. However, we are currently seeing that many retail workers have not yet realised the potential productivity gains available using these tools. Therefore, the challenge and opportunity sit with businesses to equip their people with more training and the right tools to help do their jobs even better. Businesses that invest in the technology, upskill colleagues, and focus on the tasks that really matter will be best placed to unlock the real benefits of GenAI.”

items.title: The AI agent boom is creating a new product data challenge for retailers
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Retailers and brands rushing to deploy AI agents risk creating a new generation of disconnected technology, unless they address the product data, governance, and operating models required to make multiple agents work together, according to a new whitepaper from Akeneo. The Agentic PIM Playbook examines the transitional phase as organisations move beyond individual AI experiments […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Retailers and brands rushing to deploy AI agents risk creating a new generation of disconnected technology, unless they address the product data, governance, and operating models required to make multiple agents work together, according to a new whitepaper from Akeneo.
The Agentic PIM Playbook examines the transitional phase as organisations move beyond individual AI experiments and begin deploying multiple specialised agents across the product lifecycle.
Akeneo argues that while the first AI agent may solve a relatively straightforward use case, the challenge changes fundamentally as organisations deploy more of them. As the whitepaper states, “Your first agent is a use case. Your tenth is an operating model.”
The paper identifies ten potential agents spanning the product lifecycle, including product modelling, supplier data, enrichment, content creation, localisation, asset intelligence, quality and compliance, activation, market intelligence, and insights.
While individual AI agents are likely to become widely available, Akeneo argues this accessibility to the technology itself will therefore provide relatively little competitive differentiation. What will matter is whether agents can share trusted data, business rules, workflows, and governance.
The warning comes as retailers and brands increasingly explore agentic AI to automate activities that have traditionally required significant manual intervention. Rather than relying on a single general-purpose AI assistant, Akeneo expects product teams will increasingly work alongside fleets of specialised agents, each responsible for different elements of managing, enriching and distributing product information.
But adding more agents also increases the consequences of poor underlying and unstructured data. “AI does not fix fragmented product data. It scales what it is given,” the whitepaper warns.
Akeneo identifies five foundations required to support this new environment: trusted product data; business context and repeatable intelligence; human expertise in the loop; channel intelligence; and trust, traceability and authority.
As the number of agents grows, situating these foundations correctly becomes increasingly important, and requires four shared capabilities. Agents need to work from the same governed product record; tasks and approvals need to occur in the correct sequence; taxonomies, policies and channel requirements need to be governed by shared rules; and businesses need a clear record into what has changed, why, and who, or what, made these changes.
This becomes particularly important as AI changes not only how businesses manage products, but also how consumers discover them.
As search and shopping become increasingly AI-mediated, products will need structured and authoritative information that can be understood not just by people visiting ecommerce sites, but by AI systems interpreting consumer intent, comparing products and potentially making recommendations or purchasing decisions.
The result, Akeneo argues, is that product information management is moving beyond the question of how businesses can use AI to create content faster. The larger challenge is establishing an authoritative product information environment within which multiple AI agents can operate safely and effectively.
Human expertise also remains central. Rather than removing people from product information management, the whitepaper argues that agentic AI changes where their value lies. AI can undertake repetitive work at scale, while people remain responsible for business context, exceptions, judgement and accountable decisions.
For retailers and brands, this means looking beyond the next process to automate. They need to consider how today’s individual AI projects will eventually operate as part of a much larger product intelligence ecosystem.
The whitepaper suggests organisations start with a simple question: if the business could automate one part of the product lifecycle tomorrow, which would create the greatest impact?
Justin Thomas, VP Sales – EMEA North, Akeneo said, “The interesting question is rapidly moving from, what can an AI agent do for us? to, what happens when we have ten of them? Individual agents will become increasingly easy to deploy. The harder problem is making sure they are working from the same trusted product information, following the same rules and operating within a framework the business can understand and govern.”

The new service expands the range of specialist healthcare available through Boots Online Doctor, giving eligible patients another treatment option […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
Boots Online Doctor today announces the launch of SureLeaf, a specialist medical cannabis service giving eligible patients living with chronic pain, generalised anxiety disorder or insomnia access to consultant-led assessment, treatment and ongoing clinical care.
The new service expands the range of specialist healthcare available through Boots Online Doctor, giving eligible patients another treatment option to consider and greater access to clinical expertise.
Jamie Kerruish, Chief Healthcare Officer, Boots, said: “At Boots, we’re committed to making healthcare more accessible and helping people find the right support for their individual needs. Millions of people live with ongoing pain and for some, conventional treatments do not provide adequate symptom relief. This can have a significant impact on everyday life, from working and sleeping well to spending time with family and doing the things they enjoy. Medical cannabis is a specialist area of healthcare and, through SureLeaf, we’re giving eligible patients another treatment option to consider, supported by clinical expertise and robust ongoing care. Ultimately, it’s about helping people explore appropriate options that could help them better manage their symptoms and improve their quality of life.”
SureLeaf brings together specialist consultants, multidisciplinary clinical oversight and ongoing patient monitoring throughout treatment. Patients aged 25 or over with an eligible condition can begin their assessment online, with suitability reviewed by the clinical team before progressing to a video consultation with a consultant in the relevant medical specialty who is on the General Medical Council Specialist Register.
Any proposed prescription will be independently reviewed by a multidisciplinary clinical team that includes a second, independent consultant, before treatment begins. Patients must have previously tried conventional treatments without achieving adequate symptom relief.
Once treatment begins, patients will receive ongoing clinical support and monitoring, including an initial review after 28 days followed by reviews at least every three months. Validated questionnaires will be used throughout treatment to assess relevant areas including quality of life, pain, anxiety, sleep and mood, helping clinicians monitor the effectiveness of treatment.
Dr David Gwynne, medical director, Boots Online Doctor, said: “Medical cannabis is not appropriate for everyone and prescribing decisions need to be made carefully on an individual patient basis. SureLeaf has therefore been designed with strong clinical safeguards and specialist oversight at every stage, so treatment is only considered for patients where it is clinically appropriate. Our priority is to ensure patients receive responsible, clinically led care, from their initial specialist assessment through to ongoing monitoring and review once treatment begins.”
Alongside the launch, Boots and the University of Nottingham are exploring a collaborative research programme to build on the existing real-world evidence and understanding of medical cannabis in chronic pain management.
The work would build on the existing partnership between the two organisations, which is based on a shared commitment to improve patient care through evidence led innovation and aims to help inform future clinical practice, support responsible service development and contribute to the broader understanding of the role medical cannabis could play.
SureLeaf will operate as a private healthcare service through Boots Online Doctor and will support people living with the following eligible conditions:
- Chronic pain conditions including chronic primary and neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, complex regional pain syndrome, chronic back or neck pain, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, sciatica, peripheral neuropathy, trigeminal neuralgia, phantom limb pain,
- chronic migraine, endometriosis-related pelvic pain and chronic abdominal or pancreatic pain
- Generalised anxiety disorder
- Insomnia disorder
Further information, including full eligibility criteria and how to access the service, is available on the dedicated service page here.

items.title: Grocery Horizons: tackling the biggest challenges facing grocery retail

This Wednesday [18 November], RG Events will bring together senior industry figures at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium for Grocery Horizons 2026, a one-day event exploring the forces shaping...
items.body:
With grocery retailers navigating changing shopper behaviour, rising operating costs and an increasingly complex trading environment, the need to rethink how the sector operates has never been greater.
This Wednesday [18 November], RG Events will bring together senior industry figures at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium for Grocery Horizons 2026, a one-day event exploring the forces shaping the future of grocery retail.
The event will provide a platform for retailers and industry experts to examine the commercial, operational and technological challenges facing the sector, while considering how businesses can adapt to remain competitive.
The morning programme will open with a discussion on one of the sector’s most pressing operational challenges: loss prevention. With retailers facing persistent threats from theft, organised retail crime and violence against shopworkers, the session will explore how technology and new approaches to security can help businesses protect their estates.
Delivered in partnership with Trigo, the discussion will feature Hannah Cleary, senior manager of crime and security at Morrisons and Richard Lim, chief executive and founder of Retail Economics
The conversation will consider how retailers can move beyond traditional checkout controls to develop more effective approaches to loss prevention, while balancing security investment with the wider store experience.
The second session, in partnership with SSI SCHÄFER, will turn to visibility across the retail estate, examining how better access to operational data can improve stock management, product tracking and supply chain efficiency.
Sarah Mayer, senior director of product and customer at HelloFresh, will join Eleanor Mansell, head of sourcing at SPAR, to discuss the role of data and technology in connecting different parts of retail operations.
As grocery retailers manage increasingly complex supply chains and store networks, having an accurate picture of inventory, product movement and operational performance is becoming central to improving availability and reducing inefficiencies.
The final discussion will explore another challenge facing grocery businesses: how to deliver a better customer experience without compromising the employee experience.
In partnership with Satalia, Mei Pang, principal applied AI strategist at the business, will join Chris Chandler, head of store support at OurCoop, to examine how retailers can use technology and artificial intelligence to improve the experience for both shoppers and colleagues.
With retailers under pressure to improve productivity while maintaining service standards, the session will consider how businesses can make technology work for frontline teams rather than simply adding complexity to their roles.
Beyond the panel discussions, Grocery Horizons will provide dedicated opportunities for senior grocery leaders to exchange ideas and share experiences with peers from across the industry.
The morning programme will be followed by lunch and networking, before delegates have the opportunity to take part in an F1 driving experience at the stadium.
Returning for its second year, Grocery Horizons aims to give grocery leaders practical insight into the issues shaping the sector, from loss prevention and supply chain visibility to the growing role of AI in retail operations.
With contributions from retailers, technology providers and industry analysts, the event will bring together different perspectives on how grocery businesses can respond to an evolving operating environment.
Grocery Horizons 2026 takes place on Wednesday 18 November at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. Attendance is free for senior retail leaders. The full agenda and registration details are available at Retail Gazette Grocery Horizons

items.body:
Drawing on more than 150 years of expertise in soups and broths, iconic Scotland-based food manufacturer Baxters launches Baxters Super Good Beef Bone Broth and Baxters Super Good Chicken Bone Broth, presented in easy-to-use pouch packaging.
Thanks to Baxters’ dedication to great flavour, 10-hours of slow-cooking has brought unique, naturally cloudy bone broths to supermarket shelves, delivering on three key areas – great taste, convenience and nutritional benefits.
Each bone broth is high in protein, provides a natural collagen boost, is low in fat, gluten and dairy-free, and contains no artificial colours, flavours or preservatives.
Sam Cameron, Baxters’ marketing and customer director, said: “We believe Baxters Super Good Beef and Super Good Chicken Bone Broths are a market-first for taste, convenience and nutritional benefits thanks to our long-established expertise and dedication in creating delicious soups, packed with flavour.
“Slow-cooked for 10-hours, both of our bone broth recipes reflect the flexible needs of today’s time-poor foodies, who, like us, don’t want to compromise on taste.
“Our bone broths can be used in a variety of ways, sipped straight from the mug or used as a base for sauces, soups, stews, casseroles and ramen dishes.”
Baxters Super Good Beef Bone Broth and Baxters Super Good Chicken Bone Broth are available UK-wide Sainsbury’s and Morrisons stores and Tesco in Scotland and are priced at £4.50 each.

items.title: Battle against retail crime backed in top-level Portsmouth summit
items.summary: Efforts to combat retail theft, harassment and rogue traders continued last week as members of the Federation of Independent Retailers (the Fed) met police and leaders of Portsmouth City Council to discuss the problems. The meeting came shortly after the Fed had been involved in… This story continues at Battle against retail crime backed in top-level Portsmouth summit Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The meeting came shortly after the Fed had been involved in similar talks with the Mayor of Manchester.
The event was arranged by the Fed’s former national president and prominent Portsmouth retailer, Linda Sood, whose family has operated Falcon News in the city centre for more than 40 years.
She was accompanied by other local independent retailers who are Fed members in Portsmouth and Hampshire.
The group particularly highlighted the apparent growth of rogue traders in Portsmouth selling illicit tobacco, which fuels organised crime and undercuts responsible retailers.
Retailers were encouraged to use the UK-PAC (Partners Against Crime) reporting system to help improve retail crime intelligence.
The Fed’s political engagement coordinator, Douglas Oliver, explained the work the Fed was doing at a national level to encourage the government to better resource neighbourhood police and trading standards enforcement.
Chief inspector Samuel Warne, deputy district commander of Portsmouth police, emphasised the importance of reporting, because of the crucial role he said it played in intelligence gathering and criminal investigations.
Edward Skinner of Portsmouth City Council’s trading standards team spoke about its work with intelligence to target those who might sell illegal products and its efforts to use closure orders, fines and criminal penalties to stop it.
Sood said: “Our members remain greatly concerned about retail crime and also rogue trade in illegal tobacco in the city.
“However, I would like to thank councillor Pitt, the police and the team at the council for their time and interest.
“It was reassuring to receive the update from the local police and trading standards but we know we need to keep on working together to challenge these problems we discussed.”.
Pitt – Liberal Democrat leader of the council since May 2023 – added: “As someone who worked as a publican for many years before going into city politics, I am sympathetic to those who run shops locally and face a range of challenges including theft, harassment and being undercut by criminal rogue traders.
“However, the message from the meeting was clear: please do report either using 999 in an emergency or using UK-PAC for retail crime intelligence purposes.
“UK-PAC is a really powerful new tool that retailers can try for free for the first year before making a long term commitment, because of partnership between the police and the council.”

items.title: Boots to begin prescribing medical cannabis in UK
items.summary: Online service will be offered to patients with eligible conditions, in a first for a British high street pharmacy Boots is to start prescribing medical cannabis, it has announced, in a first for a UK high street pharmacy. The online service is being offered to patients in the UK aged 25 and older who have an eligible condition such as chronic pain, anxiety or insomnia. Continue reading...
items.body:
Boots is to start prescribing medical cannabis, it has announced, in a first for a UK high street pharmacy.
The online service is being offered to patients in the UK aged 25 and older who have an eligible condition such as chronic pain, anxiety or insomnia.
The chain is launching its SureLeaf service alongside a collaborative research programme with the University of Nottingham that will examine patient outcomes, prescribing practices and experience in the treatment of chronic pain.
Patients will be invited to start an assessment online. Their suitability will then be reviewed by a clinical team, before they are invited to a video consultation with a consultant, according to Boots.
Boots said any prescription would be “independently reviewed by a multidisciplinary clinical team that includes a second, independent consultant, before treatment begins”. It said any patient wishing to be prescribed medical cannabis must first have tried conventional treatments without success. And the pharmacy said patients would be regularly reviewed.
Boots’ chief healthcare officer, Jamie Kerruish, said: “Millions of people live with ongoing pain and, for some, conventional treatments do not provide adequate symptom relief. This can have a significant impact on everyday life, from working and sleeping well to spending time with family and doing the things they enjoy.
“Ultimately, it’s about helping people explore appropriate options that could help them better manage their symptoms and improve their quality of life.”
Dr David Gwynne, the medical director of Boots’ online service, said: “Medical cannabis is not appropriate for everyone and prescribing decisions need to be made carefully on an individual patient basis.
“SureLeaf has, therefore, been designed with strong clinical safeguards and specialist oversight at every stage, so treatment is only considered for patients where it is clinically appropriate. Our priority is to ensure patients receive responsible, clinically led care, from their initial specialist assessment through to ongoing monitoring and review once treatment begins.”
The prescription of cannabis-derived medicines was legalised in 2018 after the mother of a young boy from Northern Ireland with severe epilepsy had cannabis oil seized at airport customs. Many private clinics have been treating patients with them for years.
Hopes have been expressed that cannabis could revolutionise some areas of medicine. Only people with rare forms of epilepsy, those dealing with certain side-effects of chemotherapy, and those with certain multiple sclerosis symptoms, can get it on the NHS. But, besides chronic pain, private clinics have also been prescribing the medicines for various psychiatric disorders and neurological conditions.
This year, researchers from universities in Sydney, Brisbane and Melbourne in Australia, and Bath in England, found “very little evidence” that cannabis was effective in treating anxiety, anorexia nervosa, psychotic disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder or opioid use disorder.
They found some evidence the medical products could reduce dependence on cannabis, relieve the symptoms of Tourette syndrome and help insomniacs sleep better.

items.title: Avoid this Black Friday scam - how to check it's a real deal
items.summary: Sales and the looming tax deadline mean more scams - here's how to make sure you don't get caught out.
items.body:
Avoid this Black Friday scam - how to check it's a real deal
- Published
This month's Black Friday and the tax return deadline at the end of January are both opportunities for fraudsters to scam you.
That's because people are more likely to expect emails, texts and other correspondence at this time of year.
Fraudsters will use the dates to impersonate genuine organisations and retailers by pushing victims towards fake websites to steal personal information.
Here's how to spot a scam and how you can avoid being caught out.
Is it really HMRC? Here's how to tell
If you are self-employed or have more than one source of income you will need to file a tax return by the end of January.
Fraudsters seize on this deadline to blitz people with messages that look like they are official and from the UK's tax authority, HMRC.
Any such calls or messages should be ignored, but you can also check whether an email, external, text message, external or phone call, external claiming to be from HMRC is genuine.
"Reporting scams helps us shut them down and protect others," adds Lucy Pike, HMRC's chief security officer.
New figures from HMRC, shared with the BBC, show that it received 95,340 reports of suspected scams in the year to the end of October.
There were 900 reports of one specific scam which used emails containing a malicious attachment which directed customers to a fake gov.uk webpage designed to steal personal and financial information.
To avoid being caught out, HMRC says:
- it never contacts people by email, text or phone to tell them they are due a refund or ask them to claim one
- it never asks for personal or financial information by email or text message
- it never leaves threatening voicemails about legal action or arrest
Is it a real deal? Here's how to check
In the run-up to Black Friday you may be looking around for discounts, but fraudsters will impersonate genuine retailers to steal personal details or take payment for a product that will never be delivered.
Kirsty Adams, a fraud and scams expert at High Street bank Barclays, says make sure you pause before you buy.
"When you're scrolling on the sofa and a countdown timer starts ticking, or a deal pops up in your feed from an account that looks just like a brand you trust, it's easy to get swept up and pay before you've had a chance to check.
"No deal is worth rushing for. So take a moment before you buy."
The bank also advises doing these four things:
- Pause and check, rather than being blinded by a countdown timer
- Pay safely using a credit or debit card via a trusted payment service, not a bank transfer to a stranger
- Open an official website or app yourself rather than clicking on links in emails, ads or social posts
- Talk to a friend, family or your bank if you think something does not feel right, and calling your bank straight away if you think you've been scammed
