items.title: Give shop workers the protection they need from high street thugs as festive rush gets underway, say retail chiefs
items.summary: Each of the three million people working in the retail sector have a 'story' relating to theft, abuse or violent crime, where 'an ordinary shift can turn into a nightmare', retail chiefs said.
items.body:
Give shop workers the protection they need from high street thugs as festive rush gets underway, say retail chiefs
Shop workers must be given the protection they need from High Street thugs as the festive rush gets underway, retail chiefs and unions say.
In a joint plea, they are warning Labour that workers’ safety must not ‘be the cost of Government inaction’ as retailers see over 118 violent incidents a day.
‘With Black Friday and Christmas on the horizon, retail workers will be working harder than ever. They deserve to know that the law, and we as customers, are firmly on their side,’ they argue.
Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium (BRC), a trade body, is among those behind the plea in an op-ed published by This is Money.
The Government’s Crime and Policing Act, which includes new protections aimed at discouraging criminals from shoplifting and abusing shop workers, was passed in April - but has not yet been put into action.
The new laws make assaulting a retail worker a standalone offence and remove a threshold which meant that thieves felt they could get away with stealing goods worth £200 or less.
Shocking figures: Retail staff are subject to around 1,600 incidents of violence or abuse a day.
Retailers want to see an official commencement date given for this law so it can be put into practice.
Dickinson, together with Chris Brook-Carter, chief executive of workers’ support charity Retail Trust, Joanne Thomas, general-secretary of shopworkers’ union Usdaw, and Ed Woodall, chief executive of the Association of Convenience Stores, are urging the government to do so.
‘Every day of Government delay is another day of retail workers being asked to work without the protections Parliament agreed they should have. Their safety cannot be the cost of Government inaction.
‘Ministers must now seize the moment to announce a commencement date for these overdue protections, and send a clear message to millions of retail workers: safety at work is not an aspiration. It is a basic expectation, backed by law, and enforced by police.’
Each of the three million people working in the retail sector have a ‘story’ relating to theft, abuse or violent crime, where ‘an ordinary shift can turn into a nightmare’, they said.
Shop workers are subject to around 1,600 incidents of violence or abuse a day, nearly four times pre-pandemic levels, according to the BRC.
As Black Friday and Christmas approach, the busiest time of year for shops, it is ‘critical’ to draw attention to the scale of crime facing workers, the letter continued.
The op-ed was cosigned by Dickinson, as well as Chris Brook-Carter, chief executive of Retail Trust, Joanne Thomas, general-secretary of shopworkers' union Usdaw, and Ed Woodall, chief executive of Association of Convenience Stores.
They added: ‘Ministers must now seize the moment to announce a commencement date for these overdue protections, and send a clear message to millions of retail workers: safety at work is not an aspiration. It is a basic expectation, backed by law, and enforced by police.’
Time to unleash full police powers to tackle retail crime once and for all
Helen Dickinson, Chief Executive, BRC
Chris Brook-Carter, Chief Executive, Retail Trust
Joanne Thomas, General-Secretary, Usdaw
Ed Woodall, Chief Executive, Association of Convenience Stores
Speak to anyone in retail and one thing becomes clear: everyone has a story.
For too many of the three million people working in the industry, fear has become part of the working day. From teenagers in their first job to parents juggling childcare with part-time work, all retail workers have seen how an ordinary shift can turn into a nightmare: abuse shouted across a checkout, gangs swarming aisles to steal, and threats from armed criminals.
An incident may be over in a moment. But its impact can last far longer, leaving people shaken and anxious. Those experiences follow them home, affecting friends and families.
Everyday retail workers endure around 1,600 incidents of violence or abuse, nearly four times pre-pandemic levels. Behind every incident is a person who went to work expecting to do their job, not fearing for their safety.
Most troubling is where it turns violent. Within those 1,600 daily incidents, 118 involve physical violence and 36 involve a weapon, typically a knife.
This behaviour is unacceptable. Our high streets are centres of our communities and a source of local pride. They should be places we feel safe. This is why urgent action is needed.
There has been important progress. Retail organisations have collaborated closely with police forces nationwide, through initiatives such as Project Pegasus and the Retail Crime Action Plan, to improve intelligence-sharing and crack down on repeat offending.
We welcomed the passage of the Government’s Crime and Policing Act in April. After years of campaigning, it created a standalone offence for assaulting a retail worker and removed the outdated £200 threshold for low-level theft. These interventions sent an important message that all crime will be taken seriously, and violence against retail workers will be met with a harsh response.
Yet, half a year after becoming law, the Government still haven’t put these changes into practice.
A law designed to protect retail workers cannot protect them until an official commencement date is given. Every day of Government delay is another day of retail workers being asked to work without the protections Parliament agreed they should have.
Their safety cannot be the cost of Government inaction.
We recently marked a nationwide week of coordinated action against retail crime and abuse. Campaigns led by the Retail Trust, ACS, NBCC and Usdaw, supported by the BRC, and involving retail business across the country are championing respect for retail workers and to forge safer, more resilient high streets. And tackling this issue isn't just about catching offenders but making sure all of us treat retail workers with respect.
Putting a spotlight on this issue is critical as we enter the busiest and most important quarter of the year. With Black Friday and Christmas on the horizon, retail workers will be working harder than ever. They deserve to know that the law, and we as customers, are firmly on their side.
Ministers must now seize the moment to announce a commencement date for these overdue protections, and send a clear message to millions of retail workers: safety at work is not an aspiration. It is a basic expectation, backed by law, and enforced by police.
We all want to ensure our high streets thrive; the first step is to make them safe and protect the people that work there.

items.title: Uniqlo’s UK expansion: how the Japanese fashion giant is building a nationwide presence
items.summary: Uniqlo is stepping up its UK expansion, with its first store in Wales scheduled for autumn 2027, the Japanese fashion retailer is looking to take its LifeWear proposition to more shoppers across the country. The retailer will open a two-floor store spanning approximately 940 sq m at Cardiff’s St David’s shopping centre. It will stock...
items.body:
Uniqlo is stepping up its UK expansion, with its first store in Wales scheduled for autumn 2027, the Japanese fashion retailer is looking to take its LifeWear proposition to more shoppers across the country.
The retailer will open a two-floor store spanning approximately 940 sq m at Cardiff’s St David’s shopping centre. It will stock womenswear, menswear, childrenswear and baby clothing, marking another milestone in the brand’s UK growth.
Cardiff is one of five new locations planned for 2027, alongside Bath, Brighton, Leeds and Canary Wharf in London. The openings will take Uniqlo into new regional markets while strengthening its presence in established retail destinations.
The expansion follows a period of accelerated investment in the UK, with the retailer opening its first stores in Bristol and Cambridge in 2026, alongside a second Manchester location at the Trafford Centre.
Having arrived in the UK 25 years ago, Uniqlo currently operates 26 stores across the UK, according to parent company Fast Retailing, as of 31 October 2026.
From London launch to nationwide ambitions
Uniqlo used the UK capital as it launchpad with four locations in and around London marking its debut outside Japan.
However, its initial expansion proved overly ambitious. The retailer rapidly grew its UK estate to 21 stores within two years, before withdrawing from most locations in 2003 following mounting losses.
The business subsequently adopted a more measured approach, rebuilding its presence around larger stores and a stronger brand proposition.
London remained central to its strategy, with the opening of its global flagship on Oxford Street in 2007 establishing a platform for the brand.
Since then, Uniqlo has gradually expanded beyond the capital, entering major regional cities including Manchester, Edinburgh, Liverpool, Glasgow and Birmingham.
Its latest investment signals a further shift towards regional growth.
In April 2026, the retailer opened its first South West store at Bristol’s Cabot Circus, spanning two floors and offering its LifeWear collections across womenswear, menswear and childrenswear.
This was followed by its Cambridge debut in September, with a 9,472 sq ft store at Grand Arcade.
October saw another major opening at Manchester’s Trafford Centre. At approximately 24,000 sq ft, the store is significantly larger than its existing Market Street location, making Manchester the first UK city outside London to have two Uniqlo stores.
The expansion is not limited to opening new locations. Uniqlo also reopened its enlarged Covent Garden store earlier in 2026, increasing its footprint by 30 per cent to approximately 18,300 sq ft.
The investment demonstrates the retailer’s willingness to commit to larger retail spaces, as it looks to showcase more of its product range and improve the customer experience.
Why regional cities matter
Uniqlo’s next phase of expansion will take it into several markets where it has previously relied on online sales to reach customers.
The planned Cardiff opening is “another important step in Uniqlo’s UK expansion”, according to chief operating officer Alessandro Dudech.
He stressed the retailer had already established a base of Welsh customers shopping online. The retailer believes its presence at St David’s will make its offering more accessible to customers across Wales, while giving shoppers the opportunity to experience its products in person.
There is a similar rationale behind its planned openings in Bath, Brighton and Leeds.
Each represents an opportunity to establish the brand in a new regional market, rather than simply adding further stores to its existing London-heavy estate.
Dudech has previously described the locations selected for expansion as vibrant retail destinations with strong local communities and long-term growth potential.
Speaking to Retail Gazette following the opening of its 25th UK store in Cambridge, he said: “Our ambition is to make LifeWear more accessible to customers across the UK by investing in both major cities and thriving regional locations, bringing the Uniqlo experience closer to where people live, work and shop.”
The approach also reflects the importance of physical retail in building awareness of a brand whose proposition centres on everyday wardrobe essentials rather than seasonal fashion trends.
The LifeWear proposition
At the heart of Uniqlo’s growth strategy is LifeWear, its philosophy of creating high-quality, functional clothing designed to improve everyday life.
Rather than competing solely on seasonal trends, the retailer focuses on versatile wardrobe staples, with an emphasis on fabric innovation, practicality and affordability.
Its collections include products such as HEATTECH thermal clothing, AIRism garments and lightweight outerwear, alongside everyday basics including T-shirts, knitwear and denim.
This positioning gives Uniqlo a distinctive place in the UK fashion market, sitting between traditional value retailers and more premium casualwear brands.
Its offer also allows it to appeal to a broad customer base, spanning different generations and demographics.
The retailer has increasingly used its physical stores to communicate this proposition, combining product displays with services and experiences that encourage shoppers to spend time in-store.
Its Cambridge opening, for example, included collaborations with the University of Cambridge and local illustrator Lele Saa, with exclusive designs celebrating the city’s identity.
Dudech said stores were about “much more than retail space”, describing them as places where the business could connect directly with customers and contribute to local communities.
This emphasis on local relevance is likely to become increasingly important as Uniqlo enters new UK markets.
International growth provides further momentum
The UK expansion is taking place against a backdrop of strong international performance for Uniqlo’s parent company, Fast Retailing.
For the year ended 31 August 2026, the Japanese group reported revenue of ¥3.96trn (£18.7bn), up 16.6 per cent year on year, while business profit increased 30.4 per cent to ¥718.4bn.
Uniqlo International was a major contributor, reporting revenue growth of 26.2 per cent to ¥2.41trn and business profit growth of 44.1 per cent.
The group attributed its performance partly to opening high-quality stores that effectively communicate the value of LifeWear, alongside closer coordination between products, store displays and customer communications.
Europe has become an increasingly important part of this international growth story, with Fast Retailing reporting double-digit revenue and profit growth across the region.
The company’s wider ambitions are substantial. Founder and chief executive Tadashi Yanai has set out an ambition to grow Fast Retailing into a ¥10trn business, placing further importance on international markets.
Therefore, expanding its physical presence in the UK provides an opportunity to build brand recognition, attract new customers and strengthen the relationship between its online and store operations.
What next for Uniqlo in the UK?
With 26 stores already operating and five further openings planned for 2027, Uniqlo is entering a new phase of its UK growth strategy.
Its expansion into Cardiff, Bath, Brighton and Leeds will extend its geographical reach, while the Canary Wharf opening will strengthen its London presence.
The challenge will be ensuring that each new store delivers sustainable performance in an increasingly competitive fashion market.
Its earlier UK experience offers a reminder that rapid expansion does not necessarily translate into long-term success. The retailer’s more considered approach in recent years, prioritising established shopping destinations and larger-format stores, suggests it is keen to avoid repeating those mistakes.
For now, the focus is on making LifeWear accessible to more UK consumers. As Dudech has made clear, reaching 25 stores is not a finishing line but another step in the retailer’s longer-term growth journey.
With more regional markets still to explore, Uniqlo’s UK expansion looks far from over.

items.title: Big change on the horizon | Viewpoint: Ed Woodall
items.summary: The end of 2026 has seen some significant shifts in regulation when it comes to the tobacco, vape and nicotine category. New rules on giving away vaping products and introducing an age restriction on zero-nicotine vapes shouldn’t affect many convenience retailers, who typically will already… This story continues at Big change on the horizon | Viewpoint: Ed Woodall Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
New rules on giving away vaping products and introducing an age restriction on zero-nicotine vapes shouldn’t affect many convenience retailers, who typically will already have those age restrictions in place to avoid any confusion.
But the introduction of vape duty stamps and the vaping duty itself will affect everyone when only compliant stock is mandatory in the spring. Our hope for these changes is that it will make it easier to identify illicit product (and those selling illicit product), and that the revenue raised from the duty can be used to fund enforcement and back responsible retailers who follow the law.
We are also now just weeks away from a major change in the way age-restricted sales will work for tobacco products. On 1 January 2027, the generational ban will come into force, meaning anyone born on or after 1 January 2009 will never be able to legally purchase tobacco.
What this means for retailers and colleagues in practice is that there will now be a single date of birth beyond which tobacco sales are illegal, as well as the long-established 18-plus check for many other age-restricted products.
While this might seem complicated, we’ve been working with trading standards, the Department of Health and lots of retailers across the country on a campaign to simplify the rules as much as possible. The Decline09 campaign has a very straightforward message – if the customer is born in 2009 or afterwards, you must decline the sale of tobacco.
There are lots of resources that we’ve made available as part of the campaign, including new A3 mandatory tobacco notices that every store that sells tobacco needs to replace on 1 January. Please check these out and use them to support your colleagues in getting to grips with the change.
Ed Woodall is chief executive at the Association of Convenience Stores (ACS)

items.summary: Tesco is expanding its support for parents and carers of premature babies by making free Pampers Preemie Protection nappies available from an additional 150 Tesco Express stores close to neonatal…
items.body:
Tesco widens access to free Pampers premature baby nappies to support families
Tesco is expanding its support for parents and carers of premature babies by making free Pampers Preemie Protection nappies available from an additional 150 Tesco Express stores close to neonatal units around the country.
The partnership between Tesco and Pampers was launched last year, with Pampers donating its Pampers Preemie Protection nappies, and Tesco making them accessible to families at over 350 Tesco Pharmacies.
Since then, over 200,000 premature baby nappies have been given out through Tesco Pharmacies, helping families at what can be a difficult and worrying time. This activity forms part of Pampers’ commitment to supporting families of premature babies, and to date, more than 4 million premature baby nappies have been donated in the UK since 2017.
The nappies are currently available through Tesco Pharmacies across England, Scotland and Wales, but Tesco will now be bringing the service even closer to families with premature babies, by expanding the offering to nearly 150 Tesco Express stores near neonatal units, giving parents and carers another convenient way to access the specialist nappies when and where they might need them, from a local store.

“Having a premature baby can be an overwhelming experience, and we know how much of a difference practical support and a little help can make for parents and carers. That’s why we’re making these nappies in the smallest sizes even easier to access, by bringing them to nearly 150 Tesco Express stores for the first time, supporting families when and where they may need it most.”

items.title: Waitrose set to axe thousands of products in major range overhaul
items.summary: Waitrose is considering axing thousands of products from its shelves as part of a major overhaul aimed at simplifying its range and repositioning as the ‘home of food lovers’. The…
items.body:
Waitrose set to axe thousands of products in major range overhaul
Waitrose is considering axing thousands of products from its shelves as part of a major overhaul aimed at simplifying its range and repositioning as the ‘home of food lovers’.
The upmarket grocer, which stocks more than 15,000 products in its larger stores, is reviewing underperforming and duplicate lines to make shopping easier for customers while creating space for new brands.
The decision follows a presentation to suppliers earlier this year, which revealed that a quarter of Waitrose’s products accounted for less than three per cent of total sales.
One supplier suggested that the number of brands stocked in some categories could be reduced by as much as half within months, while another said the supermarket was looking to concentrate greater sales volumes across fewer product lines.
However, Waitrose insisted the review would not necessarily mean reducing its specialist offering, which has traditionally helped differentiate it from rivals Tesco and Sainsbury’s.
Instead, it plans to use customer loyalty and sales data to identify which products to retain, while continuing to introduce new and exclusive ranges.
The company has added around 100 brands over the past year, including its recently launched seafood collaboration with celebrity chef Rick Stein.
A Waitrose spokesperson said the business was growing sales and customer numbers, with further opportunities to build on that momentum through its ‘home of food lovers’ strategy.
Waitrose said its focus was on offering a more distinctive range that combined familiar favourites with new products, while maintaining its commitment to quality.
The proposed shake-up forms part of the John Lewis Partnership’s wider £1bn investment programme, led by chairman Jason Tarry, which includes store refurbishments, new openings and improvements to its online operations.
Waitrose opened its first new full-line supermarket in eight years in Cricklewood, north London, last month, followed by a 15,000 sq ft store in Hale Barns, Greater Manchester, last week.
It is also carrying out 29 store refurbishments this year, with upgrades focused on fresh food counters, bakeries and an improved in-store shopping experience.
The overhaul comes as Waitrose continues to gain market share, with sales rising 2.2 per cent in the 12 weeks to 1 November, according to Worldpanel by Numerator.
Its share of the UK grocery market increased from 4.4 per cent to 4.5 per cent over the period, making it one of only three major grocers to gain share alongside Lidl and Ocado.

items.title: Lidl crowned UK’s top berry retailer for second consecutive year
items.summary: Lidl has been named Overall Berry Retailer of the Year for the second year running, securing three awards as sales of British berries across UK retailers climbed by more than…
items.body:
Lidl crowned UK’s top berry retailer for second consecutive year
Lidl has been named Overall Berry Retailer of the Year for the second year running, securing three awards as sales of British berries across UK retailers climbed by more than ten per cent in 2026.
It took home the top prize at the British Berry Growers annual retailer awards, alongside Blackberry Retailer of the Year and Blueberry Retailer of the Year, recognising its strong growth in British berry sales.
Co-op was named Strawberry Retailer of the Year, while Tesco secured Raspberry Retailer of the Year.
Meanwhile, Ocado received the Special Recognition Award for the second consecutive year, recognising its significant year-on-year growth in British berry sales.
The awards, announced at the British Berry Growers Retailer Conference on 12 November, recognise supermarkets achieving the strongest percentage growth in sales volumes of British-grown strawberries, raspberries, blackberries and blueberries.
The overall award is based on combined growth across all four berry categories, using sales tonnage data reported by British Berry Growers members.
British Berry Growers executive chair Nick Marston said: “Congratulations to Lidl on winning three awards, and to Co-op, Tesco and Ocado for their achievements.
“The awards and honourable mentions recognise strong performances in growing sales of British berries.”
He added: “Retail partners play an important role in supporting British growers and bringing their berries to consumers. These awards celebrate that contribution and encourage continued support for British fruit.”
Lidl also received honourable mentions in the strawberry and raspberry categories, while Co-op was recognised for its overall performance and blackberry sales growth. Morrisons received an honourable mention for blueberries.
The awards come as British berry sales continue to gain momentum, with total sales across retailers rising by more than 10 per cent this year.
The British berry industry contributes more than £2bn to the UK economy, with British Berry Growers members supplying over 95 per cent of the berries sold in UK supermarkets.
The trade body also supports research and consumer campaigns aimed at promoting British-grown fruit and strengthening the sector’s long-term growth.

items.title: Jeremy Clarkson’s Hawkstone Brewery invests in solar power to cut energy costs
items.summary: Jeremy Clarkson’s Hawkstone Brewery is set to install its first solar power system as the company hopes to reduce energy costs and improve its sustainability. The brewer, founded by the…
items.body:
Jeremy Clarkson’s Hawkstone Brewery invests in solar power to cut energy costs
Jeremy Clarkson’s Hawkstone Brewery is set to install its first solar power system as the company hopes to reduce energy costs and improve its sustainability.
The brewer, founded by the broadcaster and farmer in 2021, has appointed Nottinghamshire-based renewable energy specialist Geo Green Power to install rooftop solar panels at its production facility in Bourton-on-the-Water, Gloucestershire.
Work is expected to begin this month, with the system set to generate 24.25MWh of electricity annually and reduce the brewery’s carbon emissions by an estimated 4.9 tonnes each year.
The installation will help power energy-intensive brewing processes, including milling, heating and cooling, while reducing the business’s reliance on grid electricity.
Hawkstone said the investment would also provide greater protection against rising energy prices, which have continued to put pressure on businesses across the food and drink sector.
Hawkstone Brewery head brewer Ben Bonham said: “We’re always looking for ways to improve how we operate, and investing in solar energy is a natural next step for us.
“Brewing is an energy-intensive process, so generating our own renewable electricity will help us reduce our environmental impact while making the brewery more efficient and resilient.”
The rooftop installation will use Canadian Solar panels alongside SolarEdge inverters and optimisers, with Geo Green Power overseeing installation and ongoing maintenance.
Geo Green Power managing director James Cunningham said the project reflected the company’s experience supporting businesses in the hospitality and agricultural sectors.
“We’re incredibly excited to get started on this fantastic project and with our extensive solar experience within the hospitality industry, we know what a great opportunity this is for Hawkstone Brewery,” he said.
Cunningham added that the partnership was particularly fitting given both companies’ connections to British farming.

items.title: Ray-Ban to open landmark Oxford Street flagship in historic tube station building
items.summary: Ray-Ban is set to open a new flagship store on Oxford Street next summer, taking over part of the Grade II-listed Oxford Circus Underground station building. The 2,000 sq ft store, located at 241-243 Oxford Street on the corner of Argyll Street, will bring together two existing ground-floor retail units and a mezzanine level currently...
items.body:
Ray-Ban is set to open a new flagship store on Oxford Street next summer, taking over part of the Grade II-listed Oxford Circus Underground station building.
The 2,000 sq ft store, located at 241-243 Oxford Street on the corner of Argyll Street, will bring together two existing ground-floor retail units and a mezzanine level currently used as office space.
The opening, targeted for summer 2027, will make Ray-Ban one of the first retailers to launch a new flagship on the recently pedestrianised section of the shopping street.
The new store will combine the building’s historic architecture with a contemporary retail experience, including dedicated consultation spaces and an eye test room to support the brand’s prescription eyewear offering.
Built in 1906 and designed by architect Leslie Green, the former station building is known for its distinctive oxblood-red tiled façade, which closely resembles Ray-Ban’s signature branding.
The retailer is working with Transport for London’s property company, Places for London, to restore and repurpose the historic site.
EssilorLuxottica managing director for retail UK and Nordics, Southeast Asia and Southern Africa Andre Kitshoff said: “As we approach Ray-Ban’s 90th anniversary, there is no better place to invest in our future than Oxford Street.
“This landmark flagship will celebrate our heritage while showcasing the next chapter of the brand in one of the world’s most iconic retail destinations.”
He added that transforming the historic building into an immersive retail destination made the project particularly special.
Places for London senior asset manager Andrew Foulds said the property company had received multiple proposals for the site, but Ray-Ban’s plans stood out.
He said the development presented an opportunity to create a flagship retail destination while restoring and showcasing one of London’s historic buildings.
Oxford Street is undergoing a major transformation, with almost a kilometre of the shopping destination becoming traffic-free on 26 October.
The pedestrianisation scheme, spearheaded by the Mayor of London, is aimed at revitalising the West End shopping destination, with further public realm improvements planned for 2027.
Four & Co acted on behalf of Ray-Ban in securing the site, while Cushman & Wakefield represented Places for London.

items.title: TFG London launches new Fivefold fashion concept with new store
items.summary: TFG London has unveiled its new multi-brand fashion concept, Fivefold, opening its first store in Inverness. The store, which opened at Eastgate Shopping Centre on 12 November, brings together Hobbs, Whistles, Phase Eight and Karen Millen under one roof, offering shoppers a mix of contemporary fashion, everyday clothing and occasionwear. The launch is the first...
items.body:
TFG London has unveiled its new multi-brand fashion concept, Fivefold, opening its first store in Inverness.
The store, which opened at Eastgate Shopping Centre on 12 November, brings together Hobbs, Whistles, Phase Eight and Karen Millen under one roof, offering shoppers a mix of contemporary fashion, everyday clothing and occasionwear.
The launch is the first store to operate under the Fivefold name, with a second location set to open at Bournemouth’s Castlepoint shopping centre later this month.
The new concept builds on TFG London’s existing boutique department store format, which has already been rolled out at Fosse Park, Aberdeen and Liverpool One.
The group opened its largest UK store at Liverpool One last year, building on its strategy of combining multiple brands in larger retail destinations rather than relying solely on standalone stores.
Fivefold aims to offer customers a more personalised shopping experience, with a focus on curated collections, expert styling advice and enhanced fitting rooms.
TFG London group retail director Caraline Money said: “Fashion should be one of life’s pleasures, and that’s the idea behind Fivefold.”
She added: “We’ve already seen how much customers value being able to shop these brands together in one destination, and our opening in Inverness Eastgate is an exciting next step.”
The Inverness opening also marks the revival of a prominent retail unit that has stood empty for five years following the closure of Topshop.
Situated on the upper level of Eastgate Shopping Centre, next to H&M, the space has undergone a transformation to accommodate the new premium fashion destination.
Eastgate Shopping Centre manager Jon Carter said securing the first Fivefold store was an important milestone for Inverness and would strengthen the centre’s fashion offering.
TFG London is continuing to reshape its retail estate amid challenging trading conditions.
The South African-owned group’s London division reported a 29.4 per cent increase in retail turnover to £488m for the financial year ended March 2026, largely driven by its acquisition of White Stuff in October 2024.
However, sales across its existing brands remained flat when the contribution from White Stuff was excluded, highlighting the challenging environment facing premium fashion retailers.
TFG London has continued investing in larger, multi-brand destinations as part of its efforts to strengthen its physical retail offering and give shoppers access to a broader range of its labels.
Its next Fivefold opening in Bournemouth will mark a further step in the rollout of the concept as the retailer seeks to build on its established multi-brand shopping model.

items.title: Inside Poundland’s £21m Christmas restock as it races to secure rescue deal
items.summary: Poundland has launched a major Christmas restocking operation after its owner Gordon Brothers released £21m in emergency funding. The company is rushing more than 16 million grocery items into around 600 stores across the UK and Ireland in a five-day replenishment drive ahead of the festive trading period. Reportedly dubbed ‘Operation Gloria‘ by Poundland staff,...
items.body:
Poundland has launched a major Christmas restocking operation after its owner Gordon Brothers released £21m in emergency funding.
The company is rushing more than 16 million grocery items into around 600 stores across the UK and Ireland in a five-day replenishment drive ahead of the festive trading period.
Reportedly dubbed ‘Operation Gloria‘ by Poundland staff, in a nod to Gloria Gaynor’s hit I Will Survive, the initiative has seen more than 50 suppliers resume deliveries to the retailer’s distribution centres in Makerfield, near Wigan, and Harlow in Essex.
Products including Yorkshire Tea and Pot Noodles have been pictured making their way from warehouses to stores, alongside crisps, confectionery, health and beauty products and household essentials such as kitchen towels and tin foil.
The emergency operation follows Gordon Brothers’ decision to unlock £21m from a £50m funding pot, providing much-needed breathing space for the retailer as it continues negotiations with prospective buyers.
Poundland had reportedly been unable to pay suppliers for new stock since late October, leaving stores increasingly reliant on existing inventory and raising concerns about its ability to trade through Christmas.
However, Poundland insisted its general merchandise and clothing ranges were already well stocked for the festive season, with the latest deliveries focused on replenishing grocery aisles.
In a statement, Poundland said: “Despite the current circumstances, Poundland continues to trade strongly.”
It added that stores remained open as usual and thanked suppliers, colleagues and customers for their continued support.
The £21m funding release also comes as the retailer faces a critical deadline to secure its survival.
Poundland, which employs around 12,000 people, has until 26 November to find a buyer after securing an extension of its legal protection from creditors.
The chain is understood to be in discussions with three potential buyers, with Northern Ireland-based Martin Property Group emerging as the preferred bidder.
However, talks have reportedly stalled over the repayment terms of a loan provided by Gordon Brothers, while other retailers, including Tesco, are understood to be interested in acquiring parts of Poundland’s store estate.
Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland from Pepco Group for a nominal £1 last year, has faced growing criticism from MPs over its handling of the business.
The investment firm has denied allegations that it has improperly withheld funds, pointing to the financial support it has provided to the retailer.
It confirmed that funding would be made available to cover November’s payroll, alongside further support to maintain trading.
Business secretary Jonathan Reynolds is expected to hold further discussions with Poundland and its owner ahead of the rescue deadline.
For now, Poundland’s focus remains on getting products back onto shelves, maintaining supplier relationships and protecting Christmas trading while efforts continue to secure a buyer.

items.title: British activewear brand Sweaty Betty boosts Insiders loyalty programme with Antavo AI platform
items.summary: Antavo has partnered with Sweaty Betty to revamp its Insiders programme. Powered by the former's AI driven loyalty platform, the omnichannel offering is live in the UK, with Ireland planned for the next phase.Members earn five points for every £1 spent, whether they shop online, through the app, or
items.body:
Antavo has partnered with Sweaty Betty to revamp its Insiders programme. Powered by the former's AI driven loyalty platform, the omnichannel offering is live in the UK, with Ireland planned for the next phase.
Members earn five points for every £1 spent, whether they shop online, through the app, or in a Sweaty Betty store. They also collect bonus points for joining the programme, downloading the Sweaty Betty app, and following the brand on Instagram and TikTok, with more point earning opportunities coming in the future. Points unlock three tiers: Betty Mover to begin with, Betty Shaker at 1,200 points, and Betty Legend Maker at 2,500 points.
The revamped programme is built around repeat visits. Members earn bonus points for their second purchase and for their first purchase in a store. Milestone rewards add a further pull, with £10 off at the 5th purchase and £20 off at the 10th. The aim here is to shorten time to second purchase, lift purchase frequency and store footfall, and grow CLV and community engagement.
Melissa Mullen, Sweaty Betty President, says :“Our customers have always been at the heart of Sweaty Betty, and our Insiders programme gives us a more meaningful way to celebrate them, whether they shop with us online, in-app, or visit our stores. We’re excited to reward every purchase and every moment of engagement, and we look forward to growing the programme with Antavo as we bring Insiders to even more of our community.”
Insiders is woven into Sweaty Betty’s wider tech stack. mParticle acts as the central customer data platform, sharing member identity and engagement events with Antavo and passing loyalty events on to Braze for tier and programme messaging.
Salesforce Commerce Cloud powers the online experience, NewStore POS brings the programme into Sweaty Betty’s stores, and purchase and return data, down to individual items, flows in through MuleSoft and Antavo’s API.
Attila Kecsmar, CEO & Co-Founder, Antavo AI Loyalty Cloud, says: “For more than 25 years, Sweaty Betty has built a community of women who move with confidence, and the revamped Insiders program gives that community even more reasons to keep coming back. With our flexible, AI powered platform, Sweaty Betty can recognise every purchase and interaction across every channel. We’re proud to support such an iconic British brand and can’t wait to see the programme thrive.”

items.body:
Sergey Nivens - Fotolia
Government science advisers: ‘No framework for datacentre demand’
Government science advisers, chaired by Angela McLean, say the UK has no framework to size onshore datacentre demand – grid delays are a key siting obstacle
The UK has no agreed method for working out how much onshore datacentre capacity it needs, and delays in securing grid connections are a key factor in where new sites go.
That’s according to the Government Office for Science, which published a report of a meeting chaired by chief scientific adviser Angela McLean in February. The report represents “the combined views of roundtable participants” and is explicitly “not a statement of government policy” but does provide useful insight into the datacentre debate at national planning level.
According to the report, the group found “no obvious frameworks to determine how much onshore datacentre capacity the UK will need in the future”, and said demand was “very hard to estimate”. Sizing decisions should start from what UK capacity is essential – where offshore provision is not an option, it said – and from tasks datacentres perform across the economy, rather than from sector-by-sector demand.
“Water is not a major constraint on datacentre siting in the UK,” it said. The notes state that datacentres can be cooled without water using closed-loop systems and ventilation, given the UK’s climate, and that Amazon Web Services’ facilities reportedly run waterless for around 97% of the year. It notes the trade-off is power, and using less water means using more electricity.
The roundtable recommended the UK build a national interactive map of every datacentre, plotting sites alongside fibre routes, power lines and other infrastructure. The aim is to give developers, planners and communities a shared picture of where capacity sits, from hyperscale campuses down to small edge sites.
The notes draw a line between workloads that need to stay in the UK and those that do not. Regulated public services and industries under data protection rules such as GDPR generally require onshore sites, it said, and there are “strong arguments” for onshore capacity to serve national security and defence. Ultra-low-latency tasks – high-frequency trading and growing financial artificial intelligence (AI) use among them – also tie capacity to specific locations.
Much of the rest can go elsewhere, says the report. The notes say many workloads tolerate some latency or are not sensitive to data location, so they can use offshore facilities or, in future, centralised mega datacentres. They cite Ukraine’s experience of hostile actors as a reason to favour offshore or distributed capacity for resilience.
Grid connections are cited as a pinch point. The notes say delays in establishing a grid connection are a key factor in siting and “risk undermining the UK’s digital growth objectives”. They float removing the government requirement for new power generation to be connected to the grid as a way to cut delays and improve national resilience.
Planning is another gap identified. There is currently no national planning guidance for datacentre siting, and the notes point to strategies in the Netherlands and Saudi Arabia as references. They argue clearer guidance would give developers and communities more certainty, and that public acceptance depends on people seeing a national need, clear local benefits and developers they trust.
The timing coincides with lively debate decisions on planning, grid connections and datacentre location.
The debate nationally lacks reliable figures. Computer Weekly analysis published this week has highlighted the dearth of reliable data around datacentre planning, in particular with regard to electricity draw, water use, and even the numbers of datacentres in existence and in the pipeline.
Computer Weekly has spent several months attempting to build reliable estimates. It has drawn on the Barbour ABI construction database and Energy Performance Certificate registers and found 88 verified existing UK datacentre sites with a combined capacity of about 1.6GW, against a committed pipeline of 173 schemes and about 14.6GW. The recommendation for a national map echoes that work. The numbers are contested because no shared, verified inventory exists.
Demand uncertainty runs through the meeting notes. The roundtable said future capacity would be variable and geographic, would depend on balance between small firms and large consumers, and would hinge on the pace of AI adoption – which itself depends on domestic datacentre capacity. It acknowledged that over-provisioning may be necessary to absorb that uncertainty, and that AI and non-AI services are already blurring as cloud sites evolve into combined general and AI facilities.
It acknowledged that workloads differ sharply. Training AI models is generally less latency-sensitive than running them, and for some large language models, demand has shifted from training to inference, which the notes say carries a significantly greater environmental impact at scale. Image processing for agriculture and transport is among the fastest-growing uses and typically needs localised capacity because of the volume of data involved.
Nine people took part in the roundtable. Alongside Angela McLean, the roundtable included Clive Richardson (Amazon Web Services), Dawn Childs (Pure Data Centres Group), Dimitra Simeonidou (University of Bristol), Eve Schooler (University of Oxford), John Booth (BCS, The Chartered Institute for IT), Luisa Cardani (TechUK), Patrick Devine-Wright (Exeter University) and Tim Watson (Loughborough University).
No grid or energy system operator sat at the table, and no water or planning regulator, even though grid delays and planning are two of the report’s central themes. The notes also carry the caution that they are advice, not a decision. The government has not committed to the map, to planning guidance or to changing grid connection rules.
The eight-month gap between meeting and publication points to a slow clearance loop in a fast-moving area. In that time, the UK pressed ahead with AI growth zones and datacentre planning decisions against capacity and demand figures that, by the advisers’ own account, nobody has a framework to test.
Waste heat and climate add further constraints. The notes say reuse needs datacentres sited near infrastructure that can use the heat, and that opportunities are limited without district heat networks and when sites sit on former industrial or greenfield land. Possible use cases include laundry, food preparation and greenhouses. Siting must also adapt to flooding, temperature and water availability.
Read more about datacentres

- Data dive – government 2030 datacentre capacity targets look shaky: We look at current and projected UK capacity and find the 2030 target for AI-capable capacity currently out of reach.

items.body:
Bill Quinn is starting a new position as Omnichannel Director-UK & EMEA at JD Sports Fashion.
He joins from Hibbett where he spent almost 11 years, most recently serving as Chief Information Officer. Quinn's CV also includes stints at 24 Hour Fitness and David's Bridal.
Zebra Technologies
Zebra Technologies says that it has helped JD Sports to achieve 98% on-shelf availability and 20% faster replenishment, so high demand sizes move from the storeroom to the shelf when and where customers want them.
JD Sports has nearly 5,000 stores across 46 countries. As the retailer scaled, inventory visibility in stores remained a challenge. To reliably offer one-hour Click & Collect or 30-minute delivery, the stock count needed to be accurate. It sought a real-time inventory visibility solution that could support omnichannel retail, was easy for retail assistants to use and fast to roll-out across stores.
A pilot across five stores highlighted the capabilities of Zebra’s TC2 Series mobile computers paired with RFD40 UHF RFID sleds to read tags faster and at greater range. JD Sports also selected Zebra OneCare which allows its store associates to address everyday wear and tear and accidental damage by simply swapping devices at no cost if something breaks.
Alongside Zebra, JD Sports worked with Renovotec, a Zebra partner who led the device deployment, and Checkpoint Systems, a Zebra eegistered ISV who integrated its ItemOptix software, giving a single view of inventory data across the retailer.
"What Zebra gives us is the ability to scale with trust,” says Daniel McGrath, Head of Customer Operations, JD Sports. “Things just land and work. Colleagues open a box, turn it on, and they are up and running. That lets our teams spend their time where it matters: with the customer.”
The first store went live in 76 days, with roll-out at 26 additional stores a week on average, reaching 414 locations across the UK and Ireland in roughly three months.
An associate clips a RFID sled onto the mobile computer they already use for daily tasks and walks the floor and stockroom, sweeping rails and shelves as the reader logs every tagged item in range and builds a live count on screen. In some cases, a whole store can be covered in a single pass.
Store associates now move 95% more inventory from the storeroom to shop floor and spend less time on stock counting. Stores can run this process from twice a week, or even daily, allowing them to keep shelves and the inventory management system in sync.
The same visibility is also helping JD Sports proactively tackle loss, as teams can identify and investigate issues much sooner. They can see where loss is happening rather than waiting for a 90- or 180-day audit.
“Retailers like JD Sports demonstrate the effectiveness of Zebra’s Modern Store framework, and the outcomes we and our partners deliver for both retailers and their shoppers,” says Mark Thomson, Retail Strategy Director EMEA, Zebra Technologies. “Together, we’re making work better every day for retailers and their frontline workers.”

items.title: DoorDash linked with Lyft acquisition deal as quick commerce firm aggressively builds commerce ecosystem
items.summary: DoorDash recently pulled off what is arguably the biggest retail technology acquisition of the year, snapping up Instacart for $17 billion.And it is already planning its next move, an acquisition of Lyft, according to Brittain Ladd, a supply chain consultant and former Amazon executive.In a LinkedIn
items.body:
DoorDash recently pulled off what is arguably the biggest retail technology acquisition of the year, snapping up Instacart for $17 billion.
And it is already planning its next move, an acquisition of Lyft, according to Brittain Ladd, a supply chain consultant and former Amazon executive.
In a LinkedIn post, in which he cited multiple unnamed sources, Ladd noted that discussions are at an early stage. He also observed that DoorDash and Lyft already have a partnership through Lyft Go and DashPass, connecting rides, delivery and membership benefits.
He commented: "DoorDash is aggressively building a commerce ecosystem. Deliveroo adds international delivery reach. SevenRooms adds reservations and guest relationships. Symbiosys adds advertising technology. Instacart will increase grocery, retail technology and merchant relationships. The missing piece is mobility. Uber already connects rides and delivery through one platform and one membership. Acquiring Lyft would give DoorDash a stronger foundation to compete across both."
There are various benefits here, according to Ladd, including more reasons to use DoorDash. "A ride to work. Groceries for the week. Dinner delivered home. Connecting these occasions creates more opportunities to serve the same customer and earn a larger share of everyday spending. This alone justifies acquiring Lyft."
A membership also becomes harder to cancel when customers use it for transportation, meals and groceries. Lyft Go with DashPass already provides a foundation. Ownership could support deeper coordination of benefits, rewards and customer experience.
DoorDash could also introduce delivery customers to Lyft, while Lyft introduces riders to DoorDash. "The opportunity is to generate incremental business through existing customer relationships rather than continually paying to acquire customers separately," Ladd said.
Eligible drivers also could access both passenger and delivery demand. That could expand earning opportunities and improve network productivity. The economics must be validated market by market; vehicle requirements, insurance and overlapping demand peaks matter.
But why acquire Lyft if a partnership already exists? "Because ownership could align customer strategy, technology investment and network operations under one economic model. A partnership connects benefits. Ownership could enable decisions about the entire platform: where to invest, how to allocate incentives and how to coordinate human driven and autonomous networks," Ladd said.
He concluded: "I believe there is a compelling case to pursue. DoorDash has expanded what it can deliver. Lyft would expand how it participates in everyday life. DoorDash can’t ignore what Walmart is doing related to food and grocery delivery. It will eventually offer ride hailing. Walmart’s partnership with Nash, is a strategic advantage. Amazon is a growing threat.
The acquisition will likely be announced in 2027, according to Ladd. If it does happen, it would be the first DoorDash deal aimed squarely at the dining room.
DoorDash did not respond to our request for comment.

items.body:
New Era has opened a flagship UK store on London's Oxford Street. This is its sixth location in the capital.
In a LinkedIn post, New Era's Natalie Defries said: "We're thrilled to announce that our new store at 386 Oxford Street, London W1C 1JT is now open, on the UK's busiest shopping street. Delivered in partnership with CM Delta, it marks another big step in our retail expansion across the region."
Across more than 117m² and three floors, the store offers: Ground floor: a curated selection of the brand's key silhouettes, plus a dedicated area for product exclusive to Oxford Street; Basement: a broader seasonal range of headwear and apparel, centred around a permanent customisation space offering embroidery and exclusive custom designed store patches; First floor: dedicated entirely to the 59FIFTY, in a bespoke environment with an additional customisation station
Shoppers will find the latest headwear, apparel and accessories, alongside collections from MLB, NBA, NFL, Oracle Red Bull Racing and Williams F1 Team.
Patrik Söderström, Vice President EMEA, commented: "Oxford Street is one of the world's most recognised retail destinations, making it the perfect location for New Era."

items.body:
Footstop has launched an AutoStore powered automated warehouse in Prague.
The retailer, which specialises in footwear and apparel, was founded in 2012 by Peter Hajduček. Revenue in 2025 reached almost CZK 1.9 billion, with over 80% of sales generated outside its country of birth, Czech Republic. It operates seven bricks and mortar stores in Prague (2x), Budapest, Bucharest, Bratislava, Warsaw and Paris, partners with brands such as adidas, Nike, New Balance, Asics and Vans, and develops its own brands FTSHP and Queens.
In a LinkedIn post, CEO Aleš Pitro said: "Somewhere in Paris, someone just ordered a pair of sneakers. Let me tell you what happens next. The order lands in our system in Prague. Within minutes, our automated warehouse finds the right size among hundreds of thousands of pairs, packs it and sends it on its way. Tomorrow it's at their door. Simple, right? It took us a long time to make it that simple."
He added: "More than 80% of what we sell goes outside the Czech Republic. In e-commerce, logistics isn't a back office function - it's an essential part of a successful business. This year we invested in a robotic warehouse and an automated packing line, and they are a big reason why we're now able to scale efficiently."
"Our Q3 results confirm how much of a change for the better this has been: revenue grew 20% and EBITDA 58% year-on-year, and we confirmed our full-year outlook. I like numbers, but I like this picture more: a Czech company delivering limited edition and exclusive sneakers all across Europe every single day, and getting better at it. A huge thank you to our warehouse and IT teams for their amazing work on this project."
