items.title: David Jones’ future looks grim. Is Myer next?
items.summary: With Myer’s profitability battered and share price languishing near all-time lows, DJs’ slide into administration raises an uncomfortable question Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast When the retailer’s doors slide open, shoppers are greeted by rows of slashed price tags, frantic discounting, and all the other hallmarks of a department store closing down. Except this isn’t David Jones, the embattled upmarket retailer that is shutting half its 38 stores . Continue reading...
items.body:
When the retailer’s doors slide open, shoppers are greeted by rows of slashed price tags, frantic discounting, and all the other hallmarks of a department store closing down.
Except this isn’t David Jones, the embattled upmarket retailer that is shutting half its 38 stores.
This is its longtime rival, Myer, where entire floors are seemingly permanently on sale.
With Myer’s profitability battered and share price languishing near all-time lows, DJs’ slide into administration raises an uncomfortable question: is Myer next?
‘Sustained erosion of relevance’
At first glance, Myer’s headline numbers seem to defy the retail gloom, with double-digit sales growth to $4.1bn last financial year.
That lift, however, was not driven by surging demand, but by adding sales from the newly acquired apparel chains, Just Jeans, Jay Jays, Portmans, Dotti and Jacqui E, bought from billionaire businessman Solomon Lew’s Premier Investments.
Meanwhile, to keep registers ringing, Myer employed “higher than planned promotional activity to stimulate demand”, according to its annual report, which reduced its profitability.
The department store has also slashed the value of its brands, down more than $200m in one year alone, in an admission that its labels are worth far less than they once were.
Department stores have faced a “sustained erosion of relevance over the past five years”, according to IBISWorld market researchers, as online platforms win over bargain-hunters and specialists like beauty retailer Mecca prove more nimble in capturing shifting tastes.
DJs and Myer, on the other hand, have been weighed down by long-running physical property leases tied to underperforming stores in their sprawling networks.
The era of Australian families being fiercely loyal to either David Jones or Myer is long gone, replaced by a grim battle for both chains to stay relevant.
The stress on big department store profitability has been exacerbated by a period of cost of living pressures that have “entrenched deal-hunting behaviour, reshaping how and when consumers engage with department stores”, according to IBISWorld.
Myer was contacted for comment.
Survival tactic or slow-motion bankruptcy
Myer, however, has a critical advantage over David Jones: time.
While DJs fell into administration under mounting debts, Myer finished last financial year with a $100m net cash buffer, buying management breathing space to fix the business.
It has been reducing store numbers and with it lease liabilities – down to 56 stores from 60 before the pandemic – which is something David Jones is only doing now that it has collapsed into administration.
For the moment, Myer is leaning into the discounts demanded by shoppers, in the hope that more profitable trading conditions will emerge.
Richard Hemming, the editor at Under The Radar Report, says in retail “volume is everything”.
“If you get the volumes through, that customer base will eventually be in a position to pay more, and when volumes and margins both improve, you get that double effect,” Hemming says.
While analysts have mixed views on whether permanent discounting is a smart survival tactic or a slow-motion way to go bankrupt, department stores do need to move huge volumes of stock to keep cash flowing and clear seasonal goods.
They can use those discounts to get more people signed up to their loyalty programs – such as the successful Myer One scheme – in the hope they will become long-term customers.
Hemming sees the upside in Myer’s current pain, noting the retailer is “cleaning house earlier than rivals” precisely because investors have long priced it “like it’s going to go broke”.
Myer is revamping the business to aggressively pursue online sales.
Advantage over old rival
Myer shares have been heavily sold down over the years, and now hover around the 24c mark, representing a fraction of its $4.10 float price from 2009.
It did, however, receive a price bump on the day DJs fell into administration.
With roughly two in five Myer stores sharing a shopping centre with a David Jones outlet, investors are betting the coming closure of 19 DJs sites will hand Myer an easy market-share boost, even as its own long-term turnaround demands further store cuts.
In the short term, the pain is likely to intensify for Myer as the David Jones stores marked for closure are under orders to clear stock with widespread promotions, luring customers.
Broader retail sentiment is also souring, as a string of interest rate rises and escalating cost-of-living pressures force cash-strapped shoppers to pare their discretionary spend.
The Retail Doctor Group’s chief executive, Brian Walker, says the main long-term advantage Myer has over its old rival is financial flexibility.
“Whereas David Jones was incredibly encumbered, Myer doesn’t have that issue right now,” Walker says.
“As we sit here today, Myer is financially stronger, but strategically still pretty vulnerable.”

Complaints about parcel deliveries are on the rise, and now Ofcom is warning companies to raise their game or face tighter regulation. We hear from James Stinson of Ofcom in Belfast. items.title: Could Comet return to the high street? New owner has ambitions to revive former electrical retail giant
items.summary: Electricals retailer Comet collapsed in 2012 and was one of the biggest high street casualties Britain has seen. Its new boss has big ambitions for the revived company.
items.body:
Could Comet return to the high street? New owner has ambitions to revive former electrical retail giant
Electricals retailer Comet collapsed in 2012 and was one of the biggest high street casualties Britain has ever seen.
It's now back, but online only, and its boss, Cas Paton, has major ambitions for the group.
Notably, he is not ruling out a return to the high street in Britain for Comet.
The 236-shop business, which at the time employed around 7,000 people, was acquired in 2011 for the nominal sum of £1 by private equity group OpCapita.
OpCapita failed to revive Comet's fortunes, as the retailer suffered amid the decline in consumer spending during the recession and the seismic growth of online rivals.
The chain collapsed in November 2012. Thousands of people lost their jobs and were left out of pocket as a result of the administration, and taxpayers had to foot a bill of approximately £50million for unpaid taxes and redundancy costs.
Comet, which was founded in Hull in 1933 and began life selling batteries and radios, was acquired by London-based online marketplace OnBuy in 2025.
Nothing ruled out: Cas Paton told This is Money he had not ruled out a return to the high street for Currys
OnBuy has said it wants to be a 'serious challenger' to rivals like Amazon and Currys.
Last year, OnBuy said it planned to resurrect Comet 'as a marketplace at the apex of e-commerce'.
This is Money asked Paton, founder and chief executive of OnBuy, if shoppers could expect to see Comet return to high streets across Britain.
Paton told This is Money: 'Never say never. We've launched online because that's the right model for Comet now, but I'd love to see the name back on British high streets in some form.
'We're already exploring partnerships that could make that happen.
'I don't think the answer is simply to recreate the old stores and pretend retail hasn't changed.
'It would have to be relevant, exciting and give people a reason to walk through the door.'
Paton said Comet had been revived as a 'specialist electricals marketplace, to be a modern-day champion of tech, gadgets, and built around how people actually want to shop now'.
He added: 'We are onboarding more suppliers and brands every day, so we expect the range, and the number of deals available, to keep growing over the coming months.'
The chief executive said shoppers 'did not need another website selling everything'.
He said: 'Britain needs great retail destinations that actually know what they stand for.
'If I'm looking for a new TV, laptop or washing machine, I want proper choice, a great price and a shopping experience built around electricals.
'More competition matters because it gives customers greater choice. It forces everyone to work harder on price, range and the experience they offer. That's healthy.'
Star deals: Comet collapsed in Britain in 2012, triggering thousands of job losses
Get what you can: A photo from 2012 of a Comet shop closing down
It's personal: For Cas Paton, the revival of Comet is personal as he visited the shops as a boy
Paton said he also believed the Government was not doing enough to support retailers.
He said: 'The Government is treating retailers as a source of revenue rather than an engine for growth.
'At the moment, businesses feel they are succeeding despite the system, not because of it.
'You can't keep increasing costs, adding regulation and then act surprised when shops close or investment goes elsewhere.
'Retailers need stability. They need to know that employing another person, opening another location or investing in better technology won't be punished by the next Budget.
'Stop trying to choose between online retail and the high street as well. The future is both.
'Give businesses the conditions to grow and let retailers work out how customers want to shop.'
For Paton, the revival of Comet is personal. He remembers visiting Comet's Trafford Park store with his late dad Nigel as a boy and being blown away by the technology on display.
So, Comet's back online, but it is operating in a tough environment. Competition from the likes of Amazon, Currys and AO World will not be going away any time soon.
There were 738,144 British businesses in 'significant' financial distress in the third quarter of 2026, according to the latest quarterly 'red flag alert' report from BTG Consulting PLC, a Manchester-based insolvency adviser formerly known as Begbies Traynor.
It comes against a backdrop of rising inflation in Britain, with energy bills set to increase further in January 2027 as the impact of the Middle East energy shock continues to feed through into the cost of living.

items.title: Rip out ugly clutter to help revive UK high streets, says thinktank
items.summary: Exclusive: Report says restricting cars and freeing up pavement space could be a cheap way to bring shoppers back The long decline of the high street is a problem that has gripped British governments for years. But what if there was a solution no one had considered before – doing it all on the cheap? Spending less money is, admittedly, just one element of a report led by the urban thinktank Create Streets. But it does argue that rather than multimillion-pound revamps, a better answer could be smaller changes aimed at making town and city centres more appealing. Continue reading...
items.body:
The long decline of the high street is a problem that has gripped British governments for years. But what if there was a solution no one had considered before – doing it all on the cheap?
Spending less money is, admittedly, just one element of a report led by the urban thinktank Create Streets. But it does argue that rather than multimillion-pound revamps, a better answer could be smaller changes aimed at making town and city centres more appealing.
Central to this, the study says, is trying to banish, or at least tame, motor traffic, because too often urban centres are places “designed to be driven through, not for time to be spent in”.
As well as citing a lack of imagination, the report, which is co-produced by bike storage company Cyclehoop, blames planning regulations that favour conformity and clutter and too often treat speeding cars as a given, to which everything else must adjust.
“The default high street is engineered for traffic and furnished from a catalogue: a tarmac pavement, guardrails penning people at the kerb, litter bins ordered from a procurement catalogue, a row of plastic planters – public investment that is joyless,” it says.
While planners have traditionally focused on car access as a metric for thriving town centres, calculations for the Create Streets report suggest that replacing parking with other kerbside infrastructure, including bike spaces or outside drinking and dining areas, creates more economic value.
It found that one parking space in the high street of a market town is typically used by about 3.5 vehicles a day, bringing in just over £73,000 a year in spending to nearby shops.
But the same 12 square metres, if used to hold nine share e-bikes, generates an average of 13 trips a day, with over £146,000 a year in spending, even taking into account the lower average spend per person.
In a busier city, where share bikes would be used more frequently, the estimated total annual spend rises to more than £300,000.
Repurposing the space for outside dining brings less dramatic gains, but in a city centre it can still amount to about £120,000 in extra annual spending.
The report calls for a cultural rethink involving low-cost tweaks that rip away ugly and unnecessary street furniture and make better use of kerbsides.
Calling use by families “the indicator species of a healthy high street”, the report cites what is known as “the wrist test” – whether it feels safe to let go of a young child’s wrist so they can roam with some freedom.
This is best done, it argues, by removing the threat of speeding motor vehicles and not by trying to mitigate their impact. It calls the removal of pedestrian guardrails next to roads “the most cost-effective upgrade for the majority of high streets”, saying they are an eyesore with minimal safety benefits.
The report says “the absurdity of modern public realm management” is exemplified by Secured by Design, policy guidelines on cutting neighbourhood crime. These can, critics point out, mean benches and plants are removed on the advice of police, supposedly to discourage antisocial behaviour.
Andy Burnham, the prime minister, has pledged to try to reverse the decline of high streets, announcing in September a £210m regeneration fund.
However, the bulk of the money will go into buildings: turning old shops into shared workspaces or community cafes, or keeping pubs and clubs in business.
The report argues that renovating buildings is pointless if the street outside is unappealing. To reduce clutter, it says, there should be “a presumption of removal where an item cannot be justified”.
The effects can be dramatic, the report says, pointing to examples including Altrincham in Cheshire, where the creation of a walkable, car-free urban area helped see retail vacancies fall from over 30% to 7% in less than a decade.
Such initiatives do not have to be expensive, it claims, noting the example of an unused patch of land next to a church in Grimsby which was turned into a park for less than £20,000.
“Streets that are ugly are not so because councils lack the desire to change them, but because the system is counting the maintenance liabilities, not the benefits,” said David Milner of Create Streets.
“What works is cheap: trees in the ground, benches people want to sit on, clutter taken away.
“So much of what is built now seems to be temporary, looking more like road works than public realm improvements, so we encourage the concept of permanence; more trees in the ground, not in giant plant pots, for example.”
A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: “We support local leaders to make decisions on pedestrianisation based on their communities’ needs.
“Our Hope on the High Street strategy will help local people revive town centres by protecting community assets, bringing derelict buildings back into use and tackling the spread of vape and gambling shops.
“Funding is available for local leaders to spend on their priorities, including pedestrianising and regenerating their high streets if they so wish.”

items.title: Asda stems sales slide as new boss takes reins at struggling supermarket chain
items.summary: Sales suffered last year after a botched IT transformation disrupted operations. But it has hailed signs of improvement in recent weeks after slashing prices and improving services.
items.body:
Asda stems sales slide as new boss takes reins at struggling supermarket chain
Asda has revealed that it staunched a sales slide as its new boss takes the reins.
Britain’s third biggest supermarket said its food sales flatlined in the third quarter, up 0.1 per cent over the three months to 30 September. This was the first time the grocer has seen a lift since the first quarter of 2024.
It comes as former Morrisons boss David Potts last week joined the business, saying it had ‘made good progress but significant opportunities remain.’
Asda has lost sales to discounter Lidl and Aldi and grappled with debt pressures since a takeover by private equity firm TDR Capital in 2021.
Sales suffered in the same quarter last year when a botched IT transformation disrupted operations.
But it has hailed signs of improvement in recent weeks after slashing prices on staples and insisting it has improved its online service.
New boss David Potts last week said the grocer had ‘made good progress but significant opportunities remain.’
Online grocery sales rose 6.9 per cent over the quarter, which the company credited to ‘strong participation’ in its loyalty scheme Asda Rewards
Total revenues rose 3.1 per cent to £6.5billion, including fuel, which has seen a dramatic increase in prices since the outbreak of the war in the Middle East in February. Without fuel, sales fell by 0.1 per cent.
The retailer has previously hailed a good performance in categories including hot drinks, ice cream and chilled poultry.
The retailer said it was seeing signs of green shoots across the business, including its clothing line George. Former chief executive of fashion brand New Look, Helen Connolly, took over the job of running the fashion range this summer.
Asda’s chief financial officer, Michael Gleeson, said: ‘The work we've done through the period to deliver against our strategy was reflected in our third-quarter performance.
‘Asda's key strength is the breadth of our business, spanning food, clothing, fuel, pharmacy and other services. This means we can meet more of our customers' everyday needs and gives us more opportunities to grow.’
New boss Potts has already told the supermarket's 1,100 store managers to spend more time on the shop floor helping staff and checking stores are ready for customers.
He began his career at Tesco on the shop floor aged 16 and, after failing his O-Levels, worked his way up to run its Ireland business, its UK business and its Asia business. He was also on the board of the supermarket giant from 1998 to 2012.
He led Morrisons from 2015 to 2023, a period which included the group’s £10billion sale to private equity group Clayton Dubilier & Rice in 2021. Morrisons has also struggled in the wake of its debt-fuelled takeover and even lost its spot as Britain’s fifth biggest grocer to discounter Lidl.
Pots has replaced Asda veteran Allan Leighton, who steered the ship as executive chairman for two years from November 2024. Earlier this year, Leighton said that Asda was 'about a third' of the way through its recovery.

items.summary: Asda has reached the milestone of lowering its operational carbon emissions by 50 per cent, having achieved a 55 per cent reduction since 2015 according to the latest Environmental, Social…
items.body:
Asda surpasses carbon emissions reduction target
Asda has reached the milestone of lowering its operational carbon emissions by 50 per cent, having achieved a 55 per cent reduction since 2015 according to the latest Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) report.
The supermarket retailer lowered carbon emissions from its transport fleet by 18 per cent year-on-year, driven by the shift from diesel to liquified natural gas and bio-liquified natural gas fuels.
Asda also reached an 80 per cent LEAF Marque certification across its global fresh produce growers in over 40 countries.
Additionally, the retailer lowered operational water consumption to 2.2m³, down from 2.6m³ in 2024.
The supermarket retailer also supported biodiversity and habitat restoration schemes across over 8,500 acres of farmland through the Asda Lamb Group Habitat Project during the year.
Subscribe to Grocery Gazette for free
Sign up here to get the latest grocery and food news each morning
Asda also invested in charitable initiatives, raising over £100m through the company’s Ticked Pink campaign over the reporting period, which supports Breast Cancer Awareness.
The supermarket retailer also made significant progress across its zero-waste goals, increasing its recycled content across own-brand plastic packaging from 21.6 per cent to 32.7 per cent.
An Asda spokesperson said: “This year’s report highlights strong progress in areas where we can have the greatest impact. We’ve exceeded our operational carbon reduction target and continued to improve the nutritional profile of products sold.
“We’re also proud to have surpassed £100m raised through Tickled Pink during the reporting period, with the total now reaching £110m as we celebrate the campaign’s 30th anniversary this year. While there’s more to do, we’re committed to building on this progress and focusing on the issues that matter most to our business and stakeholders.”
Asda also reported donating over £3.2m to 2,326 community groups across the UK through the Asda Foundation.

items.title: Asda slashes fuel prices as new boss David Potts doubles down on value
items.summary: Asda has cut petrol and diesel prices by an average of 4p per litre nationwide, as new chief executive David Potts wastes little time putting his stamp on the struggling…
items.body:
Asda slashes fuel prices as new boss David Potts doubles down on value
Asda has cut petrol and diesel prices by an average of 4p per litre nationwide, as new chief executive David Potts wastes little time putting his stamp on the struggling supermarket.
The reductions took effect at 5pm on Thursday across fuel stations attached to Asda’s larger stores, offering motorists savings of around £2.20 on a typical 55-litre tank.
The price cut is among Potts’ first customer-facing changes since taking the reins earlier this month, as he looks to win back shoppers following a prolonged period of falling market share and fierce competition from Tesco, Sainsbury’s and the discounters.
Earlier this week, the former Morrisons boss ordered Asda’s 1,100 store managers to open more staffed checkouts, spend more time on the shop floor and improve product availability.
Now, attention has turned to the forecourt, with Asda looking to strengthen its value credentials ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period.
Potts said: “When we get the fundamentals right, customers notice.”
He added that cutting fuel prices was part of a broader effort to improve value across the shopping trip, alongside the supermarket’s food and clothing ranges.
The decision comes as falling wholesale fuel costs put pressure on supermarkets to pass savings on to motorists.
According to the AA, average UK petrol prices have already fallen by around 5p per litre since early October, with further reductions potentially on the way as wholesale costs continue to ease.
Asda has long used competitive fuel pricing to attract customers to its larger stores, making the latest reduction a potentially useful weapon as supermarkets battle for festive spending.
The cut also follows Asda’s recent investment in grocery prices, including reductions across 1,000 products held until after Christmas.
For Potts, the challenge now is to translate sharper pricing and improvements to the shopping experience into sustained sales growth after more than two years of difficulties at the supermarket.

items.body:
Jysk reports completion of an important step in its unified commerce journey. All of the retailer's stores in the Netherlands, Belgium, the UK and Ireland are now operating on a new platform powered by Enactor.
With these four countries fully onboard, more than 2,200 Jysk stores have gone live on the platform.
"Our store colleagues are already seeing the benefits," says Melissa Hessing, Store Manager at Jysk Alkmaar. “We moved through it very quickly. The checkout system is very user-friendly and largely self-explanatory. It will be especially easy for new colleagues."
"The implementation has been an exciting and busy process, filled with training, learning and valuable discussions about new ways of working. And there is no doubt that unified commerce will bring significant benefits to our customers, our stores and our colleagues."
Enactor's Olena Opalko comments: "What a year for Jysk and Enactor! Seven countries rolled out in 2026, more than 2,200 stores now live on the platform, and every roll-out delivered on time and smoothly. A huge achievement for everyone involved. Proud to keep supporting Jysk's global unified commerce journey."
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards
Unified commerce was a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
The awards celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world. Our winners were revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.
The event consisted of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.

items.title: lululemon CTO search continues as Morrisons goes live with Emerald: this week's biggest retail technology stories
items.summary: It's Friday, the weekend is almost upon us, so let’s kick back and reflect on another eventful week for the retail tech space. Here's your briefing on the most important stories from the past few days, including Vinted, eBay, Depop, J.Crew, Stripe, Simbe, ASICS, Corvus Robotics, Greggs, Auror, Cadbu
items.body:
It's Friday, the weekend is almost upon us, so let’s kick back and reflect on another eventful week for the retail tech space. Here's your briefing on the most important stories from the past few days, including Vinted, eBay, Depop, J.Crew, Stripe, Simbe, ASICS, Corvus Robotics, Greggs, Auror, Cadbury, and THG Ingenuity.
1. Vinted, eBay and Depop set to be hit by under-16s ban as grooming concerns grow
The UK government is set to ban under-16s from Vinted and eBay amid fears that the online platforms' messaging functions allow strangers to groom children.
Culture Secretary, Lisa Nandy, is gearing up to discuss expanding the social media ban announced earlier in the year to cover online marketplaces. Depop and Facebook Marketplace are also expected to be included.
The Children’s Society claims that some young users are being “asked for indecent photos in exchange for money” or gifts on these sites.
A government source told The Times: “There is an increasing body of evidence that says under-16s are accessing these services a lot and are potentially accessing risk. We need to take a comprehensive approach to protecting children from harm online."
Vinted, eBay, Depop, and Facebook Marketplace did not respond to our request for comment.
2. CTO search continues as lululemon appoints Emily Sunderland as Chief Strategy Officer
lululemon has announced the appointment of Emily Sunderland as Chief Strategy Officer, effective 23rd November. She will report to Chief Financial Officer Meghan Frank and joins from Boston Consulting Group.
With expertise across activewear, apparel, and specialty retail, she will play an important role in developing lululemon's long-term strategy, identifying future growth opportunities, and strengthening strategic planning.
Searches remain underway for a Chief Technology Officer and Chief Communications Officer. lululemon is building out a leadership team under a new structure announced in October. Sunderland coming onboard follows the appointments of Maggie Gauger as President & Chief Product Officer and Joseph Godsey as Chief Operating Officer.
3. J.Crew brings Stripe in to technology stack as it boosts BNPL options and makes agentic commerce move
J.Crew has added Stripe to its technology stack as it looks to boost its position in the alternative payments space.
In a LinkedIn post, Ruchika Julapalli, SVP Digital Experience, Product, Technology & AI at J.Crew, said: "We wanted to give customers more choice in how they pay, and bring in new customers who like to shop with changing wallets. So excited that we brought Stripe into the J.Crew Group tech stack. One integration opens up a range of alternative payment methods, where before each one would have been its own build."
She added: "We started by expanding our buy now, pay later options, launching Klarna and Affirm within weeks of each other across J.Crew, Madewell and J.Crew Factory. Double the fun. Stripe also positions us well for agentic commerce."
4. McDonald’s and Uber ramp up global partnership across delivery and loyalty in 14 markets
Uber Technologies and McDonald's have announced a multi-year expansion of their partnership, bringing new delivery and rewards features to customers in 14 markets across the world.
This includes the US, Australia, Belgium, Canada, France, Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Switzerland, and the UK.
The pair first partnered in 2017 in the US, and McDonald’s is now available on Uber Eats in 30 countries. Uber will now be the preferred delivery partner for orders placed in the McDonald's app, and the two companies will connect Uber with MyMcDonald's Rewards.
As McDonald's expands delivery capabilities within its app, Uber Eats will serve as the preferred integrated delivery fulfillment partner for orders placed through the McDonald's app in participating markets including the US, Australia, Canada, France, Germany, and the UK. Customers will be able to order delivery and track their orders from checkout to doorstep without leaving the app. They will also have the option to order directly through the Uber Eats app.
McDonald’s app orders will primarily be fulfilled through Uber Direct, Uber’s white labelled delivery solution, in partnership with Deliverect. Uber will also serve as the fast food giant's exclusive delivery and rideshare rewards partner in participating markets.
5. US retailer DeCicco & Sons expands Simbe Store Intelligence technology roll-out following pilot
US grocery retailer DeCicco & Sons has expanded Simbe’s Store Intelligence platform chainwide following a 35% reduction in out-of-stocks within the first 60 days at its pilot locations.
Simbe’s autonomous shelf scanning robot, Tally, captures detailed shelf conditions multiple times daily. That intelligence flows into the retailer’s existing systems, helping teams identify and resolve issues faster while supporting applications spanning store operations, e-commerce, and business intelligence.
“Our customers count on us to have the products they love and a team ready to help,” says John DeCicco Jr., CEO, DeCicco & Sons. “Simbe helps us deliver on both. Digitising our shelves is foundational to our broader technology strategy, because it gives every system we run an accurate picture of what’s happening in our stores. With real-time visibility into stores, our teams can address corrective fixes sooner and spend more time providing the personal service that brings people back to DeCiccos.”
6. Morrisons kicks off Emerald checkout software roll-out across stores in partnership with NCR Voyix
Morrisons has gone live in its first store with Emerald, the UK grocery retailer's new checkout software. It is working with NCR Voyix on the project.
In a LinkedIn post, Laura Critchley, Support Office Specialist- Front End Operations, said: "This is a project that I, alongside so many fantastic colleagues across the business, have been working on for the last two years, so seeing it finally come to life in store is a brilliant feeling."
She added: "Emerald will replace our existing Storeline software across checkouts and cash offices, bringing a more streamlined, modern and user-friendly experience for colleagues, while helping to make everyday processes easier and improve the customer experience."
"It’s been a huge collaborative effort to get us to this point, and it’s fantastic to see all the hard work starting to pay off. A brilliant step forward for our Front End teams, and we can’t wait to see Emerald rolled out across our stores from next year."
7. Cadbury connects with THG Ingenuity for new direct-to-consumer gifting platform
Cadbury has appointed THG Ingenuity to power its new direct-to-consumer Cadbury Shop.
This will see THG Commerce deliver a cloud native digital storefront and interactive customisation software, THG Studios produce end-to-end e-commerce creative assets and visual digital merchandising, while THG Fulfil will provide warehousing, pick-and-pack, temperature controlled confectionery handling, courier management and customer service solutions.
Central to the launch is an interactive product customisation engine developed to power the flagship Cadbury Heroes Pick & Mix, which allows shoppers to hand-pick a combination of miniature favourites.
The platform also introduces on-demand personalisation across giftboxes, including the dedicated Cadbury Build Your Own Letterbox Gift service, where shoppers can pick any six Cadbury tablets to be packaged and delivered straight to someone's doorstep.
8. ASICS deploys Corvus Robotics drones to manage inventory for three million plus shoes in DC outside Memphis
Corvus Robotics reports that ASICS is running Corvus One autonomous inventory drones inside its Byhalia, Memphis, USA distribution centre, where nightly flights have increased counting frequency 6x in two of the building's highest risk storage areas, which are now counted monthly.
ASICS reports recovering misplaced inventory roughly 60% faster since the system went in and has redirected about 200 hours of monthly counting labour into inventory research and exception resolution.
The facility holds close to three million units, 2.3 million pairs of footwear and 700,000 pieces of apparel and accessories, across roughly 44,000 SKUs, all managed in a Manhattan Associates warehouse management system. It fills e-commerce orders and ships to wholesale accounts, along with ASICS full price and outlet retail stores.
Corvus One covers two storage profiles in the building: the singles area, where returned and single pair product gets stored and picked, and case reserve. Both were counted twice a year under ASICS cycle count policy.
9. Morrisons Media Group announces retail media proposition expansion across 1,700 convenience stores
Morrisons Media Group (MMG) is expanding its retail media proposition to include Morrisons' approximately 1,700 convenience stores, with the aim of giving brands and suppliers a more joined up approach to planning campaigns across the grocery retailer's supermarket and convenience estates.
Steve Newbould, Head of Commercial Data & Media, Morrisons Media Group, says: "Expanding our proposition into convenience is an important step in how we support our supplier partners. Our customers shop across different formats for different reasons, and bringing these opportunities together allows us to offer brands a more comprehensive way to engage with them. This is about building on the strength of our existing retail media proposition while recognising the growing importance of convenience."
The expanded proposition combines Morrisons' first-party customer insights with SMG's retail media capabilities. Suppliers will benefit from MMG's existing support, including insights informed by Morrisons' first-party data ecosystem, MoreViu, to help shape campaign planning around relevant customer missions and commercial objectives.
10. Greggs taps Auror technology across stores as prolific shoplifter avoids jail
Greggs reports that it is rolling out Auror crime reporting and intelligence technology across its stores amid a rise in shoplifting.
The British bakery and fast food chain made the announcement as a shoplifter who stole more than £2,000 worth of soft drinks from a single Greggs store returned to the community after being handed a suspended sentence.
Since May, Tiffany O'Neill, 28, has been arrested, charged and remanded to court 11 times. She was ultimately charged with 69 theft offences.
Yet when she appeared for sentencing at Croydon Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday, having pleaded guilty to a total of 80 offences, she avoided being sent to prison and was handed a 26 week sentence, suspended for 12 months.
New constraints on magistrates and judges that came into force earlier this year require a sentence of less than a year to be suspended unless very specific exceptions apply.

items.title: Hanshow a winner at 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards for Merlin Smart Cart with shopreme and Lucky cart
items.summary: Hanshow has been named a winner at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards in the Retail Media category for its Merlin Smart Cart solution with shopreme and Lucky cart.Now in to its eighth edition, the RTIH Innovation Awards celebrate global technology innovation across the fast moving omnichannel
items.body:
Hanshow has been named a winner at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards in the Retail Media category for its Merlin Smart Cart solution with shopreme and Lucky cart.
Now in to its eighth edition, the RTIH Innovation Awards celebrate global technology innovation across the fast moving omnichannel retail landscape and are judged by an independent panel of retail, technology, data and digital leaders from organisations including Walmart, Amazon, Boots, Ikea, Fabletics, Holland & Barrett, CVS Health, and IGD.
Our 2026 winners were announced at a ceremony in Central London last week.
Retail Media Innovation is a new category for 2026, reflecting the growing role of technology platforms in helping retailers develop retail media propositions across physical and digital channels. The category recognises projects that use innovative technologies to create new opportunities for shopper engagement, strengthen retailer-brand relationships, and unlock new commercial value from retail media.
At the heart of the award winning solution is a new approach to in-store retail media: treating media as part of the shopper service rather than as a standalone advertising touchpoint. Merlin Smart Cart brings relevant engagement closer to product discovery and purchase decisions while supporting practical shopper needs throughout the journey.
Hanshow provides smart cart technology and in-store digital infrastructure, shopreme delivers the software layer, self-checkout experience and retailer-system integration, while Lucky cart adds personalisation and retail media capabilities. Together, these complementary technologies connect shopping context and loyalty identification with product discovery, relevant offers, basket visibility and streamlined checkout within the smart cart journey.
By combining shopper utility with retail media capabilities, Merlin Smart Cart creates opportunities for more relevant, contextual and measurable engagement within the physical shopping journey. For retailers and brands, this opens new ways to connect media activity with shopper interaction and commercial value, while supporting new models of collaboration across the retail media ecosystem.
Designed for practical, modular deployment, Merlin Smart Cart uses a clip-on format that works with existing trolley fleets, enabling retailers to introduce digital shopping and retail media capabilities without extensive infrastructure changes. The solution also gives retailers the flexibility to tailor the experience to their own brand and commercial strategy.
Scott Thompson, Founder and Editor of Retail Technology Innovation Hub, says: “Merlin Smart Cart stood out to the judging panel for a number of reasons, but chief among them was how the solution's entry showed that in-store media has dramatically changed in recent years. It has moved beyond traditional channels and now happens on the shelf, on the label and in the shopping cart, at the exact moment that shoppers make their decisions. And it can also be measured. Congratulations to Hanshow on building something both powerful and innovative in this dynamic space.”
“This recognition reflects an important shift in physical retail: retail media is moving closer to where purchase decisions actually happen. Smart Cart has the potential to become a new interaction layer in the physical store, bringing together shopper utility, personalisation, and measurable brand engagement at the point of decision,” says Philippe Brochard, Chairman of the Advisory Committee at Hanshow.
“With our ecosystem partners, we are bringing more of the precision and relevance of digital commerce into the physical retail journey, while keeping the shopper experience at the centre.”

items.title: Look at the Poundland scandal and see a crisis that goes beyond Britain’s high streets | Polly Toynbee
items.summary: ‘I look out for my team,’ a store manager tells me, but Poundland’s US owner doesn’t care. Labour may be too late to prevent it becoming yet another casualty of venture capital In the Poundland I visit, a treasure trove of bargains, the staff are dejected. The shelves are emptying because the owners have withheld £50m needed for new stock and paying wages. It’s just one of 600 stores in peril, and these employees just a few of 12,000 at risk of losing their jobs – with 30,000 jobs at risk in supply chains. On Tuesday £10m was released : not enough, but preventing instant collapse. Gordon Brothers, the US owner that bought Poundland for a symbolic £1 last year, specialises in buying and “restructuring” distressed companies. Under pressure, it extended the deadline by 10 working days before putting this profitable business into administration. It profits more by closing Poundland down and breaking it up. Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...
items.body:
In the Poundland I visit, a treasure trove of bargains, the staff are dejected. The shelves are emptying because the owners have withheld £50m needed for new stock and paying wages. It’s just one of 600 stores in peril, and these employees just a few of 12,000 at risk of losing their jobs – with 30,000 jobs at risk in supply chains.
On Tuesday £10m was released: not enough, but preventing instant collapse. Gordon Brothers, the US owner that bought Poundland for a symbolic £1 last year, specialises in buying and “restructuring” distressed companies. Under pressure, it extended the deadline by 10 working days before putting this profitable business into administration. It profits more by closing Poundland down and breaking it up.
The manager, whom I’ll call Jim for anonymity, is at work an hour and a half after his paid shift ended. “I look out for my team,” he says, though Gordon Brothers doesn’t seem to be looking out for him. He says the outsourced security staff vanished this week as their pay was stopped. “The shoplifting is very bad now. Look, the high-end stuff has gone first”: the well-known brands, not unknown cheaper makes. Despite everything, he is remarkably proud of the shop and boasts of how much cheaper brands are than in Sainsbury’s. He pats the shelf with red velvet Santa stockings and glittery bows, glad some Christmas stock is in before the closure. “But no one is telling us anything.”
Will the staff get jobs if it closes? He introduces me to a man in his late 50s with an easy manner and a wide grin. “My best man, by far,” he says. “He’s been here 15 years, and never a single day off sick, not one. Will any other shop see how good he is? No, because his English is bad and they won’t know his worth to any manager. I don’t know what he’ll do. I keep putting him on the till to try to improve his English, to help him along.” Jim is proud of his eye for picking good staff and keeping them on warm terms, and is fearful for their future.
This is may not be the sort of shop where you expect steadfast dedication to the company. Jim’s attitude is just another reminder of what I often find reporting on work, that most people are attached to their jobs, despite recent British Social Attitudes research reporting their frustrations. Often the greatest aggravations are about lack of control. Jim says he could increase sales if he was allowed to be the buyer. “I know our customers in this area; the centre doesn’t.”
He belongs to Usdaw, the shopworkers’ union, but says there’s nothing it can do. Time and again the union has watched helplessly as these private equity and venture capital buyouts bring down viable retailers. As we talk, a customer asks indignantly why there are no packs of Boost in the cold drinks cabinet. Jim explains the situation and the man looks shocked. “No! You can’t close down! I’m always in here.”
Our surroundings, our streetscape is at the mercy of distant forces. Gap-toothed high streets and boarded-up shops cause us all an ache of loss. Poundland stores teetering on the edge are “anchor stores” drawing people to high streets, but may join those great voids just weeks before Christmas. Woolworths’ 807 stores closed after being taken over, losing 27,000 jobs and lifetimes of local history. BHS, sold for £1, is gone. Debenhams, WHSmith, Toys R Us, Maplin, TM Lewin and plenty more, adversely transformed or taken over by private equity for unkindly “restructure” that usually ends in closures. Some, bought with debts that are loaded on to their balance sheets, stagger but survive – think Asda and Morrisons.
Now it’s Poundland’s turn. At Wednesday’s closed-session select committee on business and trade, MPs heard its long-serving managing director, Barry Williams, challenge the owners, trying to save the business and showing that it made a £18.1m operating profit in the year to September. But Gordon Brothers has turned down offers, notably one from Martin Property Group, owners of NCP car parks.
Through complex financing, it would make more by breaking Poundland up. It has £30m debt to recover but, as it is both the owner and the creditor, it comes top of the list for repayment in administration: after paying tax, it gets paid before any staff who are owed wages. If there’s no money left, redundancy is paid by the taxpayer.
Andy Burnham weighed in demanding answers, but Gordon Brothers has no legal obligation to worry about staff, let alone social or public concerns. The chair of the Commons business and trade committee, Liam Byrne, is campaigning hard to save Poundland, calling Gordon Brothers “much like a wolf on Wall Street, on the British high street”, and adding: “It’s clear that they’ve taken millions out of Poundland at a time when they themselves said the business was on a knife-edge.”
But there’s nothing anyone can do if pressure and shame fails. Why should a company, especially a foreign one, care what anyone thinks when the bottom line says close it down?
Byrne is campaigning to prevent this in future, calling for changes to company law that at present gives shareholders primacy above all else, unlike the much preferable situation in Germany. He would stop pension funds making it their sole obligation to maximise short-term gains and thus investing ever more in venture capital. He’d also impose stress tests to stop asset strippers overloading a business with debt then taking the lion’s share when it’s broken up.
On the Poundland shop floor, Jim and the rest of his team serve their customers and wait another two weeks to discover their fate. A future change in the law is essential. Maybe it will come. But it will probably be too late for them.
- Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

items.title: Morrisons rolls out flashing digital shelves - is dynamic pricing coming to supermarkets?
items.summary: Shoppers can search for a specific product via the Morrisons loyalty app's 'product finder tool'. The correct shelf-edge label in the supermarket will then light up.
items.body:
Morrisons rolls out flashing digital shelves - is dynamic pricing coming to supermarkets?
Morrisons has launched flashing electronic shelf labels designed to help shoppers find products faster, amid fears dynamic pricing could soon be introduced in British supermarkets.
Shoppers can search for a specific product via the its More Card loyalty app's 'product finder tool'.
The correct shelf-edge label in the supermarket will then light up.
Supermarkets are working at pace to figure out new ways to get shoppers to increase their spending in stores.
For now, Morrisons' flashing shelves are aimed at guiding shoppers to the right product.
But some are concerned supermarket chains across Britain could eventually introduce dynamic pricing.
Dynamic pricing is where the cost of groceries can change by the minute thanks to computer-controlled digital price labels.
Morrisons says it has partnered with French firm Vusion to 'digitise pricing across its entire supermarket estate using electronic shelf labels to automate price updates and improve pricing accuracy'.
Flashy tech: Morrisons is rolling out flashing electronic shelf labels designed to help shoppers find products faster
Andrew Opie, director of food and sustainability at the British Retail Consortium (BRC), said: 'Digital pricing displays are simply a way of updating and checking thousands of prices in a fast and cost-effective way, so they can continue to offer great value for customers.'
Morrisons told This is Money it was aligned to the BRC statement on the topic of dynamic pricing.
In April 2026, the Bank of England warned that more businesses were planning to use 'market-responsive pricing tools', with around a third of companies expected to adopt them.
Dynamic pricing technology is already used on shopping websites like Amazon, but supermarkets such as the Co-op have been trialling it in 700 stores nationwide.
While supermarkets in Britain are not currently using dynamic pricing, many, including Co-op and Morrisons, are shifting towards digital shelf labels, which will, in turn, make price changes quicker to implement.
Taking an example, if dynamic pricing was introduced across British supermarkets, a pack of yoghurts could be £1.10 in the morning and £1.50 in the afternoon.
A bottle of wine could be priced 10 per cent higher on a Friday evening – essentially, supermarkets would use customer spending data in an attempt to price 'dynamically'.
Any move towards dynamic pricing in British supermarkets would prove controversial, given that food is an essential purchase unlike concert tickets or flights.
Advocates of dynamic pricing claim shoppers already benefit when prices fall, and have claimed consumers can limit the impact by choosing where and when they buy.
Clive Black, of Shore Capital, told The Times earlier this year: 'Changing prices is very expensive.
'When Tesco changes prices, it has to replace a piece of plastic or cardboard across thousands of stores.
'The initial drive for these displays is operating efficiency, standardisation and compliance, but the longer-term possibility is dynamic pricing.
'Whether that is in the interest of shoppers or shareholders is a moot point.'
Morrisons previously said it would launch its digital flashing shelf units in September this year.
Morrisons said: 'The app will share the in-store location, ask the customer to confirm if they are in the right aisle, and then the corresponding digital shelf label will flash magenta, making it easier for the customer to spot the exact product they want.'
It added: 'The feature is ideal for navigating high-density product aisles like herbs, spices, or sauces, as well as locating popular seasonal items such as cranberry sauce.'
The new technology, which Morrisons claimed was the first of its kind in a British supermarket, will be live in all 270 Morrisons shops that currently have electronic shelf-edge labels installed before Christmas.
Gordon Macpherson, of Morrisons, said: 'We know that Christmas is one of the busiest times of the year for our customers, and we’re always looking for new ways to make their shopping experience as easy and convenient as possible.
'Our new "shop to light" feature is a great example of how we’re using technology to make a real difference in store, helping our customers find the products they need quickly, whether they’re shopping for their Christmas dinner or just popping in to pick up a few last-minute essentials.'
Marks and Spencer has also been testing the use of 'pick to light' shopping technology in its wine aisles.
In its latest half-year results, Tesco said it had more than 7,500 digital advertising screens across the group, including at Booker and convenience chain One Stop.

items.title: Next extends Costa Coffee partnership for another decade
items.summary: Next will continue working with Costa Coffee until 2036, as it continues to expand its in-store food and drink offering. The agreement will see Costa Coffee continue to operate across Next’s UK retail estate, where it currently has more than 140 locations. The partnership began in 2011 with a single concession and has since grown...
items.body:
Next will continue working with Costa Coffee until 2036, as it continues to expand its in-store food and drink offering.
The agreement will see Costa Coffee continue to operate across Next’s UK retail estate, where it currently has more than 140 locations.
The partnership began in 2011 with a single concession and has since grown into a nationwide network, with further openings and investment planned over the next decade.
In 2026, Costa Coffee opened seven new locations within Next stores, including a 3,000 sq ft site at the retailer’s flagship Bluewater destination. It is the largest Costa Coffee location within the retailer’s estate and among the first to feature the coffee chain’s latest store design.
Costa Coffee has also refurbished 26 existing locations across Next’s stores this year, as both businesses look to improve the customer experience and adapt to changing shopping habits.
The extension until January 2036 provides a long-term commitment for Next as it continues to develop its wider retail proposition, using food and drink concessions to complement its core fashion, home and lifestyle offer.
Tom Falk, head of property at Costa Coffee said: “Next has been a valued partner for many years and we’re delighted to extend our relationship through to 2036. This milestone reflects the strength of our partnership and creates an exciting platform for future growth.
“Together, we’ve grown from a single location to a network of more than 140 stores, adapting to changing consumer needs and investing in great coffee experiences along the way.
“The success of landmark locations such as Bluewater demonstrates what can be achieved when two customer-focused brands work together with a shared ambition. This agreement gives us a fantastic opportunity to build on that momentum in the years ahead.”
The deal underlines the growing role of hospitality within traditional retail environments, as retailers look to give shoppers additional reasons to visit stores and extend their time on site.
The continued presence of Costa Coffee strengthens Next’s in-store food and drink offer, supporting its wider strategy to develop larger destination stores.

Following a series of […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Luxury organic food and lifestyle retailer Daylesford is unveiling its Christmas 2026 film, With Love From the Cotswolds, narrated by acclaimed actor Richard E. Grant.
Produced in-house in collaboration with local filmmaker Freddie Jewson, the film places Daylesford’s people, craftsmanship and organic Cotswolds farm at the heart of its festive storytelling.
Following a series of handwritten invitations delivered across the farm, the film brings together Daylesford’s growers, bakers, cheesemakers and florists for an intimate Christmas gathering in a candlelit polytunnel. Narrated through an original poem written in-house and recorded at the farm by Richard E. Grant, the story celebrates the value of slowing down, thoughtful craftsmanship and human connection during the festive season.
Rather than relying on elaborate sets or large-scale production, the creative team adopted a deliberately understated approach, using natural light, real Daylesford team members and the farm’s existing surroundings to create an authentic, cinematic celebration of Christmas.
The film reflects Daylesford’s wider brand philosophy, highlighting the people, provenance and care behind its products while bringing its seasonal campaign, From the Cotswolds, with Love, to life.

items.title: Poundland owner secures two extra weeks to ensure retail chain’s survival
items.summary: US investment firm Gordon Brothers is ‘taking due care’ to consider if one of three bidders has enough funds Business live – latest updates Poundland’s owner has said it is “taking due care” to consider if one of three bidders had enough funds to ensure its survival after the troubled budget retail chain secured two more weeks to find a deal. The management of Poundland , which employs approximately 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, won approval from the high court for an extension of legal protection from creditors on Thursday morning. Continue reading...
items.body:
Poundland’s owner has said it is “taking due care” to consider if one of three bidders had enough funds to ensure its survival after the troubled budget retail chain secured two more weeks to find a deal.
The management of Poundland, which employs approximately 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, won approval from the high court for an extension of legal protection from creditors on Thursday morning.
Poundland’s board said it had sought the extra time “with a view to identifying the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and our people”.
It added: “Our stores remain open as usual during this period and we thank our colleagues, suppliers and customers for their incredible and continued support.”
The retail chain’s owner, the US investment firm Gordon Brothers, has been under pressure to accept a bid for the company that would save retail jobs and protect thousands of suppliers since Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators two weeks ago.
A spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said on Thursday: “We support the board’s decision to extend the legal moratorium over the company by a further 10 working days. This brings additional stability amid an ongoing sale process in the backdrop of increasing cost pressures and a difficult inflationary economic environment.
“With this decision, we are today able to confirm to Poundland employees that funds will be released to allow payroll to be made in full this month, while additional funds continue to be released to support Poundland’s ongoing trading.
“We are in discussions with three parties for a sale of the whole business, and we have also received several offers from established high street retailers for significant parts of the business.
“While our preference remains a sale of the whole company, we are taking due care to ensure that any successful offer can provide the funds required to acquire the business and see it through to sustainable cash generation. We, the board, and all involved are working to secure a credible plan that delivers certainty, preserves value and protects as many jobs as possible.”
Gordon Brothers confirmed it had provided £85m of financing, understood to be via an asset-backed loan that Poundland has only partially used over the past year.
That financing is in addition to a £30m shareholder loan largely taken on by Gordon Brothers when it bought the business for a nominal £1 last year.
Gordon Brothers fought back after MPs on Wednesday accused the Poundland owner of extracting millions of pounds from the retailer when it was on a “knife-edge”.
Documents provided to MPs showed the finance firm had taken close to £20m in interest payments and various fees, including those relating to store closures since acquiring Poundland.
Gordon Brothers said it had provided finance for Poundland “when no one else was willing to finance the company – and has contributed substantial efforts to support a turnaround.
“Had we not, the company would have collapsed into insolvency in August 2025. Our efforts have continuously focused on the company’s value and its people, not prioritising one over the other.”

items.title: Poundland secures more time as rescue talks continue
items.summary: Poundland has applied for a second notice of intention (NOI) to appoint administrators after its initial 10-working-day protection period expired on Thursday [12 November 2026]. The extension provides a further 10 working days to secure a buyer and avoid insolvency. The discount retailer, which has been grappling with financial difficulties and restructuring its UK store...
items.body:
Poundland has applied for a second notice of intention (NOI) to appoint administrators after its initial 10-working-day protection period expired on Thursday [12 November 2026].
The extension provides a further 10 working days to secure a buyer and avoid insolvency.
The discount retailer, which has been grappling with financial difficulties and restructuring its UK store estate, is seeking further support to protect its operations and safeguard jobs across its network.
Poundland’s board said funding had been agreed to allow the business to continue trading while negotiations progress. Stores will remain open as usual during the extended period.
The development follows mounting political pressure on owner Gordon Brothers, which acquired Poundland for £1 last year, over its handling of the retailer’s financial position.
Following a private meeting with Parliament’s Business and Trade Committee on Wednesday, its chair Liam Byrne accused Gordon Brothers of taking millions of pounds out of the business while it was financially vulnerable.
Gordon Brothers has denied prioritising its financial returns over the retailer’s future, saying it had provided £85m in new financing to support the business.
The investment firm confirmed it was in discussions with three potential buyers for the entire business, alongside receiving several offers from established high street retailers interested in acquiring significant parts of its estate.
Potential buyers include investment firm Xyra Holdings and Irish business Martin Property Group. Tesco has also reportedly explored acquiring up to 150 stores, while Iceland and Lidl are among retailers understood to have expressed interest in parts of the estate.
Around 600 UK stores and 11,000 jobs remain at risk if a rescue cannot be secured.
If negotiations fail, corporate advisory firm AlixPartners is understood to be lined up to oversee an administration process.
The additional breathing space gives Poundland another opportunity to secure a deal that preserves its store network and workforce, as well as maintaining continuity for suppliers ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period.

items.title: ‘Workers being left behind’ as government cracks down on retail crime, says policy group
items.summary: Westminster policy group, the Policy Liaison Group on Workplace Wellbeing says employers have an “absolute duty” to provide greater employee protection. It was a conclusion drawn from a Wembley Stadium roundtable during CX Vision Live 2035, which took place on Thursday 5 November. As Respect… This story continues at ‘Workers being left behind’ as government cracks down on retail crime, says policy group Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
It was a conclusion drawn from a Wembley Stadium roundtable during CX Vision Live 2035, which took place on Thursday 5 November.
As Respect Week highlights abuse towards retail workers, leading wellbeing experts called for a rethink on how to protect customer-facing employees.
Key insights included:
- Employees are often left to absorb workplace trauma without adequate recovery support.
- Employers must apply the same design discipline to psychological hazards as they do to physical safety.
- Customer-facing staff should actively co-design workplace policies, tools and training.
- Lower-paid workers are typically trapped between customer hostility at the counter and disciplinary action.
- The discussion took place on 5 November and brought together workplace wellbeing and customer experience leaders from the UK, the US and the Gulf.
According to the British Retail Consortium, retail workers experience approximately 1,600 incidents of violence and abuse every day, more than three times pre-pandemic levels. Despite retailers investing an estimated £5bn in security measures over five years, participants questioned whether enough is being done to protect employees (see roundtable summary for more insights).
The discussion identified three priorities for employers and policymakers:
- Invest in employees, not just security measures
While legislation and security measures help tackle retail crime, participants warned that they often overlook the employees dealing with the aftermath. Workers may be expected to return to work immediately following an abusive encounter, with little opportunity to recover.
Gethin Nadin, chair of the PLG, questioned this imbalance, arguing that “there’s an employee in the middle of this, and they’re not the person that’s being invested in.”
Participants called for greater post-incident care, financial support and staffing arrangements that allow employees time to recover.
- Design workplaces for psychological safety
Employers routinely assess physical hazards, but participants questioned whether psychological risks receive the same attention. The discussion highlighted three priorities: practical skills, appropriate tools and workplace design, including de-escalation training and employee involvement in shaping policies.
As Nadin asked, “If you were to prioritise psychological safety or mental health, how would you change the design of your organisation or the processes that you have in place?”
Employees should have a direct role in identifying risks and developing solutions.
- Stop leaving employees to bear the consequences of corporate decisions
Customer-facing workers often enforce pricing changes and restrictive policies they had no role in developing, leaving them exposed to customer frustration.
One participant described employees as “literally the representation of the decision”. Others highlighted the pressure to enforce policies despite personal safety concerns, describing it as “a choice between do I get fired or attacked?”
Participants called for senior leaders to spend more time in customer-facing roles and involve employees in decisions likely to provoke confrontation.
During the discussion, David Liddle, founder and CEO of The TCM Group, said: “I propose that retailers, trade associations, community safety partnerships, police forces, and restorative practitioners explore a new RISE (Retailers Investing in a Safer Environment) pilot.
“The ambition is clear: equip people to recognise risk, manage conflict safely, prevent harm where possible, and create communities in which everyone feels respected and protected. Safer shops can become a starting point for safer communities.”
Clemens Moehring, COO at Hastee, said: “When a retail worker experiences abuse, security deals with the incident and payroll deals with their pay. But who is looking at the connection between the two?
“Financial insecurity can make it harder for employees to report abuse, take time off to recover or even consider leaving an unsafe working environment. Financial wellbeing needs to be part of how employers prevent and respond to workplace violence.”
The PLG will share its findings with parliamentarians and policymakers, calling for closer collaboration between government, employers and trade unions to protect employees before, during and after incidents of abuse.
Joanne Thomas, general secretary of Usdaw, commented: “Nobody should be afraid to go to work, so it is of grave concern that Usdaw’s latest survey findings show that 12% of retail workers were assaulted last year, with around three-quarters being abused or threatened.
“The government is making a difference with investment in police, but they need to bring into force the protection of shop workers law passed by Parliament in April. Usdaw works closely with retailers to make shops safer.
“Usdaw’s volunteer health and safety reps are regularly risk assessing workplaces and discussing mitigations with managers. We encourage retail employers who don’t currently engage with Usdaw to work with us to help make their workplaces safer.”
The Retail Trust commented: “Our country’s shop workers have had enough of being shouted at, threatened, and treated with contempt.
“We’re hearing from people who are frightened to come into work because they don’t know what they’ll face that day, and from others who have been pushed to breaking point by repeated abuse.
“Retail is one of the few places where millions of strangers still interact face-to-face and there has been a disturbing shift over the last few years where behaviour that would once have been considered completely unacceptable is increasingly being seen as part of the job. This is damaging people’s confidence, destroying morale and driving good people out of a sector they once loved.
“Most people do the right thing, but when a minority don’t, the rest of us have a role to play in making sure shop workers still feel seen and valued.
“No one should face abuse at work and respect can start with something as simple as looking someone in the eye, showing a little patience or simply saying, ‘hello.’”

items.title: Matalan set to open four stores in time for Christmas
items.summary: As Matalan prepares for the peak rush, the fashion retailer is investing in its store network with four openings this November. The openings are in Aylesbury, Clacton-on-Sea, and Newport in Wales, as well as Bangor as part of its Northern Ireland investment. They form part of a wider programme of investment to modernise Matalan’s stores...
items.body:
As Matalan prepares for the peak rush, the fashion retailer is investing in its store network with four openings this November.
The openings are in Aylesbury, Clacton-on-Sea, and Newport in Wales, as well as Bangor as part of its Northern Ireland investment.
They form part of a wider programme of investment to modernise Matalan’s stores and bring its improved shopping experience to more customers.
James Dorling, property director at Matalan, commented: “Our stores play a huge role in how customers experience Matalan, so it’s essential that they reflect the improvements we’re making to our product and brand.
“That’s been the focus of our investment over the past two years – not just making stores look better, but making them easier to shop and better at showcasing what we have to offer. It’s about investing in the right locations, improving the shopping environments, and giving our customers even more reasons to choose Matalan.”
The new locations represent nearly 100,000 sq ft of new retail space and will employ around40 colleagues per store.
Additionally, the sites are designed to showcase the improvements being introduced across Matalan’s wider estate, including brighter interiors, simpler layouts and enhanced visual merchandising. The retailer has also worked to boost its fashion and homeware collections.
Matalan said its store investment has been delivering encouraging results, with the retailer’s Derby store, which opened earlier this year and introduced Matalan’s latest, more modern store format, becoming its most successful opening to date, reaching £1m in sales in just 51 days.
Dorling added: “The response to the changes we’ve made has been really positive, with Derby a particular highlight. The four openings this November mark another important milestone in our investment programme, and we’re delighted to be bringing the latest Matalan experience to more communities in time for Christmas.”

The openings are in Aylesbury, Clacton-on-Sea, and Newport in Wales, as well as Bangor as part of its Northern Ireland investment.
They form part of a wider programme of investment to modernise Matalan’s stores and bring its improved shopping experience to more customers.
James Dorling, property director at Matalan, commented: “Our stores play a huge role in how customers experience Matalan, so it’s essential that they reflect the improvements we’re making to our product and brand.
“That’s been the focus of our investment over the past two years – not just making stores look better, but making them easier to shop and better at showcasing what we have to offer. It’s about investing in the right locations, improving the shopping environments, and giving our customers even more reasons to choose Matalan.”
The new locations represent nearly 100,000 sq ft of new retail space and will employ around40 colleagues per store.
Additionally, the sites are designed to showcase the improvements being introduced across Matalan’s wider estate, including brighter interiors, simpler layouts and enhanced visual merchandising. The retailer has also worked to boost its fashion and homeware collections.
Matalan said its store investment has been delivering encouraging results, with the retailer’s Derby store, which opened earlier this year and introduced Matalan’s latest, more modern store format, becoming its most successful opening to date, reaching £1m in sales in just 51 days.
Dorling added: “The response to the changes we’ve made has been really positive, with Derby a particular highlight. The four openings this November mark another important milestone in our investment programme, and we’re delighted to be bringing the latest Matalan experience to more communities in time for Christmas.”

items.body:
Cornish Bakery has secured an eight-figure funding package from its new banking partner, HSBC UK, to support its next phase of growth and investment.
The funding will support expansion and investment in its people, bakeries and customer experience. The business is also spending more than £1.6m on refurbishments this winter, with its new Guildford bakery due to open on 25th November.
The backing follows five years of growth during which Cornish Bakery has doubled its number of bakeries, quadrupled profit and created jobs for 1,000 people. Cornish Bakery reports strong like-for-like sales growth over summer 2026, alongside six new bakery openings.
This year also saw the launch of RISE by Cornish Bakery, its larger-format concept. The first opened in Betws-y-Coed, followed by a two-storey, 3,500 sq. ft. bakery at Gunwharf Quays in Portsmouth, its largest location to date.
As Cornish Bakery continues to expand, protecting the individuality of its people and bakeries remains fundamental to its approach. Rather than pursuing the traditional cookie-cutter model of national expansion, the business is embracing what founder Grocutt describes as an ‘anti-brand strategy’, with each new bakery individually designed and curated to reflect the community it serves.
Mat Finch, managing director of Cornish Bakery, said: “Our next phase is about investing intelligently, finding brilliant locations and building bakeries that belong in their communities. We’re delighted to have HSBC UK’s support which will really help us to maximise our potential.”
Liam Gover, relationship director at HSBC UK, said: “Cornish Bakery has a clear sense of what makes its business distinctive and how it wants to grow. We’re pleased to support investment in its bakeries and new locations while helping it retain the individual character of each site.”
Cornish Bakery has 81 bakeries and a team of more than 1,000. For more information on the company and its bakeries, visit www.thecornishbakery.com.

Houston Hot Chicken (HHC), the cult favourite US chicken brand known for serious heat, queues round the block and openings that feel like a party, is bringing its fire to Watford for its third UK restaurant.
Watford, your chicken game is about to get a serious upgrade. Houston Hot Chicken (HHC) is landing in town with juicy buttermilk-marinated chicken, hand-breaded then dialled up to whatever heat you can handle. Think stacked hot chicken sandwiches, sensational tenders, loaded fries, house-made lemonades and irresistible shakes – you better come hungry.
After debuting in Stevenage in October and with Brunswick Centre next in line, HHC is moving fast to bring its bold American flavours to more UK neighbourhoods as part of the PizzaExpress House of Brands.
Watford’s chicken fans have a new name to add to the must-try list. HHC’s menu is all about the chicken. There are stacked hot chicken sandwiches dripping with sauce, hand-breaded tenders made for dunking, and loaded fries piled high. Add ice-cold house lemonades and thick slurpable shakes and you’ve got everything covered for a quick lunch or full-on feast with friends.
Every order starts with a choice of heat, from a gentle kick all the way up to the top of the scale. That’s where you’ll find “Houston, We Have A Problem” A scorching two million on the Scoville scale. It’s so hot it comes with paperwork… waiver signed, bragging rights secured. If you’re not chasing glory? Every level further down the scale still delivers the big, bold flavour with zero compromises.
Ben Lawrence, International Director at PizzaExpress, said: “Watford, get ready. Houston Hot Chicken is coming to town and we can’t wait for you to try it.
We’re moving quickly. After Stevenage and with Brunswick Centre coming up next, Watford is a big step in taking HHC’s bold flavours and energy to more people across the UK. The momentum is real and this is only the beginning.”
The brand isn’t messing around, and not only is it landing in Watford, for some, it’s coming straight to the door. From Monday 16 November, HHC is also launching its Crouch End delivery kitchen, which will bring the heat to North London through Deliveroo. Whether it’s a Friday night feast, a midweek pick-me-up or the centrepiece of your next mates’ night in, just pick your heat, place your order and let HHC handle dinner.
For those in Watford, the exact opening date and launch-day celebrations will be revealed soon. To be the first to hear follow @HHC_UKI on Instagram and TikTok.
Watford, we have lift-off. Countdown to the first bite starts now.
